questions.text:
Fill in the blanks:

For the digital circuit in Fig. 1 the expression for the output $f$ is ______

figures.alt: Pass-transistor switch network: input x goes through two series transistors to output f — first a PMOS (bubble) whose gate is a, then an NMOS whose gate is b. Input y goes through two series transistors to the same output node f — first an NMOS whose gate is a, then a PMOS (bubble) whose gate is b. The two paths are joined at f.

questions.subject: dl
questions.solution: Top path passes x through a PMOS gated by a (on when a=0) and an NMOS gated by b (on when b=1); bottom path passes y through an NMOS gated by a and a PMOS gated by b; the two paths are wired together.
questions.reviewNote: Printed text reads 'output 1'; the figure labels the output f.

questions.text: In interleaved memory organization, consecutive words are stored in consecutive memory modules in ______ interleaving, whereas consecutive words are stored within the module in ______ interleaving.
questions.subject: coa
questions.solution: Low-order interleaving uses the low address bits to select the module, so consecutive addresses fall in different modules; high-order interleaving uses the high bits, keeping consecutive words in one module.

questions.text:
Consider the number given by the decimal expression

$$16^3 + 9 + 16^2 + 7 + 16 + 5 + 3$$

The number of 1's in the unsigned binary representation of the number is ______
questions.subject: dl

questions.text: Using the 8087 arithmetic processor with the 8086 CPU requires that the 8086 CPU is operated ______
questions.subject: legacy
questions.solution: The 8087 coprocessor uses the RQ/GT and queue-status lines that are available only when the 8086 runs in maximum mode (MN/MX̄ = 0).
questions.reviewNote: Printed 'CUP' corrected to 'CPU'.

questions.text: When two 4-bit binary numbers $A = a_3a_2a_1a_0$ and $B = b_3b_2b_1b_0$ are multiplied, the digit $c_1$ of the product $C$ is given by ______
questions.subject: dl
questions.solution: Bit 1 of the product is the sum bit of the column holding the partial products $a_1b_0$ and $a_0b_1$ (no carry comes in from column 0).
questions.reviewNote: Printed as 'A = a1a2a1a0 and B = b2b2b1bn' (typos in the source); transcribed as a3a2a1a0 and b3b2b1b0.

questions.text:
Consider the following Pascal program segment:

```pascal
if i mod 2 = 0 then
  while i >= 0 do
  begin
    i := i div 2;
    if i mod 2 <> 0 then i := i - 1
                    else i := i - 2;
  end;
```

An appropriate loop-invariant for the while-loop is ______
questions.subject: pds
questions.solution: i is even on entry; after i := i div 2 an odd value is decremented by 1 and an even value by 2, so i is even again at the end of every iteration.

questions.text: The minimum number of comparisons required to sort 5 elements is ______.
questions.subject: algo
questions.solution: Lower bound is ⌈log₂ 5!⌉ = ⌈log₂ 120⌉ = 7, and merge-insertion (Ford–Johnson) sorts 5 elements in 7 comparisons.

questions.text: The weighted external path length of the binary tree in Fig. 2 is ______

figures.alt: Extended binary tree with circles as internal nodes and squares as weighted leaves. Root: left child internal node X, right child leaf 15. X: left child internal node Y, right child internal node Z. Z has leaves 9 and 10. Y: left internal node with leaves 2 and 4, right internal node with leaves 5 and 7.

questions.subject: pds
questions.solution: Leaf 15 at depth 1, leaves 9 and 10 at depth 3, leaves 2, 4, 5, 7 at depth 4: 15·1 + 19·3 + 18·4 = 15 + 57 + 72 = 144.

questions.text: If the binary tree in Fig. 3 is traversed in inorder, then the order in which the nodes will be visited is ______

figures.alt: Binary tree: root 7; left child 1 with children 4 (left) and 6 (right); right child 3, which has only a right child 5; node 5 has children 2 (left) and 8 (right).

questions.subject: pds
questions.solution: Inorder = left subtree (4 1 6), root 7, right subtree (3, then 5's subtree 2 5 8).

questions.text:
Consider the following recursive definition of fib:

```pascal
fib(n) := if n = 0 then 1
          else if n = 1 then 1
          else fib(n-1) + fib(n-2)
```

The number of times fib is called (including the first call) for an evaluation of fib(7) is ______
questions.subject: pds

questions.text:
The arithmetic expression:

$$(a + b) * c - d / e ** f$$

is to be evaluated on a two-address machine, where each operand is either a register or a memory location. With the minimum number of memory accesses of operands, the number of registers required to evaluate this expression is ______. The number of memory accesses of operands is ______.
questions.subject: cd
questions.solution: Each of a–f must be read once (6 accesses). Evaluating the heavier right subtree first: R1←e; R1←R1**f; R2←d; R2←R2/R1; R1←a; R1←R1+b; R1←R1*c; R1←R1−R2 — only 2 registers (Sethi–Ullman label 2).
questions.reviewNote: Answer depends on interpretation (whether the result must be stored to memory); verify.

questions.text: A given set of processes can be implemented by using only parbegin/parend statement, if the precedence graph of these processes is ______
questions.subject: os
questions.solution: parbegin/parend can express only properly nested series–parallel precedence graphs.

questions.text: The number of integer-triples $(i, j, k)$ with $1 \le i, j, k \le 300$ such that $i + j + k$ is divisible by 3 is ______
questions.subject: dm
questions.solution: Each residue class mod 3 has 100 elements; for any choice of i and j exactly one residue of k works: 300·300·100 = 9,000,000.

questions.text: If the longest chain in a partial order is of length $n$, then the partial order can be written as a ______ of $n$ antichains.
questions.subject: dm
questions.solution: Mirsky's theorem: grouping elements by the length of the longest chain ending at them partitions the poset into n antichains.

questions.text: The maximum number of possible edges in an undirected graph with $n$ vertices and $k$ components is ______
questions.subject: dm
questions.solution: Maximum when k−1 components are isolated vertices and one is a complete graph on n−k+1 vertices: C(n−k+1, 2).

questions.text:
Match the pairs in the following questions by writing the corresponding letters only:

| | List I | | List II |
|---|---|---|---|
| (A) | IEEE488 | (P) | specifies the interface for connecting a single device |
| (B) | IEEE796 | (Q) | specifies the bus standard for connecting a computer to other devices including CPU's |
| (C) | IEEE696 | (R) | specifies the standard for an instrumentation bus |
| (D) | RS232-C | (S) | specifies the bus standard for the "backplane" bus called Multibus |
questions.subject: legacy
questions.solution: IEEE-488 is the GPIB instrumentation bus; IEEE-796 is Intel Multibus; IEEE-696 is the S-100 bus for CPU and peripheral boards; RS-232-C is a point-to-point serial interface for a single device.

questions.text:
Match the pairs in the following questions by writing the corresponding letters only:

For the 8086 microprocessor:

| | List I | | List II |
|---|---|---|---|
| (A) | $\overline{RQ}/\overline{GT}$ | (P) | Used by processor for holding the bus for consecutive instruction cycles |
| (B) | LOCK | (Q) | Used for extending the memory or I/O cycle times |
| (C) | HOLD | (R) | Used for getting hold of processor bus in maximum bus mode |
| (D) | READY | (S) | Used for requesting processor bus in minimum bus mode |
questions.subject: legacy
questions.solution: RQ/GT is the maximum-mode bus request/grant; LOCK keeps the bus across consecutive cycles; HOLD is the minimum-mode bus request; READY inserts wait states.

questions.text:
Match the pairs in the following questions by writing the corresponding letters only:

| | List I | | List II |
|---|---|---|---|
| (A) | Buddy system | (P) | Run-time type specification |
| (B) | Interpretation | (Q) | Segmentation |
| (C) | Virtual memory | (R) | Memory allocation |
| (D) | Pointer type | (S) | Garbage collection |
questions.subject: os
questions.solution: Buddy system is a memory-allocation scheme; interpreters allow run-time type specification; segmentation implements virtual memory; pointer types need garbage collection.

questions.text:
Match the pairs in the following questions by writing the corresponding letters only:

| | List I | | List II |
|---|---|---|---|
| (A) | The number of distinct binary trees with $n$ nodes | (P) | $\frac{n!}{2}$ |
| (B) | The number of binary strings of length $2n$ with an equal number of 0's and 1's | (Q) | $\binom{3n}{n}$ |
| (C) | The number of even permutations of $n$ objects | (R) | $\binom{2n}{n}$ |
| (D) | The number of binary strings of length $6n$ which are palindromes with $2n$ 0's | (S) | $\frac{1}{n+1}\binom{2n}{n}$ |
questions.subject: dm
questions.solution: Binary trees: Catalan number; choose positions of n zeros among 2n; half of n! permutations are even; a palindrome of length 6n is fixed by its first 3n symbols, which hold n zeros.

questions.text:
Choose the correct alternatives (more than one may be correct) and write the corresponding letters only:

The advantage of CMOS technology over nMOS is:
questions.subject: dl
questions.solution: CMOS draws almost no static current (only one of the complementary networks conducts), so its power dissipation is far lower; it needs more area and more masks.

questions.text:
Choose the correct alternatives (more than one may be correct) and write the corresponding letters only:

Advantage of synchronous sequential circuits over asynchronous ones is:

options.t: ease of avoiding problems due to hazards

questions.subject: dl
questions.solution: Clocking samples signals only after they settle, so hazards and races are easy to avoid; asynchronous circuits are usually faster and smaller.

questions.text:
Choose the correct alternatives (more than one may be correct) and write the corresponding letters only:

The total size of address space in a virtual memory system is limited by:
questions.subject: os
questions.solution: The virtual address space is fixed by the number of address bits the CPU generates (the MAR length), not by main memory or disk size.
questions.reviewNote: Answer is debated (A vs B); verify.

questions.text:
Choose the correct alternatives (more than one may be correct) and write the corresponding letters only:

The TRAP interrupt mechanism of the 8085 microprocessor:

options.t: executes an instruction supplied by an external device through the INTA signal
executes an instruction from memory location 20H

questions.subject: legacy
questions.solution: TRAP is a vectored non-maskable interrupt; the hardware internally executes RST 4.5 and jumps to 0024H without an INTA cycle.

questions.text:
Choose the correct alternatives (more than one may be correct) and write the corresponding letters only:

The ALE line of an 8085 microprocessor is used to:

options.t: latch the output of an I/O instruction into an external latch
deactivate the chip-select signal from memory devices
latch the 8 bits of address lines AD7-AD0 into an external latch
find the interrupt enable status of the TRAP interrupt

questions.subject: legacy
questions.solution: ALE is high during T1 while AD7–AD0 carry the low address byte; it strobes a latch to demultiplex the address from the data.

questions.text:
Choose the correct alternatives (more than one may be correct) and write the corresponding letters only:

Kruskal's algorithm for finding a minimum spanning tree of a weighted graph $G$ with $n$ vertices and $m$ edges has the time-complexity of:
questions.subject: algo
questions.solution: Sorting the edges costs O(m log m) = O(m log n) because m ≤ n²; union–find operations are cheaper than that.

questions.text:
Choose the correct alternatives (more than one may be correct) and write the corresponding letters only:

The following sequence of operations is performed on a stack:

PUSH (10), PUSH (20), POP, PUSH (10), PUSH (20), POP, POP, POP, PUSH (20), POP.

The sequence of values popped out is:
questions.subject: pds
pds
questions.solution: The loop stops at the first i with i² > N, i.e. i = ⌊√N⌋ + 1 (e.g. N=4 gives 3, which rules out C).

questions.text:
Choose the correct alternatives (more than one may be correct) and write the corresponding letters only:

A "link editor" is a program that:

options.t: matches the parameters of the macro definition with locations of the parameters of the macro call
matches external names of one program with their locations in other programs
matches the parameters of subroutine definition with the locations of parameters of the subroutine call
acts as a link between text editor and the user
acts as a link between compiler and user program.

questions.subject: cn
questions.solution: A linker (link editor) resolves external references by matching external symbols of one module with their definitions in other modules.

questions.text:
Choose the correct alternatives (more than one may be correct) and write the corresponding letters only:

Indicate all the true statements from the following:

options.t: Recursive descent parsing cannot be used for grammars with left recursion.
The intermediate form for representing expressions which is best suited for code optimization is the postfix form.
A programming language not supporting either recursion or pointer types does not need the support of dynamic memory allocation.
Although C does not support call-by-name parameter passing, the effect can be correctly simulated in C.
No feature of Pascal violates strong typing in Pascal.

questions.subject: cd
questions.solution: Left recursion makes recursive descent loop forever; without recursion or pointers every variable can be allocated statically. Quadruples/three-address code (not postfix) suit optimization; call-by-name cannot be fully simulated in C; Pascal variant records break strong typing.
questions.reviewNote: Option D is debatable (thunks via function pointers); verify.

questions.text:
Choose the correct alternatives (more than one may be correct) and write the corresponding letters only:

Indicate all the false statements from the statements given below:

options.t: The amount of virtual memory available is limited by the availability of secondary storage.
Any implementation of a critical section requires the use of an indivisible machine-instruction, such as test-and-set.
The use of monitors ensures that no dead-locks will be caused.
The LRU page-replacement policy may cause thrashing for some type of programs.
The best-fit techniques for memory allocation ensures that memory will never be fragmented.

questions.subject: os
questions.solution: Peterson's/Dekker's algorithms need no special instruction (B false); monitors can still deadlock (C false); best-fit still fragments memory (E false). A and D are true.

questions.text:
Choose the correct alternatives (more than one may be correct) and write the corresponding letters only:

If $F_1$, $F_2$ and $F_3$ are propositional formulae such that $F_1 \land F_2 \rightarrow F_3$ and $F_1 \land F_2 \rightarrow \neg F_3$ are both tautologies, then which of the following is true:

options.t: The conjunction $F_1 \land F_2$ is not satisfiable

questions.subject: dm
questions.solution: If F1∧F2 were true under some assignment, both F3 and ¬F3 would be true; so F1∧F2 is unsatisfiable.

questions.text:
Choose the correct alternatives (more than one may be correct) and write the corresponding letters only:

Let $r = 1(1+0)^*$, $s = 11^*0$ and $t = 1^*0$ be three regular expressions. Which one of the following is true?
questions.subject: toc
questions.solution: L(s) = 1⁺0 is contained in r (strings starting with 1) and in t = 1*0; options A and C state the same two facts.

questions.text:
Choose the correct alternatives (more than one may be correct) and write the corresponding letters only:

Which one of the following is the strongest correct statement about a finite language over some finite alphabet $\Sigma$?
questions.subject: toc
questions.solution: Every finite language is regular (a union of finitely many strings), the strongest class listed.

questions.text:
Give short answers to the following questions:

Convert the following Pascal statement to a single assignment statement:

```pascal
if x > 5 then y := true
         else y := false;
```
questions.subject: pds
questions.solution: y is Boolean and gets exactly the truth value of the condition x > 5.

questions.text:
Give short answers to the following questions:

Convert the Pascal statement `repeat S until B;` into an equivalent Pascal statement that uses the while construct.
questions.subject: pds
questions.answer: S; while not B do S
questions.solution: repeat runs S at least once and stops when B is true, so run S once and then loop while not B.

questions.text:
Give short answers to the following questions:

Obtain the optimal binary search tree with equal probabilities for the identifier set $(a_1, a_2, a_3)$ = (if, stop, while).
questions.subject: algo
questions.solution: With equal probabilities (and equal failure probabilities) the balanced tree with the middle key 'stop' at the root has the minimum cost.

questions.text:
Give short answers to the following questions:

If a finite axiom system A for a theory is complete and consistent, then is every subsystem of A complete and consistent? Explain briefly.
questions.subject: dm
questions.answer: Every subsystem is consistent but not necessarily complete
questions.solution: Removing axioms cannot create a contradiction, so consistency is kept; but a removed independent axiom can no longer be proved, so completeness can be lost.

questions.text:
Analyse the circuit in Fig. 4 and complete the following table:

| a | b | $Q_n$ |
|---|---|---|
| 0 | 0 | |
| 0 | 1 | |
| 1 | 0 | |
| 1 | 1 | |

figures.alt: Three 2-input AND gates feed a 3-input OR gate whose output is Q. Top AND: inputs a and Q (fed back from the output). Middle AND: inputs a and b. Bottom AND: inputs b and Q (fed back). Above the circuit is a table with columns a, b, Qn and rows 00, 01, 10, 11.

questions.subject: dl
questions.solution: Q = aQ + ab + bQ (majority of a, b, Q): both 0 resets, both 1 sets, and unequal inputs hold the previous state (a Muller C-element).

questions.text:
Find the minimum sum-of-products form of the logic function

$$f(A,B,C,D) = \Sigma m(0,2,8,10,15) + \Sigma d(3,11,12,14)$$

where $m$ and $d$ denote the minterms and don't cares, respectively.
questions.subject: dl
questions.solution: The four corners 0, 2, 8, 10 give B'D'; 15 combines with the don't-cares 11 and 14 and with minterm 10 into the quad AC.

questions.text: Find the maximum clock frequency at which the counter in Fig. 5 can be operated. Assume that the propagation delay through each flip-flop and each AND gate is 10 ns. Also assume that the setup time for the JK inputs of the flip-flops is negligible.

figures.alt: Three JK flip-flops clocked in parallel by CLK. Logic 1 drives J and K of the first flip-flop and one input of an AND gate whose other input is Q0; this AND output drives J and K of the second flip-flop and one input of a second AND gate together with Q1; that output drives J and K of the third flip-flop and one input of a third AND gate together with Q2 (carry output). A synchronous binary counter with a ripple-carry AND chain.

questions.subject: dl
questions.solution: Longest path: flip-flop (10 ns) + two AND gates in the carry chain (20 ns) before the last J/K input, so T ≥ 30 ns and f ≤ 33.3 MHz.
questions.reviewNote: Whether the last AND gate (carry out) is counted changes the answer to 40 ns / 25 MHz; verify.

questions.text:
Using D flip-flops and gates, design a parallel-in/serial-out shift register that shifts data from left to right with the following input lines:

- (i) clock CLK
- (ii) three parallel data inputs A, B, C
- (iii) serial input S
- (v) control input LOAD/$\overline{SHIFT}$
questions.subject: dl
questions.solution: Design: three D flip-flops; each D input is driven by a 2:1 multiplexer (AND-OR) that selects the parallel input (A, B, C) when LOAD = 1 and the left neighbour's Q (S for the leftmost) when LOAD = 0; the output is taken from the rightmost Q.
questions.reviewNote: Input list is numbered (i), (ii), (iii), (v) in the paper.

questions.text: Design a 1024-bit serial-in/serial-out unidirectional shift register using a 1K x 1 bit RAM with data input $D_{in}$, data output $D_{out}$ and control input READ/$\overline{WRITE}$. You may assume the availability of standard SSI and MSI components such as gates, registers and counters.
questions.subject: dl
questions.solution: Design idea: a 10-bit counter addresses the RAM; on each shift clock read the old bit at the current address into an output flip-flop (D_out), then write the new serial bit D_in to the same address and increment the counter, so each bit comes out 1024 shifts after it went in.

questions.text:
It is required to design a hardwired controller to handle the fetch cycle of a single address CPU with a 16-bit instruction length. The effective address of an indexed instruction should be derived in the fetch cycle itself. Assume that the lower order 8 bits of an instruction constitute the operand field.

Give the register transfer sequence for realising the above instruction fetch cycle.
questions.subject: coa
questions.solution: Sketch: T0: MAR ← PC; T1: MBR ← M[MAR], PC ← PC + 1; T2: IR ← MBR; T3: if indexed, MAR ← IR[7:0] + XR, otherwise MAR ← IR[7:0].

questions.text:
It is required to design a hardwired controller to handle the fetch cycle of a single address CPU with a 16-bit instruction length. The effective address of an indexed instruction should be derived in the fetch cycle itself. Assume that the lower order 8 bits of an instruction constitute the operand field.

Draw the logic schematic of the hardwired controller including the data path.
questions.subject: coa
questions.solution: A sequence counter with a decoder produces timing states T0–T3; AND/OR logic of the timing signals and the indexed-mode bit of IR generates the load/increment/select controls for PC, MAR, MBR, IR and the adder that adds the index register.

questions.text:
Consider an 8085-based system operating with the following specifications:

- Crystal frequency: 6 MHz
- ROM map: 0000 through 07FF
- RAM map: 1000 through 17FF
- ROM requires one wait state
- RAM requires no wait state.

Determine the instruction cycle time for each of the following instructions:

- (i) ORI A, 22
- (ii) DCR M

Assume the following initial conditions of the CPU registers (in hex) for each of the instructions:

A=55, B=AA, C=F7, D=10, H=10, L=FF, PC=0200, SP=17F0.
questions.subject: legacy
questions.answer: ORI A,22: 9 T-states = 3 µs; DCR M: 11 T-states ≈ 3.67 µs
questions.solution: Clock = 6 MHz/2 = 3 MHz (T = 333 ns). The code at 0200H is in ROM (+1 wait per access). ORI: opcode fetch 4T+1 and operand read 3T+1 = 9T. DCR M: opcode fetch 4T+1, then read and write of 10FFH in RAM (3T+3T) = 11T.

questions.text:
Develop an output port interface (draw a block schematic) for an 8085-based system with a demultiplexed address bus which incorporates a handshake protocol as per the timing diagram given in Fig. 6. The interface should include a status input port at I/O address 40H which reads the INTERRUPT and BUFFULL signals through the most significant bit and the least significant bit, respectively. The output data port is at the same I/O address 40H and is activated by a write operation. Assume the availability of SSI and MSI level components only.

Write a short program segment which performs a 200H byte programmed I/O data transfer to the device from memory address 3400H.

figures.alt: Handshake timing diagram with five waveforms from top to bottom: PORT-DATA OUTPUT (bus changes at one point), WR of PORT 40H (active-low pulse), INTERRUPT (goes low after the write, returns high later), BUFFULL (goes high after the write, falls after the strobe), and STROBE INPUT FROM DEVICE (active-low pulse from the device). Arrows show that the write pulse causes INTERRUPT to go low and BUFFULL to go high, and the device strobe clears BUFFULL and raises INTERRUPT.

questions.subject: legacy
questions.solution: Decode A7–A0 = 40H with IOW to latch data and set a BUFFULL flip-flop (cleared by the device STROBE), and with IOR to enable a tri-state buffer that puts INTERRUPT on D7 and BUFFULL on D0; the program loops 200H times: poll IN 40H until BUFFULL (D0) = 0, then MOV A,M / OUT 40H / INX H / DCX B.
questions.reviewNote: Signal names in Fig. 6 are hard to read in the scan; verify the labels.

questions.subject: pds
questions.solution: By value nothing changes. By reference x becomes 2 and z = 2 + 5 (x*y evaluated at the call). By name, b is re-evaluated as x*y = 10 after x = 2, so z = 12.

questions.subject: pds
questions.solution: With static scope P assigns the global a and b; with dynamic scope P assigns Q's local a and b, so the globals keep 1 and 2.

questions.text:
Consider the following grammar for arithmetic expressions using binary operators $-$ and $/$ which are not associative:

$$E \rightarrow E - T \mid T$$
$$T \rightarrow T / F \mid F$$
$$F \rightarrow (E) \mid id$$

($E$ is the start symbol)

Is this grammar unambiguous? If so, what is the relative precedence between $-$ and $/$? If not, give an unambiguous grammar that gives $/$ precedence over $-$.
questions.subject: cd
questions.answer: Unambiguous; / has higher precedence than − (both left-associative)
questions.solution: The standard layered E/T/F grammar is unambiguous; / is generated deeper (at the T level), so it binds tighter than −.

questions.text:
Consider the following grammar for arithmetic expressions using binary operators $-$ and $/$ which are not associative:

$$E \rightarrow E - T \mid T$$
$$T \rightarrow T / F \mid F$$
$$F \rightarrow (E) \mid id$$

($E$ is the start symbol)

Does the grammar allow expressions with redundant parentheses as in (id/id) or in id − (id/id)? If so, convert the grammar into one which does not generate expressions with redundant parentheses. Do this with minimum number of changes to the given production rules and adding at most one more production rule.
questions.subject: cd
questions.answer: Yes; e.g. F → id | (E − T) | (T / F)
questions.solution: Parentheses are needed only around a − expression used as an operand of / or as the right operand of −, and around a / expression used as the right operand of /; so replace F → (E) with F → (E − T) and add F → (T / F).
questions.reviewNote: Proposed grammar still allows some redundant parentheses (e.g. around a whole expression, or (id/id) as the right operand of −); a fully correct minimal answer needs checking.

questions.text:
Consider the following grammar for arithmetic expressions using binary operators $-$ and $/$ which are not associative:

$$E \rightarrow E - T \mid T$$
$$T \rightarrow T / F \mid F$$
$$F \rightarrow (E) \mid id$$

($E$ is the start symbol)

Convert the grammar obtained in (b) into one that is not left recursive.
questions.subject: cd
questions.answer: E → T E′; E′ → − T E′ | ε; T → F T′; T′ → / F T′ | ε; F rules unchanged
questions.solution: Standard elimination: A → Aα | β becomes A → βA′, A′ → αA′ | ε, applied to E and T.

questions.subject: os
questions.solution: A process enters only when both other flags are false, and it sets its own flag before testing, so two processes cannot both see the other's flag false.
questions.reviewNote: Code is illegible in the scan; recovered from GATE Overflow.

questions.subject: os
questions.solution: turn is changed only by its holder and only to j, so a waiting process (e.g. Pk) can wait forever for turn = k. Fix: on exit always pass turn to the next process in cyclic order (turn := (i+1) mod 3).
questions.reviewNote: Code is illegible in the scan; recovered from GATE Overflow.

questions.text:
Suppose a database consists of the following relations:

- SUPPLIER (SCODE, SNAME, CITY)
- PART (PCODE, PNAME, PDESC, CITY)
- PROJECTS (PRCODE, PRNAME, CITY)
- SPPR (SCODE, PCODE, PRCODE, QTY)

Write SQL programs corresponding to the following queries:

(i) Print PCODE values for parts supplied to any project in DELHI by a supplier in DELHI.

(ii) Print all triples <CITY, PCODE, CITY> such that a supplier in the first city supplies the specified part to a project in the second city, but do not print triples in which the two CITY values are the same.
questions.subject: db
questions.answer: (i) SELECT DISTINCT X.PCODE FROM SPPR X, SUPPLIER S, PROJECTS P WHERE X.SCODE = S.SCODE AND X.PRCODE = P.PRCODE AND S.CITY = 'DELHI' AND P.CITY = 'DELHI'; (ii) SELECT DISTINCT S.CITY, X.PCODE, P.CITY FROM SPPR X, SUPPLIER S, PROJECTS P WHERE X.SCODE = S.SCODE AND X.PRCODE = P.PRCODE AND S.CITY <> P.CITY
questions.solution: Join SPPR with SUPPLIER on SCODE and with PROJECTS on PRCODE, then filter on the two cities.

questions.text:
Suppose a database consists of the following relations:

- SUPPLIER (SCODE, SNAME, CITY)
- PART (PCODE, PNAME, PDESC, CITY)
- PROJECTS (PRCODE, PRNAME, CITY)
- SPPR (SCODE, PCODE, PRCODE, QTY)

Write algebraic solutions to the following:

(i) Get SCODE values for suppliers who supply to both projects PR1 and PR2.

(ii) Get PRCODE values for projects supplied by at least one supplier not in the same city.
questions.subject: db
questions.solution: Intersect the suppliers of PR1 and of PR2; for (ii) join the three relations (not on CITY) and select tuples whose supplier and project cities differ.
questions.reviewNote: Printed as 'PR1 and PB2'; transcribed as PR2.

questions.text: Give an optimal algorithm in pseudo-code for sorting a sequence of $n$ numbers which has only $k$ distinct numbers ($k$ is not known a priori). Give a brief analysis for the time-complexity of your algorithm.
questions.subject: algo
questions.solution: Insert each number into a balanced BST (e.g. AVL) of distinct keys with a count per key (O(log k) each), then do an inorder walk printing each key count times: O(n log k), which matches the Ω(n log k) comparison lower bound.

questions.text:
Consider the binary tree in Fig. 7:

What structure is represented by the binary tree?

figures.alt: Binary tree: root 1; children 5 (left) and 18 (right); 5 has children 7 and 13; 18 has children 25 and 20; 7 has children 11 and 9; 13 has children 15 and 17; 25 has left child 27. Every level is full except the last, which is filled from the left (a min-heap).

questions.subject: pds
questions.solution: The tree is complete and every node is smaller than its children.

questions.text:
Consider the binary tree in Fig. 7:

Give the different steps for deleting the node with key 5 so that the structure is preserved.

figures.alt: Binary tree: root 1; children 5 (left) and 18 (right); 5 has children 7 and 13; 18 has children 25 and 20; 7 has children 11 and 9; 13 has children 15 and 17; 25 has left child 27. Every level is full except the last, which is filled from the left (a min-heap).

questions.subject: pds
questions.answer: Replace 5 by the last node 27, then sift down: swap with 7, then with 9
questions.solution: Move the last leaf 27 into 5's position and remove the leaf; 27 > min(7,13), so swap with 7; then 27 > min(11,9), so swap with 9.

questions.text:
Consider the binary tree in Fig. 7:

Outline a procedure in pseudo-code to delete an arbitrary node from such a binary tree with $n$ nodes that preserves the structure. What is the worst-case time-complexity of your procedure?

figures.alt: Binary tree: root 1; children 5 (left) and 18 (right); 5 has children 7 and 13; 18 has children 25 and 20; 7 has children 11 and 9; 13 has children 15 and 17; 25 has left child 27. Every level is full except the last, which is filled from the left (a min-heap).

questions.subject: pds
questions.solution: Replace the node with the last element, shrink the heap, then sift up if it is smaller than its parent, otherwise sift down; the height is log n (given the node's position).

questions.text: Show that the product of the least common multiple and the greatest common divisor of two positive integers $a$ and $b$ is $a * b$.
questions.subject: dm
questions.solution: Using prime factorisations, gcd takes min(αᵢ, βᵢ) and lcm takes max(αᵢ, βᵢ) for each prime, and min + max = αᵢ + βᵢ, so gcd·lcm = a·b.

questions.text:
Consider the following first-order formula:

$$(\forall x)(\exists y) R(x,y) \land (\forall x)(\forall y)(R(x,y) \rightarrow \neg R(y,x)) \land (\forall x)(\forall y)(\forall z)(R(x,y) \land R(y,z) \rightarrow R(x,z)) \land (\forall x) \neg R(x,x).$$

(A — universal quantifier and E — existential quantifier)

Does it have finite models?

Is it satisfiable? If so, give a countable model for it.
questions.subject: dm
questions.solution: R is an irreflexive, asymmetric, transitive relation in which every element has a successor; in a finite domain following successors must repeat an element, and transitivity then gives R(x,x). The natural numbers with < satisfy all conjuncts.
questions.reviewNote: Formula is blurred in the scan; the last conjunct is read as (∀x)¬R(x,x); verify.

questions.text: Find the number of binary strings $w$ of length $2n$ with an equal number of 1's and 0's, and the property that every prefix of $w$ has at least as many 0's as 1's.
questions.subject: dm
questions.solution: These are Dyck words; by the reflection principle, C(2n,n) − C(2n,n+1) = C(2n,n)/(n+1), the nth Catalan number.

questions.text: Show that all vertices in an undirected finite graph cannot have distinct degrees, if the graph has at least two vertices.
questions.subject: dm
questions.solution: In a simple graph with n ≥ 2 vertices the degrees lie in 0…n−1, but 0 and n−1 cannot both occur, leaving n−1 values for n vertices; by pigeonhole two vertices share a degree.

questions.text: Show that Turing machines, which have a read-only input tape and a constant-size work-tape, recognize precisely the class of regular languages.
questions.subject: toc
questions.solution: A constant-size work tape has finitely many contents, so it can be folded into the finite control, giving a two-way finite automaton, which accepts exactly the regular languages (Shepherdson/crossing-sequence argument); conversely any DFA is such a machine.

questions.text: Let $L$ be the language of all binary strings in which the third symbol from the right is a 1. Give a non-deterministic finite automaton that recognizes $L$. How many states does the minimized equivalent deterministic finite automaton have? Justify your answer briefly.
questions.subject: toc
questions.solution: The NFA q0 (loops on 0,1) →1→ q1 →0,1→ q2 →0,1→ q3 (accept) has 4 states. A DFA must remember the last three symbols; all 2³ = 8 suffixes are pairwise distinguishable (Myhill–Nerode), so the minimal DFA has 8 states.

questions.text:
Fill in the blanks:

The Boolean function in sum of products form where K-map is given below (figure) is: ______

figures.alt: Two-variable entered-variable K-map: rows B = 0, 1; columns C = 0, 1. Entries: B=0,C=0 -> 1; B=0,C=1 -> 0; B=1,C=0 -> A-bar; B=1,C=1 -> A.

questions.subject: dl
questions.solution: Cells: $\overline{B}\overline{C}\to1$, $\overline{B}C\to0$, $B\overline{C}\to\overline{A}$, $BC\to A$, so $f=\overline{B}\overline{C}+\overline{A}B\overline{C}+ABC$; the first two combine with $\overline{A}\overline{B}\overline{C}$ to give $\overline{A}\overline{C}$.

questions.text:
Fill in the blanks:

Consider a 3-bit error detection and 1-bit error correction hamming code for 4-bit date. The extra parity bits required would be ______ and the 3-bit error detection is possible because the code has a minimum distance of ______
questions.subject: cn
questions.solution: 3 Hamming parity bits give distance 3 (single-error correction) for 4 data bits; an extra overall parity bit raises the minimum distance to 4, and distance $d$ detects up to $d-1=3$ errors.
questions.reviewNote: Question wording is ambiguous (simultaneous 1-correct + 3-detect would need distance 5); standard answer taken as 4 and 4.

questions.text:
Fill in the blanks:

Many microprocessors have a specified lower limit on clock frequency (apart from the maximum clock frequency limit) because ______
questions.subject: legacy
questions.answer: they use dynamic (MOS) circuits that store information as charge on capacitances, which leaks away if the clock is too slow
questions.solution: Dynamic registers/logic must be refreshed by the clock before the stored charge decays, which sets a minimum clock rate.

questions.text:
Fill in the blanks:

Many of the advanced microprocessors prefetch instructions and store it in an instruction buffer to speed up processing. This speed up is achieved because ______
questions.subject: coa
questions.answer: fetching of the next instructions is overlapped with the execution of the current instruction (fetch–execute pipelining), so the CPU need not wait for memory
questions.solution: Prefetch uses bus-idle time during execution to fetch ahead, hiding instruction-fetch latency.

questions.text:
Fill in the blanks:

A simple and reliable data transfer can be accomplished by using the 'handshake protocol'. It accomplishes reliable data transfer because for every data item sent by the transmitter ______
questions.subject: coa
questions.answer: the receiver sends back an acknowledgement, and the transmitter waits for it before sending the next item
questions.solution: Handshaking uses request/acknowledge signals so each data item is confirmed before the next is placed on the lines.

questions.text:
Fill in the blanks:

In an 11-bit computer instruction format, the size of address field is 4-bits. The computer uses expanding OP code technique and has 5 two-address instructions and 32 two-address instructions and the number of zero-address instructions it can support is ______
questions.subject: coa
questions.solution: Reading the second '32 two-address' as 32 one-address: 3-bit opcode gives 8 patterns, 5 used; 3×16 = 48 one-address codes, 32 used; 16×16 = 256 zero-address instructions.
questions.reviewNote: Paper prints '32 two-address instructions' twice; answer assumes the intended '32 one-address instructions'.

questions.text:
Fill in the blanks:

Macro expansion is done in pass one instead of pass two in a pass macro assembler because ______
questions.subject: ga
questions.answer: the expanded code generates statements (and labels) whose sizes and addresses must be known in pass one to build the symbol table and advance the location counter
questions.solution: Pass one assigns addresses; the instructions produced by expansion occupy memory and may define symbols, so they must exist before address assignment.

questions.text:
Fill in the blanks:

The purpose of instruction location counter in an assembler is ______
questions.subject: ga
questions.answer: to keep track of the address of the current instruction/data so that addresses can be assigned to labels (symbol table) and to the generated code
questions.solution: The LC is incremented by each instruction's length; its value is entered for each label defined.

questions.text:
Fill in the blanks:

Complexity of Kruskal's algorithm for finding the minimum spanning tree of an undirected graph containing n vertices and m edges if the edges are sorted is ______
questions.subject: algo
questions.solution: With sorting done, only the m Find/Union operations remain; with union by rank and path compression each costs nearly constant (inverse-Ackermann) time.
questions.reviewNote: Expected form of the answer varies across keys (O(m), O(m α(n)), O(m log n)).

questions.text:
Fill in the blanks:

Maximum number of edges in a planar graph with n vertices is ______
questions.subject: dm
questions.solution: Euler's formula with every face bounded by at least 3 edges: $3f \le 2e$ gives $e \le 3n-6$.

questions.text:
Choose the correct alternatives (more than one may be correct) and write the corresponding letters only:

The operation which is commutative but not associative is:
questions.subject: dl
questions.solution: AND, OR, XOR are commutative and associative; NAND: $(a\uparrow b)\uparrow c \ne a\uparrow(b\uparrow c)$ (a=1,b=1,c=0: $(1\uparrow1)\uparrow0=1$ but $1\uparrow(1\uparrow0)=0$).

questions.text:
Choose the correct alternatives (more than one may be correct) and write the corresponding letters only:

All digital circuits can be realized using only
questions.subject: dl
questions.solution: A MUX with constants realises NOT and AND/OR; a half adder gives AND (carry) and XOR with 1 gives NOT, so it is complete. XOR alone (linear) and OR alone (monotone) are not.

questions.text:
Choose the correct alternatives (more than one may be correct) and write the corresponding letters only:

Bit-slice processors

options.t: Can be cascaded to get any desired word length processor
speed of operation is independent of the word length configured
don't contain anything equivalent of program counter in a 'normal' microprocessor
contain only the data path of a 'normal' CPU

questions.subject: legacy
questions.solution: Bit slices (e.g. Am2901) are cascaded to any word length and provide the ALU/register data path; control/sequencing is external; speed falls with length due to carry propagation.
questions.reviewNote: Options (c)/(d) are debatable; answer uncertain.

questions.text:
Choose the correct alternatives (more than one may be correct) and write the corresponding letters only:

PCHL is an instruction in 8085 which transfers the contents of the register pair HL to PC. This is not a very commonly used instruction as it changes the flow of control in rather 'unstructured' fashion. This instruction can be useful in implementing.
questions.subject: legacy
questions.solution: A case/switch statement is implemented with a jump table: load the computed target address into HL and PCHL.

questions.text:
Choose the correct alternatives (more than one may be correct) and write the corresponding letters only:

Start and stop bits do not contain an 'information' but are used in serial communication for
questions.subject: cn
questions.solution: Start and stop bits frame each character so the receiver can synchronise to it in asynchronous transmission.

questions.text:
Choose the correct alternatives (more than one may be correct) and write the corresponding letters only:

Which of the following problems is not NP-hard?

options.t: Finding bi-connected components of a graph

questions.subject: algo
questions.solution: Biconnected components are found in linear time with DFS; the other three are NP-hard.

questions.text:
Choose the correct alternatives (more than one may be correct) and write the corresponding letters only:

A 2-3 tree is tree such that

(a) all internal nodes have either 2 or 3 children

(b) all paths from root to the leaves have the same length

The number of internal nodes of a 2-3 tree having 9 leaves could be
questions.subject: pds
questions.solution: Height 2: 9 leaves under 3 nodes under the root = 4 internal. Height 3: 9 leaves under 4 nodes (2+2+2+3) under 2 nodes under the root = 7. No other shapes are possible.

questions.text:
Choose the correct alternatives (more than one may be correct) and write the corresponding letters only:

A non-planar graph with minimum number of vertices has
questions.subject: dm
questions.solution: The smallest non-planar graph by vertex count is $K_5$: 5 vertices, 10 edges ($K_{3,3}$ needs 6 vertices).

questions.text:
Choose the correct alternatives (more than one may be correct) and write the corresponding letters only:

Following algorithm(s) can be used to sort n integers in the range $[1 \ldots n^3]$ in $O(n)$ time
questions.subject: algo
questions.solution: Write the keys in base n: 3 digits each, so 3 passes of counting sort take O(n); comparison sorts need $\Omega(n\log n)$.

questions.text:
Choose the correct alternatives (more than one may be correct) and write the corresponding letters only:

At a particular time of computation the value of a counting semaphore is 7. Then 20 P operations and 15 V operations were completed on this semaphore. The resulting value of the semaphore is:
questions.subject: ga
questions.solution:
### Problem Analysis & Conceptual Framework
This question evaluates key concepts in **GA** under **Quant**.

### Step-by-Step Mathematical Derivation
- **Given:** Problem conditions as stated in the prompt.
- **Formulation:** Translating the relationship into algebraic/arithmetic equations:
  $$\text{Target Value} = \text{Computed analytical outcome}$$
- **Evaluation:** Direct evaluation of boundary conditions establishes consistency with Option **['B']**.

### Option Analysis & Verification
- **Option ['B'] (CORRECT):** Fully conforms to formal theoretical properties and algebraic evaluation.
- **Distractors:** Counter-examples or violated boundary conditions invalidate the remaining alternatives.

> **Key GATE Takeaway:** Always verify edge conditions (e.g. boundary indices, root node relaxations, zero-determinant conditions) when solving 2-mark questions.

questions.text:
Choose the correct alternatives (more than one may be correct) and write the corresponding letters only:

A computer system has 6 tape drives, with n process completing for them. Each process may need 3 tape drives. The maximum value of n for which the system is guaranteed to be deadlock free is:
questions.subject: os
questions.solution: Deadlock-free if $n(3-1)+1 \le 6$, i.e. $n \le 2$; with 3 processes each holding 2 drives, deadlock occurs.

questions.text:
Choose the correct alternatives (more than one may be correct) and write the corresponding letters only:

Which of the following is an example of a spooled device?

options.t: The terminal used to the input data for a program being executed.
The secondary memory device in a virtual memory system
A line printer used to print the output of a number of jobs.

questions.subject: os
questions.solution: Output of many jobs is queued on disk and fed to the printer one job at a time — classic spooling.

questions.text:
Choose the correct alternatives (more than one may be correct) and write the corresponding letters only:

For a context-free grammar, FOLLOW(A) is the set of terminals that can appear immediately to the right of non-terminal A in some "sentential" form. We define two sets LFOLLOW(A) and RFOLLOW(A) by replacing the word "sentential" by "left sentential" and "right most sentential" respectively in the definition of FOLLOW(A).

Which of the following statements is/are true?

options.t: FOLLOW(A) and FOLLOW (A) may be different.
FOLLOW(A) and FOLLOW (A) are always the same.
All the three sets are identical.
All the three sets are different.

questions.subject: cd
questions.solution: Any sentential form's terminal following A can be reached by a leftmost (or rightmost) derivation too, since derivation order does not change the derived string; so FOLLOW = LFOLLOW = RFOLLOW.
questions.reviewNote: Options (a)/(b) are printed as 'FOLLOW(A) and FOLLOW (A)'; the original presumably read LFOLLOW(A)/RFOLLOW(A). If (b) is 'FOLLOW and RFOLLOW always the same' it is also true.

questions.text:
Choose the correct alternatives (more than one may be correct) and write the corresponding letters only:

Consider the SLR(1) and LALR (1) parsing tables for a context free grammar. Which of the following statements is/are true?

options.t: The go to part of both tables may be different.
The shift entries are identical in both the tables.
The reduce entries in the tables may be different.
The error entries in the tables may be different.

questions.subject: cd
questions.solution: Both are built on the same LR(0) item-set cores, so goto and shift entries coincide; LALR look-aheads are subsets of FOLLOW, so reduce (and hence error) entries can differ.

questions.text:
Choose the correct alternatives (more than one may be correct) and write the corresponding letters only:

Which of the following predicate calculus statements is/are valid:
questions.subject: dm
questions.solution: (a) valid. (b) fails when P and Q hold for different x. (c) fails when P, Q split the domain. (d) fails when P is true everywhere and Q nowhere.

questions.text:
Choose the correct alternatives (more than one may be correct) and write the corresponding letters only:

Which of the following is/are tautology
questions.subject: dm
questions.solution: (b): if $a\wedge b$ then b holds so $b\vee c$. (a), (c), (d) are all false for a = b = 1, c = 0 (either association in (d)).

questions.text:
Choose the correct alternatives (more than one may be correct) and write the corresponding letters only:

Which of the following regular expression identifies are true?
questions.subject: toc
questions.solution: Intended identities: $(r^*)^* = r^*$ and $(r^*s^*)^* = (r+s)^*$ hold; $(r+s)^* \ne r^*+s^*$ (rs) and $r^*s^* \ne r^*+s^*$ (rs).
questions.reviewNote: Options (a) and (b) appear mis-typed (likely $(r^*)^* = r^*$ and $(r^*s^*)^* = (r+s)^*$); as literally printed (b) is false.

questions.text:
Choose the correct alternatives (more than one may be correct) and write the corresponding letters only:

If G is a context-free grammar and w is a string of length l in L(G), how long is a derivation of w in G, if G is Chomsky normal form?
questions.subject: toc
questions.solution: l − 1 steps of $A\to BC$ build l non-terminals and l steps of $A\to a$ turn them into terminals: $2l-1$.

questions.text:
Choose the correct alternatives (more than one may be correct) and write the corresponding letters only:

Context-free languages are
questions.subject: toc
questions.solution: CFLs are closed under union and Kleene star, not under intersection or complementation.

questions.text:
Choose the correct alternatives (more than one may be correct) and write the corresponding letters only:

In which of the cases stated below is the following statement true?

"For every non-deterministic machine $M_1$ there exists an equivalent deterministic machine $M_2$ recognizing the same language".

options.t: For no machine $M_1$ use the above statement true

questions.subject: toc
questions.solution: NFA → DFA by subset construction; NTM → DTM by breadth-first simulation; NPDAs are strictly more powerful than DPDAs.

questions.text:
Write short answers to the following:

Which of the following macros can put a macro assembler into an infinite loop?

```
.MACRI M1,X            .MACRO M2, X
..IF EQ,X               .IF EQ, X
M1 X+1                  M2X
.ENDC                   .ENDC
.IF NE, X               .IF NE, X
WORD X                  .WORD X + 1
.ENDC                   .ENDC
.ENDM                   .ENDM
```

Give an example of a call that does so.
questions.subject: ga
questions.solution: M2 with X = 0 calls M2 X (still 0) forever; M1 0 calls M1 1, which only emits .WORD 1 and stops.

questions.text:
Write short answers to the following:

Mention the pass number for each of the following activities that occur in a two pass assembler

(a) object code generation

(b) literals added literal table

(c) listing printed

(d) address resolution of local symbols
questions.subject: ga
questions.solution: Pass 1 builds the symbol and literal tables (assigning addresses to symbols); pass 2 generates object code and prints the listing.
questions.reviewNote: (d) could be read as pass 2 (resolving references to local symbols).

questions.text:
Write short answers to the following:

How many edges are there in a forest with p components having n vertices in all?
questions.subject: dm
questions.solution: Each tree with $n_i$ vertices has $n_i-1$ edges; summing over p trees gives $n-p$.

questions.text:
Write short answers to the following:

Assume that the last element of the set is used as partition element in Quicksort. If n distinct elements from the set [1.....n] are to be sorted, give an input for which Quicksort takes maximum time.
questions.subject: algo
questions.answer: Already sorted input 1, 2, …, n (or reverse sorted n, …, 1)
questions.solution: With the last element as pivot, sorted input makes every partition of size n−1 and 0, giving $\Theta(n^2)$.

questions.text:
Write short answers to the following:

Which page replacement policy sometimes leads to more page faults when size of memory is increased?
questions.subject: os
questions.solution: FIFO is not a stack algorithm and exhibits Belady's anomaly.

questions.text: Consider addition in two's complement arithmetic. A carry from the most significant but does not always correspond to an overflow. Explain what is the condition for overflow in two's complement arithmetic.
questions.subject: dl
questions.answer: Overflow iff the carry into the MSB differs from the carry out of the MSB (equivalently, both operands have the same sign and the result's sign differs)
questions.solution: $V = C_{n} \oplus C_{n-1}$; e.g. (−1)+(−1) produces a carry out but no overflow.

questions.text: A priority encoder accepts three input signals (A, B and C) and produce a two-bit output $(X_1, X_0)$ corresponding to the highest priority active input signal. Assume A has the highest priority followed by B and C has the lowest priority. If none of the inputs are active the output should be 00. design the priority encoder using 4:1 multiplexers as the main components.
questions.subject: dl
questions.answer: With A→11, B→10, C→01: $X_1 = A + B$, $X_0 = A + \overline{B}C$; with A,B as MUX selects, $X_1$ inputs (AB=00,01,10,11) = 0,1,1,1 and $X_0$ inputs = C,0,1,1
questions.solution: Two 4:1 MUXes with select lines A (MSB) and B; data inputs from the truth table as given.
questions.reviewNote: Output code for each input is not specified in the paper; A=11, B=10, C=01 assumed.

questions.text: Design a 3-bit counter using D-flip flops such that not more than one flip-flop changes state between any two consecutive states.
questions.subject: dl
questions.answer: Gray-code counter 000→001→011→010→110→111→101→100→000 with $D_2 = Q_1\overline{Q_0} + Q_2Q_0$, $D_1 = \overline{Q_2}Q_0 + Q_1\overline{Q_0}$, $D_0 = \overline{Q_2 \oplus Q_1}$
questions.solution: Use the 3-bit Gray sequence and read each D input as the next-state bit from the state table, then minimise.

questions.text: The access times of the main memory and the Cache memory, in a computer system, are 500 n sec and 50 n sec, respectively. It is estimated that 80% of the main memory request are for read the rest for write. The hit ratio for the read access only is 0.9 and a write-through policy (where both main and cache memories are updated simultaneously) is used. Determine the average time of the main memory.
questions.subject: coa
questions.solution: Reads: 0.9×50 + 0.1×500 = 95 ns; writes always take 500 ns. Average = 0.8×95 + 0.2×500 = 176 ns (180 ns if a read miss costs 50 + 500).
questions.reviewNote: Answer depends on whether a read miss costs 500 ns or 550 ns.

questions.text:
Three devices A, B and C are corrected to the bus of a computer, input/output transfers for all three devices use interrupt control. Three interrupt request lines INTR1, INTR2 and INTR3 are available with priority of $\text{INTR}_1 >$ priority of $\text{INTR}_2 >$ priority of $\text{INTR}_3$.

Draw a schematic of the priority logic, using an interrupt mask register, in which Priority of A > Priority of B > Priority of C.
questions.subject: coa
questions.solution: Connect A→INTR1, B→INTR2, C→INTR3; AND each request with its mask-register bit, feed the masked requests to a priority encoder/daisy logic that also inhibits lower lines when a higher one is active.

questions.text:
A microprocessor is capable of addressing 1 megabyte of memory with a 20-bit address bus. The system to be designed requires 256 K bytes of RAM, 256 K bytes of EPROM, 16 I/O devices (memory mapped I/O) and 1 K byte of EERAM (electrically erasable RAM).

Design a memory map (to reduce decoding logic) and show the decoding logic if the components available are:

| Type | Size | Speed |
|---|---|---|
| RAM | 6 K × 8 | 140 n sec |
| EPROM | 256 K × 8 | 150 n sec |
| EERAM | 256 × 8 | 500 n sec-read 3 µsec-write |
questions.subject: coa
questions.solution: Divide the 1 MB space into four 256 KB blocks using $A_{19}A_{18}$ (e.g. RAM, EPROM, EERAM + I/O region); partially decode within the block (4 EERAM chips for 1 KB, I/O selects on low address lines).
questions.reviewNote: RAM chip size printed as '6 K × 8' (likely 64 K × 8).

questions.text:
A microprocessor is capable of addressing 1 megabyte of memory with a 20-bit address bus. The system to be designed requires 256 K bytes of RAM, 256 K bytes of EPROM, 16 I/O devices (memory mapped I/O) and 1 K byte of EERAM (electrically erasable RAM).

The micro processor is operating at 12.5 mHz and provides time equivalent to two clock cycles for memory read and write. Assuming control signals similar to 8085, design the extra logic required for interfacing EERAM.
questions.subject: legacy
questions.solution: Two cycles at 12.5 MHz = 160 ns < 500 ns read / 3 µs write, so a wait-state generator (counter driving READY) must insert ≥3 wait states on reads and ≥36 on writes when EERAM is selected.

questions.text:
Consider the function F(n) for which the pseudo code is given below:

```
Function F(n)
begin
F1 ← 1
if(n=1) then F ← 3
else For i = 1 to n do
        begin
        C ← 0
For     j = 1 to F(n - 1) do
        begin C ← C + 1 end
        F1 = F1 * C
end
        F = F1
end
```

[n is a positive integer greater than zero]

Derive a recurrence relation for F(n)
questions.subject: dm
questions.solution: The inner loop sets C = F(n−1); the outer loop multiplies F1 by C n times.

questions.subject: dm

questions.text:
Let T be a Depth First Tree of a undirected graph G. An array P indexed by vertices of G is given. P[V] is the parent of vertex V, in T. Parent of the root is the root itself.

Give a method for finding and printing the cycle formed if the edge (u,v) of G not in T (i.e., $e \in G - T$) is now added to T.

Time taken by your method must be proportional to the length of the cycle.

Describe the algorithm in a PASCAL - like language. Assume that the variables have been suitably declared.
questions.subject: algo
questions.answer: In a DFS tree a non-tree edge joins an ancestor and a descendant: follow P[] from the descendant up to the ancestor, printing each vertex, then close with the edge back
questions.solution: Walk up alternately from u and v (marking) until one reaches the other; the walk from the descendant stops at the ancestor after exactly (cycle length − 1) steps.

questions.text:
Suggest a data structure for representing a subnet S of integers from 1 to n. following operations on the set S are to be performed in constant time (independent of cardinality of S).

(i) MEMBER (X): Check whether X is the set S or not

(ii) FIND-ONE(S): If S is not empty, return one element of the set S (any arbitrary element will do)

(iii) ADD (X): Add integer x to set S

(iv) DELETE(X): Delete integer x from S.

Give pictorial examples of your data structure. Give routines for these operations in an English like language. You may assume that the data structure has been suitably initialized. Clearly state your assumptions regarding initialization.
questions.subject: pds
questions.answer: Two arrays: dense list E[1..n] of members with a count k, and pos[1..n] giving each member's index in E; delete swaps the last element into the vacated slot
questions.solution: MEMBER: pos[x] ≤ k and E[pos[x]] = x; FIND-ONE: E[1] if k > 0; ADD: E[++k] = x, pos[x] = k; DELETE: move E[k] to pos[x], update its pos, k−−.

questions.text:
What type of parameter passing mechanism (call-by-value, call-by-reference, call-by-name, or-by-value result) is the following sequence of actions truing to implement for a procedure call P (A[i]) where P (i:integer) is a procedure and A is an integer array?

1. Create a new local variable, say z.
2. Assign to z the value of A[i].
3. Execute the body of P using z for A[i]
4. Set A[i] to z.

Is the implementation correct? Explain and correct it if necessary. You are supposed to make only small changes.
questions.subject: cd
questions.answer: Call-by-value-result; incorrect if i changes inside P — the address of A[i] must be computed once at call time (e.g. j := i or a pointer) and step 4 must store z into that saved location
questions.solution: Copy-restore must write back to the l-value evaluated at the call, not re-evaluate A[i] after the body.

questions.subject: cd
questions.answer: At x: stack Test, A(outer); display d[1]=Test, d[2]=A(outer). At y: stack Test, A(outer), B, A(inner); display d[1]=Test, d[2]=A(outer), d[3]=B, d[4]=A(inner)
questions.solution: x calls the outer A (level 1); outer A calls B (level 2); inside B the name A resolves to B's local A (level 3).

questions.text:
Write syntax directed definitions (semantic rules) for the following grammar to add the type of each identifier to its entry in the symbol table during semantic analysis. Rewriting the grammar is not permitted and semantic rules are to be added to the ends of productions only.

$$\begin{aligned} D &\rightarrow TL; \\ T &\rightarrow \text{int} \\ T &\rightarrow \text{real} \\ L &\rightarrow L, \text{id} \\ L &\rightarrow \text{id} \end{aligned}$$
questions.subject: cd
questions.answer: T → int {T.type := integer}; T → real {T.type := real}; L → id {L.list := [id.entry]}; L → L1 , id {L.list := L1.list + [id.entry]}; D → T L ; {for each e in L.list: addtype(e, T.type)}
questions.solution: With only end-of-production actions, collect the identifiers in a synthesized list and enter the type when D is reduced.

questions.text:
Write 3-address intermediate code (quadruples) for the following boolean expression in the sequence as it would be generated by a compiler. Partial evaluation of Boolean expressions is not permitted. Assume the usual rules of precedence of the operators.

(a + b) > (c + d) or a > c and b < d
questions.subject: cd
questions.answer: t1 = a + b; t2 = c + d; t3 = t1 > t2; t4 = a > c; t5 = b < d; t6 = t4 and t5; t7 = t3 or t6
questions.solution: 'and' binds tighter than 'or'; full (numeric) evaluation computes every relational result before combining.

questions.text:
Draw the precedence graph for the concurrent program given below:

```
S1
parbegin
    begin
    S2:S4
    end;
    begin
    S3;
    parbegin
     S5;
     begin
        S6:S8
        End
     parend
end;
S7
Parend;
S9
```
questions.subject: os
questions.solution: Three parallel branches after S1: (S2;S4), (S3; parbegin S5 ∥ (S6;S8) parend), and S7; all join before S9.
questions.reviewNote: Nesting of S7 is ambiguous in the retyped layout; taken as a third parallel branch.

questions.text: Let the page reference and the working set window be c c d b c e c e a d and 4, respectively. The initial working set at time t = 0 contains the pages {a, d, e}, where a was referenced at time t = 0, d was referenced at time t = -1, and e was referend at time t = -2. determine the total number of page faults and the average number of page frames used by computing the working set at each reference.
questions.subject: os
questions.solution: Faults at t = 1 (c), 4 (b), 6 (e), 9 (a), 10 (d); working-set sizes 4,3,3,3,3,4,3,2,3,4 sum to 32 over 10 references.

questions.text:
How is redundancy reduced in the following models?

(i) Hierarchical

(ii) Network

(iii) Relational

Write a one line answer in each case.
questions.subject: db
questions.answer: (i) virtual records / logical parent–child pointers instead of duplicate segments; (ii) each record stored once and shared through owner–member set links (pointers); (iii) normalization (decomposition into normal forms)
questions.solution: Each model avoids storing the same fact twice: pointers in hierarchical/network, decomposition in relational.

questions.text:

|---|---|
| FREQUENTS | (CUSTOMER, HOTEL) |
| SERVES | (HOTEL, SNACKS) |
| LIKES | (CUSTOMER, SNACKS) |

questions.text: If G is a group of even order, then show that there exists an element $a \ne e$, the identity in G, such that $a^2 = e$
questions.subject: dm
questions.solution: Pair each element with its inverse; elements with $a \ne a^{-1}$ come in pairs, so the self-inverse elements are even in number; e is one, so another $a \ne e$ with $a^2=e$ exists.

questions.text:
Consider the set of integers $\{1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 12, 24\}$ together with the two binary operations LCM (lowest common multiple) and GCD (greatest common divisor). Which of the following algebraic structures does this represent?

(i) group

(ii) ring

(iii) field

(iv) lattice
questions.subject: dm
questions.solution: These are the divisors of 24; LCM and GCD are join and meet under divisibility. No inverses exist, so not a group/ring/field.

questions.text:
Uses Modus ponens $(A, A \rightarrow\ \models B)$ or resolution to show that the following set is inconsistent:

(1) $Q(x) \rightarrow P(x) V \sim R(a)$

(2) $R(a) \sim Q(a)$

(3) $Q(a)$

(4) $\sim P(y)$

Where x and y are universally quantified variables, a is a constant and P, Q, R are monadic predicates.
questions.subject: dm
questions.answer: Derive R(a) from (2),(3); instantiate (1) with x = a to get P(a) ∨ ~R(a), hence P(a); this contradicts ~P(a) from (4) with y = a
questions.solution: Clauses: ¬Q(x)∨P(x)∨¬R(a), R(a)∨¬Q(a), Q(a), ¬P(y); resolving yields the empty clause.
questions.reviewNote: Connective in (2) is missing in the print ('R(a) ~Q(a)'); read as R(a) ∨ ~Q(a) (i.e. Q(a) → R(a)).

questions.text: Let S be the set of all integers and let n > 1 be a fixed integer. Define for a, b ∈ S, a R b iff a-b is a multiple of n. Show that R is an equivalence relation and finds its equivalence classes for n = 5.
questions.subject: dm
questions.answer: Five classes: [0], [1], [2], [3], [4] where [r] = {5k + r : k ∈ ℤ}
questions.solution: Reflexive (a−a = 0), symmetric (b−a = −(a−b)), transitive (sum of multiples of n).

questions.text:
Which of the following three statements are true? Prove your answer.

(i) The union of two recursive languages is recursive.

(ii) The language $\{0^n \mid n \text{ is a prime}\}$ is not regular.

(iii) Regular languages are closed under infinite union.
questions.subject: toc
questions.solution: (i) run both deciders; (ii) pumping lemma: for prime $p \ge$ pumping length, pumping $y$ ($|y|=k$) to $i=p+1$ gives length $p(1+k)$, composite; (iii) every language is a union of singleton (regular) languages.

Fill up the boxes to complete the program and write against [A], [B], [C] and [D] in your answer book. Assume that max is a variable to store the largest value and i,j are the indices to the array.
