Is the above decomposition dependency-preserving? If not, list all the dependencies that are not preserved.
questions.subject: db
questions.answer: No; NO → P is not preserved
questions.solution: R1 gets L→MN, P→L, MN→P, L→P; R2 gets M→O; from these the closure of {N,O} is just {N,O}.

questions.text:
Answer the following:

The following table refers to search times for a key in B-trees and $B^+$-trees.

| B-tree: Successful Search | B-tree: Unsuccessful Search | $B^+$-tree: Successful Search | $B^+$-tree: Unsuccessful Search |
|---|---|---|---|
| $X_1$ | $X_2$ | $X_3$ | $X_4$ |

A successful search means that the key exists in the database and unsuccessful means that it is not present in the database. Each of the entries $X_1$, $X_2$, $X_3$, and $X_4$ can have a value of either Constant or Variable. Constant means that the search time is the same, independent of the specific key value; whereas Variable means that it is dependent on the specific key value chosen for the search.

Give the correct values for the entries $X_1$, $X_2$, $X_3$, and $X_4$ (for example $X_1$ = Constant, $X_2$ = Constant, $X_3$ = Constant, $X_4$ = Constant).
questions.subject: db
questions.answer: X1 = Variable, X2 = Constant, X3 = Constant, X4 = Constant
questions.solution: B-tree keys live in internal nodes too, so a hit may stop early; misses and all B+-tree searches always reach a leaf at the same depth.

questions.text:
A computer system uses 32-bit virtual address, and 32-bit physical address. The physical memory is byte addressable, and the page size is 4 kbytes. It is decided to use two level page tables to translate from virtual address to physical address. Equal number of bits should be used for indexing first level and second level page table, and the size of each page table entry is 4 bytes.

Give a diagram showing how a virtual address would be translated to a physical address.
questions.subject: os
questions.answer: VA = 10-bit level-1 index | 10-bit level-2 index | 12-bit offset; PTBR + p1 → L1 entry → L2 table base, + p2 → frame number (20 bits) concatenated with offset
questions.solution: Offset = 12 bits for 4 KB pages; remaining 20 bits split equally 10/10.

What is the number of page table entries that can be contained in each page?

$E \rightarrow E * E$

$E \rightarrow id$

In this grammar, what is the precedence of the two operators * and +?

For the grammar

If only one parse tree is desired for any string in the same language, what changes are to be made so that the resulting LALR(1) grammar is non-ambiguous?

questions.answer: E → E + T | T; T → T * F | F; F → id (or declare %left '+' then %left '*' in the parser generator)
questions.solution: Introduce one non-terminal per precedence level with left recursion for left associativity.

questions.subject: dl

questions.text: Ram and Shyam have been asked to show that a certain problem Π is NP-complete. Ram shows a polynomial time reduction from the 3-SAT problem to Π, and Shyam shows a polynomial time reduction from Π to 3-SAT. Which of the following can be inferred from these reductions?

options.t: Π is NP-hard but not NP-complete
Π is in NP, but is not NP-complete
Π is neither NP-hard, nor in NP

questions.subject: algo
questions.solution: 3-SAT ≤p Π makes Π NP-hard; Π ≤p 3-SAT puts Π in NP; hence NP-complete.

questions.text: If the strings of a language L can be effectively enumerated in lexicographic (i.e., alphabetic) order, which of the following statements is true?

options.t: L is regular but not necessarily finite
L is context free but not necessarily regular
L is recursive but not necessarily context free

questions.subject: toc
questions.solution: Enumeration in canonical order gives a decider: enumerate until w or a later string appears. So L is recursive, e.g. $a^nb^nc^n$ qualifies.

questions.subject: cd

questions.text:
Consider the following three claims

I. $(n + k)^m = \Theta(n^m)$, where k and m are constants  
II. $2^{n+1} = O(2^n)$  
III. $2^{2n} = O(2^n)$

Which of these claims are correct?
questions.subject: algo
questions.solution: I: binomial expansion leading term n^m. II: 2^{n+1}=2·2^n. III: 2^{2n}/2^n=2^n is unbounded, so false.

III. a b f h g e

questions.subject: algo
questions.solution: II fails: after a b f, DFS must continue from f to an unvisited neighbour (g or h), never jump to e (not adjacent to f). I, III, IV are valid DFS orders.

If, instead, we use binary search to identify the position, the worst case running time will
questions.subject: algo
questions.solution: Binary search reduces comparisons but shifting elements still costs Θ(n) per insertion, Θ(n²) overall.

questions.subject: pds
questions.solution: The 7th smallest lies within the top 7 levels (at most 127 nodes); searching a constant-size region is Θ(1).

questions.text: Which of the following statements is FALSE?

options.t: In statically typed languages, each variable in a program has a fixed type
In un-typed languages, values do not have any types
In dynamically typed languages, variables have no types
In all statically typed languages, each variable in a program is associated with values of only a single type during the execution of the program

questions.subject: pds
questions.solution: In dynamically typed languages a variable does carry a type at run time (the type of the value it currently holds), so C is treated as false.
questions.reviewNote: Debatable question: D is also arguably false (subtyping/polymorphism); C follows the commonly quoted key.

questions.text: Using a larger block size in a fixed block size file system leads to

options.t: better disk throughput but poorer disk space utilization
better disk throughput and better disk space utilization
poorer disk throughput but better disk space utilization
poorer disk throughput and poorer disk space utilization

questions.subject: os
questions.solution: Larger blocks mean fewer seeks per byte (higher throughput) but more internal fragmentation in the last block.

questions.text: In a system with 32 bit virtual addresses and 1KB page size, use of one-level page tables for virtual to physical address translation is not practical because of

options.t: the large amount of internal fragmentation
the large amount of external fragmentation
the large memory overhead in maintaining page tables
the large computation overhead in the translation process

questions.subject: os
questions.solution: 2^32/2^10 = 2^22 page table entries per process — several MB of page table per process.

questions.text: Which of the following assertions is FALSE about the Internet Protocol (IP)?

options.t: It is possible for a computer to have multiple IP addresses
IP packets from the same source to the same destination can take different routes in the network
IP ensures that a packet is discarded if it is unable to reach its destination within a given number of hops
The packet source cannot set the route of an outgoing packets; the route is determined only by the routing tables in the routers on the way

questions.subject: cn
questions.solution: IP supports source routing options, so the source can specify the route; the other statements are true (multihoming, datagram routing, TTL).

questions.text: Which of the following functionalities must be implemented by a transport protocol over and above the network protocol?

options.t: Packet delivery in the correct order

questions.subject: cn
questions.solution: Every transport protocol (even UDP) provides end-to-end (process-to-process) connectivity; loss recovery, duplicate detection and ordering are optional (absent in UDP).

questions.text: Which of the following scenarios may lead to an irrecoverable error in a database system?

options.t: A transaction writes a data item after it is read by an uncommitted transaction
A transaction reads a data item after it is read by an uncommitted transaction
A transaction reads a data item after it is written by a committed transaction
A transaction reads a data item after it is written by an uncommitted transaction

questions.subject: db
questions.solution: Reading uncommitted data (dirty read) can make a schedule non-recoverable if the reader commits and the writer later aborts.

$$\alpha: (\forall x)[P_x \Leftrightarrow (\forall y)[Q_{xy} \Leftrightarrow \neg Q_{yy}]] \Rightarrow (\forall x)[\neg P_x]$$

questions.text: m identical balls are to be placed in n distinct bags. You are given that m ≥ kn, where k is a natural number ≥ 1. In how many ways can the balls be placed in the bags if each bag must contain at least k balls?

| + | a | b | c |
|---|---|---|---|
| **a** | b | a | c |
| **b** | a | b | c |

| × | a | b | c |
|---|---|---|---|
| **a** | a | b | c |
| **b** | b | c | a |
| **c** | c | c | b |

For example, a + c = c, c + a = a, c × b = c and b × c = a. Given the following set of equations:

(b × x) + (c × y) = c

the number of solution(s) (i.e., pair(s) (x, y)) that satisfy the equations) is

questions.text:
Let Σ = {a, b, c, d, e} be an alphabet. We define an encoding scheme as follows:

g(a) = 3, g(b) = 5, g(c) = 7, g(d) = 9, g(e) = 11.

Let $p_i$ denote the i-th prime number ($p_1$ = 2)

For a non empty string $s = a_1 \ldots a_n$, where each $a_i \in \Sigma$, define $f(s) = \prod_{i=1}^{n} p_i^{g(a_i)}$. For a non empty sequence $\langle s_1, \ldots, s_n \rangle$ of strings from $\Sigma^+$, define $h(\langle s_1, \ldots, s_n \rangle) = \prod_{i=1}^{n} p_i^{f(s_i)}$

Which of the following numbers is the encoding, h, of a non-empty sequence of strings?

questions.text:
Consider the following system of linear equations

$$\begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 & -4 \\ 4 & 3 & -12 \\ 1 & 2 & -8 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \\ z \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} \alpha \\ 5 \\ 7 \end{bmatrix}$$

Notice that the second and the third columns of the coefficient matrix are linearly dependent. For how many values of α, does this system of equations have infinitely many solutions?

questions.text:
A 1-input, 2-output synchronous sequential circuit behaves as follows.

Let $z_k$, $n_k$ denote the number of 0's and 1's respectively in initial k bits of the input ($z_k + n_k = k$). The circuit outputs 00 until one of the following conditions holds.

- $z_k - n_k = 2$. In this case, the output at the k-th and all subsequent clock ticks is 10.
- $n_k - z_k = 2$. In this case, the output at the k-th and all subsequent clock ticks is 01.

What is the minimum number of states required in the state transition graph of the above circuit?
questions.subject: dl
questions.solution: States for difference z−n ∈ {−1, 0, +1} plus two absorbing states (output 10 and output 01): 5.

questions.text:
The literal count of a boolean expression is the sum of the number of times each literal appears in the expression. For example, the literal count of (xy + xz') is 4. What are the minimum possible literal counts of the product-of-sum and sum-of-product representations respectively of the function given by the following Karnaugh map? Here, X denotes "don't care"

| xy \ zw | 00 | 01 | 11 | 10 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **00** | X | 1 | 0 | 1 |
| **01** | 0 | 1 | X | 0 |
| **11** | 1 | X | X | 0 |
| **10** | X | 0 | 0 | X |
questions.subject: dl
questions.solution: POS: (z'+w')(y'+z')(x'+w')(x+y'+w) = 9 literals. SOP: y'w' + xyz' + x'z'w = 8 literals, so the true minimum is (9, 8); the key's option is (9, 10).
questions.reviewNote: No option matches the true minimum (9, 8); the official key gives (C) (9, 10). Source: https://gateoverflow.in/936/gate2003-45

questions.text:
Consider the ALU shown below.

If the operands are in 2's complement representation, which of the following operations can be performed by suitably setting the control lines K and $C_0$ only (+ and - denote addition and subtraction respectively)?

options.t: A + B, and A - B, but not A + 1
A + B, and A + 1, but not A - B
A + B, but not A - B or A + 1
A + B, and A - B, and A + 1

figures.alt: Ripple-carry adder/subtractor: each bit i has an XOR gate taking B_i and the common control line K; the XOR output and A_i feed a full adder with carry-in C_i (C_0 at the least significant stage), producing sum S_i and carry C_{i+1} to the next stage.

The non-inverting buffers have delays $\delta_1$ = 2 ns and $\delta_2$ = 4 ns as shown in the figure. Both XOR gates and all wires have zero delay. Assume that all gate inputs, outputs and wires are stable at logic level 0 at time 0. If the following waveform is applied at input A, how many transition(s) (change of logic levels) occur(s) at B during the interval from 0 to 10 ns?

questions.solution: A rises at 1 ns; first XOR output = A ⊕ A(t−2) is high on [1,3]; B = X ⊕ X(t−4) is high on [1,3] and [5,7]: transitions at 1, 3, 5, 7 ns.

questions.text:
The following information pertains to Q.48-49. Consider the following assembly language program for a hypothetical processor. A, B, and C are 8 bit registers. The meanings of various instructions are shown as comments.

```
    MOV B, #0    ; B ← 0
    MOV C, #8    ; C ← 8
Z:  CMP C, #0    ; compare C with 0
    JZ X         ; jump to X if zero flag is set
    SUB C, #1    ; C ← C-1
    RRC A, #1    ; right rotate A through carry by one bit. Thus:
                 ; if the initial values of A and the carry flag are a7...a0 and
                 ; c0 respectively, their values after the execution of this
                 ; instruction will be c0a7...a1 and a0 respectively.
    JC Y         ; jump to Y if carry flag is set
    JMP Z        ; jump to Z
Y:  ADD B, #1    ; B ← B + 1
    JMP Z        ; jump to Z
X:
```

If the initial value of register A is $A_0$, the value of register B after the program execution will be
questions.subject: coa
questions.solution: Each of the 8 iterations rotates one bit of A into carry and increments B when it is 1.

questions.text:
The following information pertains to Q.48-49. Consider the following assembly language program for a hypothetical processor. A, B, and C are 8 bit registers. The meanings of various instructions are shown as comments.

```
    MOV B, #0    ; B ← 0
    MOV C, #8    ; C ← 8
Z:  CMP C, #0    ; compare C with 0
    JZ X         ; jump to X if zero flag is set
    SUB C, #1    ; C ← C-1
    RRC A, #1    ; right rotate A through carry by one bit. Thus:
                 ; if the initial values of A and the carry flag are a7...a0 and
                 ; c0 respectively, their values after the execution of this
                 ; instruction will be c0a7...a1 and a0 respectively.
    JC Y         ; jump to Y if carry flag is set
    JMP Z        ; jump to Z
Y:  ADD B, #1    ; B ← B + 1
    JMP Z        ; jump to Z
X:
```

Which of the following instructions when inserted at location X will ensure that the value of register A after program execution is the same as its initial value?

options.t: LRC A, #1 ; left rotate A through carry flag by one bit

questions.subject: coa
questions.solution: A plus carry form a 9-bit ring; 8 rotations leave it rotated by 8 positions, so one more RRC completes the 9-rotation cycle and restores A.

Let S denote the set of seven bit binary strings in which the first, the fourth, and the last bits are 1. The number of strings in S that are accepted by M is

S → a S b | S S | ε

Which of the following statements is true?

There is a deterministic pushdown automaton that accepts L(G)
We can find a deterministic finite state automaton that accepts L(G)

questions.text:
Consider two languages $L_1$ and $L_2$, each on the alphabet Σ. Let f: Σ* → Σ* be a polynomial time computable bijection such that $(\forall x)[x \in L_1 \text{ iff } f(x) \in L_2]$. Further, let $f^{-1}$ be also polynomial time computable.

Which of the following CANNOT be true?

options.t: $L_1$ is recursively enumerable and $L_2$ is recursive

questions.subject: algo
questions.solution: L1 ≤ L2 via f, so if L2 were decidable L1 would be decidable too.

questions.text:
A single tape Turing Machine M has two states $q_0$ and $q_1$, of which $q_0$ is the starting state. The tape alphabet of M is {0, 1, B} and its input alphabet is {0, 1}. The symbol B is the blank symbol used to indicate end of an input string. The transition function of M is described in the following table.

|  | 0 | 1 | B |
|---|---|---|---|
| $q_0$ | $q_1$, 1, R | $q_1$, 1, R | Halt |
| $q_1$ | $q_1$, 1, R | $q_0$, 1, L | $q_0$, B, L |

The table is interpreted as illustrated below.

The entry ($q_1$, 1, R) in row $q_0$ and column 1 signifies that if M is in state $q_0$ and reads 1 on the current tape square, then it writes 1 on the same tape square, moves its tape head one position to the right and transitions to state $q_1$.

Which of the following statements is true about M?

options.t: M does not halt on any string in $(0 + 1)^+$
M does not halt on any string in $(00 + 1)^*$
M halts on all strings ending in a 0
M halts on all strings ending in a 1

questions.subject: toc
questions.solution: M halts only when q0 reads B. On a non-empty input it reaches the end in q1, moves left to q0 on a 1, then right to q1 on B, and loops forever; only ε halts.

options.t: L is recursively enumerable, but $\overline{L}$ is not
$\overline{L}$ is recursively enumerable, but L is not
Neither L nor $\overline{L}$ is recursively enumerable

questions.subject: toc
questions.solution: L contains the non-halting instances (tagged 1) so it is not RE; $\overline{L}$ contains the non-halting instances tagged 0 (plus malformed strings), so it is not RE either.

questions.text:
The following information pertains to Q. 61-62. In a permutation $a_1 \ldots a_n$, of n distinct integers, an inversion is a pair $(a_i, a_j)$ such that i < j and $a_i > a_j$.

If all permutations are equally likely, what is the expected number of inversions in a randomly chosen permutation of 1...n?
questions.subject: algo
questions.solution: Each of the $\binom{n}{2}$ pairs is inverted with probability ½.

questions.text:
The following information pertains to Q. 61-62. In a permutation $a_1 \ldots a_n$, of n distinct integers, an inversion is a pair $(a_i, a_j)$ such that i < j and $a_i > a_j$.

What would be the worst case time complexity of the Insertion Sort algorithm, if the inputs are restricted to permutations of 1...n with at most n inversions?
questions.subject: algo
questions.solution: Insertion sort runs in Θ(n + number of inversions) = Θ(n).

questions.text:
A data structure is required for storing a set of integers such that each of the following operations can be done in O(log n) time, where n is the number of elements in the set.

I. Deletion of the smallest element  
II. Insertion of an element if it is not already present in the set

Which of the following data structures can be used for this purpose?

options.t: A heap can be used but not a balanced binary search tree
A balanced binary search tree can be used but not a heap
Both balanced binary search tree and heap can be used
Neither balanced binary search tree nor heap can be used

questions.subject: pds
questions.solution: Checking membership before insertion takes Θ(n) in a heap but O(log n) in a balanced BST, which also deletes its minimum in O(log n).

questions.text: Let S be a stack of size n ≥ 1. Starting with the empty stack, suppose we push the first n natural numbers in sequence, and then perform n pop operations. Assume that Push and Pop operations take X seconds each, and Y seconds elapse between the end of one such stack operation and the start of the next operation. For m ≥ 1, define the stack-life of m as the time elapsed from the end of Push(m) to the start of the pop operation that removes m from S. The average stack-life of an element of this stack is
questions.subject: pds
questions.solution: Stack-life of m = 2(n−m)(X+Y) + Y; averaging over m = 1..n gives (n−1)(X+Y) + Y = n(X+Y) − X.

questions.text: The cube root of a natural number n is defined as the largest natural number m such that $m^3 \le n$. The complexity of computing the cube root of n (n is represented in binary notation) is

options.t: $O(n^{0.5})$ but not $O((\log n)^k)$ for any constant k > 0
$O((\log n)^k)$ for some constant k > 0, but not $O((\log \log n)^m)$ for any constant m > 0
$O((\log \log n)^k)$ for some constant k > 0.5, but not $O((\log \log n)^{0.5})$

questions.subject: algo
questions.solution: Binary search over [0, n] needs O(log n) steps, each cubing an O(log n)-bit number: polylog in n; merely reading the log n-bit input rules out O((log log n)^m).

questions.text:

Here, $x_s$ denotes the starting time and $x_e$ denotes the ending time of activity X. We need to schedule the activities in a set of rooms available to us. An activity can be scheduled in a room only if the room is reserved for the activity for its entire duration. What is the minimum number of rooms required?

questions.text:
Let G = (V, E) be a directed graph with n vertices. A path from $v_i$ to $v_j$ in G is a sequence of vertices ($v_i$, $v_{i+1}$, ..., $v_j$) such that $(v_k, v_{k+1}) \in E$ for all k in i through j−1. A simple path is a path in which no vertex appears more than once.

Let A be an n × n array initialized as follows

$$A[j, k] = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } (j, k) \in E \\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}$$

Consider the following algorithm.

```
for i = 1 to n
  for j = 1 to n
    for k = 1 to n
      A[j, k] = max(A[j, k], A[j, i] + A[i, k]);
```

Which of the following statements is necessarily true for all j and k after termination of the above algorithm?

options.t: If A[j, j] ≥ n − 1, then G has a Hamiltonian cycle
If there exists a path from j to k, A[j, k] contains the longest path length from j to k
If there exist a path from j to k, every simple path from j to k contains at most A[j, k] edges

questions.subject: algo
questions.solution: The max-plus Floyd–Warshall variant can only grow values and ends with A[j,k] at least the length of every simple j–k path (it may over-count via cycles), so D always holds; A, B, C can fail on graphs with cycles.

questions.text:
Consider the following logic program P

A(x) ← B(x, y), C(y)  
← B(x, x)

Which of the following first order sentences is equivalent to P?

options.t: $(\forall x)[(\exists y)[B(x, y) \wedge C(y)] \Rightarrow A(x)] \wedge \neg(\exists x)[B(x, x)]$
$(\forall x)[(\forall y)[B(x, y) \wedge C(y)] \Rightarrow A(x)] \wedge \neg(\exists x)[B(x, x)]$
$(\forall x)[(\exists y)[B(x, y) \wedge C(y)] \Rightarrow A(x)] \vee \neg(\exists x)[B(x, x)]$
$(\forall x)[(\forall y)[B(x, y) \wedge C(y)] \Rightarrow A(x)] \wedge \neg(\exists x)[B(x, x)]$

questions.subject: dm
questions.solution: A clause is universally closed: ∀x∀y[B(x,y)∧C(y) ⇒ A(x)] ≡ ∀x[∃y(B(x,y)∧C(y)) ⇒ A(x)]; the goal clause ← B(x,x) means ∀x ¬B(x,x) ≡ ¬∃x B(x,x); a program is the conjunction of its clauses.

Derive clause (P ∨ Q) from clauses (P ∨ R), (Q ∨ ¬R).

(P ∨ Q) ⇒ FALSE if and only if both P and Q are unsatisfiable

questions.text: Which of the following is NOT an advantage of using shared, dynamically linked libraries as opposed to using statically linked libraries?

options.t: Lesser overall page fault rate in the system
Existing programs need not be re-linked to take advantage of newer versions of libraries

questions.subject: os
questions.solution: Dynamic linking adds work (loading/resolving symbols) at program start, so startup is slower, not faster.

questions.text: A uni-processor computer system only has two processes, both of which alternate 10 ms CPU bursts with 90 ms I/O bursts. Both the processes were created at nearly the same time. The I/O of both processes can proceed in parallel. Which of the following scheduling strategies will result in the least CPU utilization (over a long period of time) for this system?

options.t: Static priority scheduling with different priorities for the two processes
Round robin scheduling with a time quantum of 5 ms

questions.subject: os
questions.solution: FCFS/SRTF/priority give a 100 ms cycle with 20 ms busy (20%); RR-5 finishes the bursts at 15 and 20 ms, stretching the cycle to 105 ms (≈19%).

questions.text:
The following information pertains to Q.78-79. A processor uses 2-level page tables for virtual to physical address translation. Page tables for both levels are stored in the main memory. Virtual and physical addresses are both 32 bits wide. The memory is byte addressable. For virtual to physical address translation, the 10 most significant bits of the virtual address are used as index into the first level page table while the next 10 bits are used as index into the second level page table. The 12 least significant bits of the virtual address are used as offset within the page. Assume that the page table entries in both levels of page tables are 4 bytes wide. Further, the processor has a translation look-aside buffer (TLB), with a hit rate of 96%. The TLB caches recently used virtual page numbers and the corresponding physical page numbers. The processor also has a physically addressed cache with a hit rate of 90%. Main memory access time is 10 ns, cache access time is 1 ns, and TLB access time is also 1 ns.

Assuming that no page faults occur, the average time taken to access a virtual address is approximately (to the nearest 0.5 ns)
questions.subject: os
questions.solution: Translation: 1 + 0.04 × (2 × 10) = 1.8 ns; data: 1 + 0.1 × 10 = 2 ns; total 3.8 ≈ 4 ns.

questions.text:
The following information pertains to Q.78-79. A processor uses 2-level page tables for virtual to physical address translation. Page tables for both levels are stored in the main memory. Virtual and physical addresses are both 32 bits wide. The memory is byte addressable. For virtual to physical address translation, the 10 most significant bits of the virtual address are used as index into the first level page table while the next 10 bits are used as index into the second level page table. The 12 least significant bits of the virtual address are used as offset within the page. Assume that the page table entries in both levels of page tables are 4 bytes wide. Further, the processor has a translation look-aside buffer (TLB), with a hit rate of 96%. The TLB caches recently used virtual page numbers and the corresponding physical page numbers. The processor also has a physically addressed cache with a hit rate of 90%. Main memory access time is 10 ns, cache access time is 1 ns, and TLB access time is also 1 ns.

Suppose a process has only the following pages in its virtual address space: two contiguous code pages starting at virtual address 0x00000000, two contiguous data pages starting at virtual address 0x00400000, and a stack page starting at virtual address 0xFFFFF000. The amount of memory required for storing the page tables of this process is
questions.subject: os
questions.solution: Code, data and stack fall in first-level entries 0, 1 and 1023: one 4 KB outer table + three 4 KB inner tables = 16 KB.

questions.text: Host A is sending data to host B over a full duplex link. A and B are using the sliding window protocol for flow control. The send and receive window sizes are 5 packets each. Data packets (sent only from A to B) are all 1000 bytes long and the transmission time for such a packet is 50 µs. Acknowledgement packets (sent only from B to A) are very small and require negligible transmission time. The propagation delay over the link is 200 µs. What is the maximum achievable throughput in this communication?
questions.subject: cn

Students: (Roll_number, Name, Date_of_birth)  
Courses: (Course_number, Course_name, Instructor)

select distinct Name
from Students, Courses, Grades
where Students.Roll_number = Grades.Roll_number
  and Courses.Instructor = Korth
  and Courses.Course_number = Grades.Course_number

Names of students who have got an A grade in at least one of the courses taught by Korth

questions.text: Consider the grammar rule $E \to E_1 - E_2$ for arithmetic expressions. The code generated is targeted to a CPU having a single user register. The subtraction operation requires the first operand to be in the register. If $E_1$ and $E_2$ do not have any common sub expression, in order to get the shortest possible code

questions.subject: coa
questions.solution: Fetch/decode 7 words x 2 = 14; three memory transfers x 3 = 9; one ADD = 1; total 24.

questions.text:
Consider a small two-way set-associative cache memory, consisting of four blocks. For choosing the block to be replaced, use the least recently used (LRU) scheme. The number of cache misses for the following sequence of block addresses is

8, 12, 0, 12, 8
questions.subject: coa
questions.solution: Two sets; all addresses map to set 0: 8 miss, 12 miss, 0 miss (evicts 8), 12 hit, 8 miss: 4 misses.

questions.text: Let A = 11111010 and B = 00001010 be two 8-bit 2's complement numbers. Their product in 2's complement is
questions.subject: dl
questions.solution: A = -6, B = 10, product = -60 = 11000100 in 8-bit two's complement.

questions.text:
The microinstructions stored in the control memory of a processor have a width of 26 bits. Each microinstruction is divided into three fields: a micro-operation field of 13 bits, a next address field (X), and a MUX select field (Y). There are 8 status bits in the inputs of the MUX.

How many bits are there in the X and Y fields, and what is the size of the control memory in number of words?

figures.alt: Control Address Register feeds Control Memory; the memory outputs a 13-bit micro-operation field, an X field (next address) going back to the address register, and a Y field going to a MUX. The MUX takes status bits as input, and its output together with a Load signal (through an incrementer) controls the Control Address Register.

questions.subject: coa
questions.solution: Y selects among 8 status bits: 3 bits; X = 26 - 13 - 3 = 10 bits; control memory has 2^10 = 1024 words.

questions.text: A hard disk with a transfer rate of 10 Mbytes/second is constantly transferring data to memory using DMA. The processor runs at 600 MHz, and takes 300 and 900 clock cycles to initiate and complete DMA transfer respectively. If the size of the transfer is 20 Kbytes, what is the percentage of processor time consumed for the transfer operation?
questions.subject: coa
questions.solution: Transfer takes 20 KB / 10 MB/s = 2 ms; CPU overhead is 1200 cycles / 600 MHz = 2 microseconds; 2 us / 2 ms = 0.1%.

questions.text: A 4-stage pipeline has the stage delays as 150, 120, 160 and 140 nanoseconds respectively. Registers that are used between the stages have a delay of 5 nanoseconds each. Assuming constant clocking rate, the total time taken to process 1000 data items on this pipeline will be
questions.subject: coa
questions.solution: Clock = 160 + 5 = 165 ns; time = (4 + 999) x 165 ns = 165.5 microseconds.

questions.text:
The following propositional statement is

$(P \to (Q \vee R)) \to ((P \vee Q) \to R)$
questions.subject: dm
questions.solution: False at P=T,Q=T,R=F (not valid), true at P=F,Q=F (satisfiable).

questions.text:
How many solutions does the following system of linear equations have?

$-x + 5y = -1$
$x - y = 2$
$x + 3y = 3$
questions.subject: la
questions.solution: Rank of coefficient and augmented matrix are both 2 = number of unknowns; x = 9/4, y = 1/4 satisfies all three.
questions.reviewNote: Right-hand side of the first equation was illegible in the scan; recovered from gateoverflow.

questions.text:
The following is the incomplete operation table of a 4-element group.

| $\cdot$ | e | a | b | c |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| e | e | a | b | c |
| a | a | b | c | e |
| b | | | | |
| c | | | | |

The last row of the table is
questions.subject: dm
questions.solution: From the table a has order 4 with a^2=b, a^3=c, a^4=e. Then c*e=c, c*a=a^4=e, c*b=a^5=a, c*c=a^6=b: c e a b.

questions.text:
The inclusion of which of the following sets into

$S = \{\{1, 2\}, \{1, 2, 3\}, \{1, 3, 5\}, \{1, 2, 4\}, \{1, 2, 3, 4, 5\}\}$

is necessary and sufficient to make S a complete lattice under the partial order defined by set containment?
questions.subject: dm
questions.solution: Meets such as {1,2,3}∩{1,3,5} = {1,3} and {1,2}∩{1,3,5} = {1} must be present, so {1} and {1,3} are needed and suffice.

questions.text: An examination paper has 150 multiple-choice questions of one mark each, with each question having four choices. Each incorrect answer fetches -0.25 mark. Suppose 1000 students choose all their answers randomly with uniform probability. The sum total of the expected marks obtained by all these students is
questions.subject: prob
questions.solution: Per question E = 1/4 - 3/4 x 1/4 = 1/16; per student 150/16 = 9.375; times 1000 = 9375.

questions.text: Mala has a colouring book in which each English letter is drawn two times. She wants to paint each of these 52 prints with one of k colours, such that the colour-pairs used to colour any two letters are different. Both prints of a letter can also be coloured with the same colour. What is the minimum value of k that satisfies this requirement?
questions.subject: dm
questions.solution: Each letter needs a distinct unordered pair (repeats allowed) of colours: k(k+1)/2 >= 26 gives k >= 7 (k=6 gives only 21).

questions.text: In an $M \times N$ matrix such that all non-zero entries are covered in a rows and b columns. Then the maximum number of non-zero entries, such that no two are on the same row or column, is
questions.subject: dm
questions.solution: Chosen non-zeros are independent (no shared row/column) and each must lie in a covered row or column, so at most a + b (bipartite matching <= vertex cover).

questions.text: The minimum number of colours required to colour the following graph, such that no two adjacent vertices are assigned the same colour, is

figures.alt: Eight vertices: a left vertex and a right vertex, a top and a bottom vertex, and an inner 4-cycle. The left and right vertices are each joined to the top, bottom, and to the two inner vertices on their side; the top vertex is joined to the two upper inner vertices and the bottom vertex to the two lower inner vertices.

questions.subject: dm
questions.solution: The graph is not 3-colourable: the two apex-side vertices force top and bottom to share a colour, which then leaves conflicting colours on the inner 4-cycle; 4 colours suffice.
questions.reviewNote: Edges read from a small figure.

questions.text: Two n bit binary strings, $S_1$ and $S_2$ are chosen randomly with uniform probability. The probability that the Hamming distance between these strings (the number of bit positions where the two strings differ) is equal to d is
questions.subject: prob
questions.solution: XOR of the strings is uniform over 2^n patterns; C(n,d) of them have d ones.

questions.text: How many graphs on n labeled vertices exist which have at least $(n^2 - 3n)/2$ edges?
questions.subject: dm
questions.solution: Total possible edges C(n,2) = (n^2-n)/2, so at least (n^2-3n)/2 edges means missing at most n edges: sum over k=0..n of C((n^2-n)/2, k).
questions.reviewNote: Binomial indices in options are blurry; read from context.

questions.text: A point is randomly selected with uniform probability in the X-Y plane within the rectangle with corners at (0,0), (1,0), (1,2) and (0,2). If p is the length of the position vector of the point, the expected value of $p^2$ is
questions.subject: prob
questions.solution: E[x^2] = 1/3 (uniform on [0,1]) and E[y^2] = 4/3 (uniform on [0,2]); sum 5/3.

questions.text: Let $G_1 = (V, E_1)$ and $G_2 = (V, E_2)$ be connected graphs on the same vertex set V with more than two vertices. If $G_1 \cap G_2 = (V, E_1 \cap E_2)$ is not a connected graph, then the graph $G_1 \cup G_2 = (V, E_1 \cup E_2)$

options.t: has chromatic number strictly greater than those of $G_1$ and $G_2$

questions.subject: dm
questions.solution: G1 and G2 are each connected but their common edges are not, so the union has more than |V|-1 edges and must contain a cycle.

questions.subject: algo
questions.solution: Each f(counter) costs proportional to the run of 1s just counted, so total f cost is at most n; the loop itself is Theta(n): Theta(n).
