questions.text:
The recurrence equation

T(1) = 1

T(n) = 2T(n-1) + n, $n \geq 2$

evaluates to
questions.subject: algo

questions.text: A program takes as input a balanced binary search tree with n leaf nodes and computes the value of a function g(x) for each node x. If the cost of computing g(x) is min{no. of leaf-nodes in left-subtree of x, no. of leaf-nodes in right-subtree of x} then the worst-case time complexity of the program is
questions.subject: algo
questions.solution: Cost per level is n/2 (nodes at depth i each cost n/2^{i+1}), over log n levels: Theta(n log n).
questions.reviewNote: Confident in the derivation but the official key may differ; check.

questions.text: The following finite state machine accepts all those binary strings in which the number of 1's and 0's are respectively

figures.alt: Six states in two rows of three. Top row (left to right): start/accepting q0, q1, q2; bottom row: p0, p1, p2. On 1: q0->q1->q2->q0 (arc from q2 back to q0) and p0->p1->p2->p0 (arc). On 0: q_i -> p_i and p_i -> q_i for each column.

questions.subject: toc
questions.solution: Top-row transitions on 1 cycle mod 3 and 0 moves between top and bottom rows (parity); the start state is the only accepting state: number of 1's divisible by 3 and 0's even.

questions.text: The language $\{a^m b^n c^{m+n} \mid m, n \geq 1\}$ is

options.t: context sensitive but not context free

questions.subject: toc
questions.solution: Context-free via S -> aSc | aBc, B -> bBc | bc; not regular by pumping.

questions.text:
Consider the following grammar G:

$S \to bS \mid aA \mid b$
$A \to bA \mid aB$
$B \to bB \mid aS \mid a$

Let $N_a(w)$ and $N_b(w)$ denote the number of a's and b's in a string w respectively. The language $L(G) \subseteq \{a, b\}^+$ generated by G is
questions.subject: toc
questions.solution: Reading a's moves S -> A -> B -> S cyclically (b's loop); derivation ends at S->b or B->a, only when the a count is a multiple of 3.

questions.text:
$L_1$ is a recursively enumerable language over $\Sigma$. An algorithm A effectively enumerates its words as $w_1, w_2, w_3, \ldots$. Define another language $L_2$ over $\Sigma \cup \{\#\}$ as $\{w_i \# w_j : w_i, w_j \in L_1, i < j\}$. Here # is a new symbol. Consider the following assertions.

$S_1$: $L_1$ is recursive implies $L_2$ is recursive
$S_2$: $L_2$ is recursive implies $L_1$ is recursive

Which of the following statements is true?

options.t: $S_1$ is true but $S_2$ is not necessarily true
$S_2$ is true but $S_1$ is not necessarily true

questions.subject: toc
questions.solution: S1: decide w_i # w_j by running A to find their indices and checking i<j and membership. S2: w in L1 iff w = w_1 or w_1 # w in L2, which is decidable if L2 is.

questions.text:
Choose the best matching between the programming styles in Group 1 and their characteristics in Group 2.

| Group 1 | Group 2 |
|---|---|
| P. Functional | 1. Command-based, procedural |
| Q. Logic | 2. Imperative, abstract data types |
| R. Object-oriented | 3. Side-effect free, declarative, expression evaluation |
| S. Imperative | 4. Declarative, clausal representation, theorem proving |
questions.subject: ga
questions.solution: Functional = side-effect free/expression evaluation; logic = clausal/theorem proving; OO = abstract data types; imperative = command-based.

questions.text:
What does the following C-statement declare?

```c
int (* f) (int * );
```

options.t: A function that takes an integer pointer as argument and returns an integer
A function that takes an integer as argument and returns an integer pointer
A pointer to a function that takes an integer pointer as argument and returns an integer
A function that takes an integer pointer as argument and returns a function pointer

questions.subject: pds
questions.solution: `(*f)` makes f a pointer; `(int *)` is the parameter list and `int` the return type, so f points to a function taking `int*` and returning `int`.

questions.text: An Abstract Data Type (ADT) is:

options.t: a data type that cannot be instantiated
a data type for which only the operations defined on it can be used, but none else

questions.subject: pds
questions.solution: An ADT is defined by its interface: values can be manipulated only through the operations defined on it; it is not the same as an abstract class and can be instantiated.

questions.text: A common property of logic programming languages and functional languages is:
questions.subject: ga
questions.solution: Both paradigms specify what to compute rather than how; only functional languages are based on λ-calculus and only logic languages use Horn clauses.

questions.text:
Which one of the following are essential features of an object-oriented programming language?

(i) Abstraction and encapsulation

(ii) Strictly-typedness

(iii) Type-safe property coupled with sub-type rule

(iv) Polymorphism in the presence of inheritance
questions.subject: pds
questions.solution: Abstraction/encapsulation and polymorphism with inheritance are essential to OOP; strict typing and type-safe subtyping are not required (e.g. Smalltalk, Python are dynamically typed).

questions.text: A program P reads in 500 integers in the range [0, 100] representing the scores of 500 students. It then prints the frequency of each score above 50. What would be the best way for P to store the frequencies?

options.t: A dynamically allocated array of 550 numbers

questions.subject: pds
questions.solution: Only scores 51..100 need counts, i.e. 50 distinct values, so an array of 50 counters suffices.

questions.text: An undirected graph G has n nodes. Its adjacency matrix is given by an n × n square matrix whose (i) diagonal elements are 0's, and (ii) non-diagonal elements are 1's. Which one of the following is TRUE?

options.t: Graph C has no minimum spanning tree (MST)
Graph G has a unique MST of cost n-1
Graph G has multiple distinct MSTs, each of cost n-1
Graph G has multiple spanning trees of different costs

questions.subject: algo
questions.solution: G is $K_n$ with all edge weights 1; every spanning tree has n-1 edges and cost n-1, and there are $n^{n-2}$ of them (multiple, for n > 2).

questions.text: The time complexity of computing the transitive closure of a binary relation on a set of n elements is known to be:
questions.subject: algo
questions.solution: Warshall's algorithm computes the transitive closure with three nested loops over n elements: $O(n^3)$.

questions.text:
Let A, B and C be non-empty sets and let

X = (A - B) - C and Y = (A - C) - (B - C)

Which one of the following is TRUE?
questions.subject: dm
questions.solution: $X = A\cap B'\cap C'$; $Y = A\cap C'\cap(B\cap C')' = A\cap C'\cap(B'\cup C) = A\cap B'\cap C'$, so X = Y.

questions.text:
The following is the Hasse diagram of the poset [{a, b, c, d, e}, ≤]

![](fig/cse-2005/cs-9-1.png)

The poset is:

options.t: a lattice but not a distributive lattice
a distributive lattice but not a Boolean algebra

figures.alt: Hasse diagram with five elements: a at the top, e at the bottom, and b, c, d in the middle level; each of b, c, d is connected upward to a and downward to e (diamond lattice M3).

questions.subject: dm
questions.solution: This is the diamond lattice $M_3$: every pair has a lub and glb, but c has two complements (b and d), so it is not distributive.
questions.reviewNote: Printed poset set reads '{a, & c, ci, e}' (typo in the reprint); transcribed as {a, b, c, d, e} from the diagram.

questions.text: Let G be a simple connected planar graph with 13 vertices and 19 edges. Then, the number of faces in the planar embedding of the graph is:
questions.subject: dm
questions.solution: Euler's formula: $f = e - v + 2 = 19 - 13 + 2 = 8$.

questions.text: Let G be a simple graph with 20 vertices and 100 edges. The size of the minimum vertex cover of G is 8. Then, the size of the maximum independent set of G is:
questions.subject: dm
questions.solution: The complement of a minimum vertex cover is a maximum independent set: $20 - 8 = 12$.

questions.text: Let f(x) be the continuous probability density function of a random variable X. The probability that $a < X \le b$, is:
questions.subject: prob
questions.solution: For a continuous random variable, $P(a < X \le b) = \int_a^b f(x)dx$.

questions.text: The set {1, 2, 4, 7, 8, 11, 13, 14} is a group under multiplication modulo 15. The inverses of 4 and 7 are respectively:
questions.subject: dm
questions.solution: $4\times4 = 16 \equiv 1$ and $7\times13 = 91 \equiv 1 \pmod{15}$.

questions.text: The grammar $A \rightarrow A\,A \mid (A) \mid \varepsilon$ is not suitable for predictive-parsing because the grammar is:
questions.subject: cd
questions.solution: The production $A \to AA$ is left-recursive, which a predictive (top-down) parser cannot handle; the grammar is also ambiguous, so both (a) and (b) are true statements.
questions.reviewNote: Grammar is both left-recursive and ambiguous; commonly accepted key is (b) left-recursive, but (a) is also defensible.

questions.text:
Consider the following circuit.

![](fig/cse-2005/cs-15-1.png)

Which one of the following is TRUE?

options.t: None of X, Y, Z is redundant

figures.alt: Three-gate circuit: a 2-input NAND gate with inputs X and complemented Y (bubble on its lower input); a 2-input AND gate with inputs Y and Z; the outputs of the NAND and the AND feed a 2-input NAND gate whose output is f.

questions.subject: dl
questions.solution: Top NAND gives $(X\overline{Y})'= \overline{X}+Y$; AND gives YZ; output $f = ((\overline{X}+Y)YZ)' = (YZ)'$, independent of X.

questions.text: The range of integers that can be represented by an n bit 2's complement number system is:
questions.subject: dl
questions.solution: n-bit 2's complement represents $-2^{n-1}$ through $2^{n-1}-1$.

questions.text: The hexadecimal representation of $657_8$ is:
questions.subject: dl

questions.text: The switching expression corresponding to $f(A,B,C,D) = \Sigma(1, 4, 5, 9, 11, 12)$ is:
questions.subject: dl
questions.solution: $BC'D'$ covers 4, 12; $A'C'D$ covers 1, 5; $AB'D$ covers 9, 11 — exactly the given minterms.

questions.text: Which one of the following is true for a CPU having a single interrupt request line and a single interrupt grant line?

options.t: Neither vectored interrupt nor multiple interrupting devices are possible
Vectored interrupts are not possible but multiple interrupting devices are possible
Vectored interrupts and multiple interrupting devices are both possible
Vectored interrupt is possible but multiple interrupting devices are not possible

questions.subject: coa
questions.solution: With daisy chaining, many devices share the single request/grant pair, and the device that receives the grant places its vector on the data bus, so both are possible.

questions.text: Normally user programs are prevented from handling I/O directly by I/O instructions in them. For CPUs having explicit I/O instructions, such I/O protection is ensured by having the I/O instructions privileged. In a CPU with memory mapped I/O, there is no explicit I/O instruction. Which one of the following is true for a CPU with memory mapped I/O?

options.t: I/O protection is ensured by operating system routine(s)
I/O protection is ensured by a hardware trap
I/O protection is ensured during system configuration

questions.subject: coa
questions.solution: With memory-mapped I/O, device registers are memory addresses; the OS protects them by not mapping those addresses into user address spaces (memory management set up by OS routines).

questions.text: What is the swap space in the disk used for?
questions.subject: os
questions.solution: Swap space holds pages/process images (process data) swapped out of main memory.

questions.text: Increasing the RAM of a computer typically improves performance because
questions.subject: os
questions.solution: More physical frames hold more of each process's working set, reducing page faults.

questions.text: Packets of the same session may be routed through different paths in:
questions.subject: cn
questions.solution: Routing is done per packet at the IP layer, independent of the transport protocol, so both TCP and UDP packets may take different paths.

questions.text: The address resolution protocol (ARP) is used for:

options.t: Finding the IP address from the DNS
Finding the IP address of the default gateway
Finding the IP address that corresponds to a MAC address
Finding the MAC address that corresponds to an IP address

questions.subject: cn
questions.solution: ARP maps a known IP address to the corresponding MAC (hardware) address on the local network.

questions.text: The maximum window size for data transmission using the selective reject protocol with n-bit frame sequence numbers is:
questions.subject: cn
questions.solution: For selective repeat, sender and receiver windows must not overlap: window ≤ half the sequence space, $2^{n-1}$.

questions.text: In a network of LANs connected by bridges, packets are sent from one LAN to another through intermediate bridges. Since more than one path may exist between two LANs, packets may have to be routed through multiple bridges. Why is the spanning tree algorithm used for bridge-routing?

options.t: For shortest path routing between LANs
For avoiding loops in the routing paths

questions.subject: cn
questions.solution: The spanning tree disables redundant bridge links so frames do not circulate forever in loops.

questions.text: An organization has a class B network and wishes to form subnets for 64 departments. The subnet mask would be:
questions.subject: cn
questions.solution: 64 subnets need 6 subnet bits borrowed from the 16 host bits: mask /22 = 255.255.252.0.

questions.text: Which one of the following is a key factor for preferring $B^+$-trees to binary search trees for indexing database relations?

options.t: Database relations have a large number of records
Database relations are sorted on the primary key
$B^+$-trees require less memory than binary search trees
Data transfer from disks is in blocks

questions.subject: db
questions.solution: A $B^+$-tree node fills a disk block with many keys, giving high fan-out and few block accesses; this matters because disk I/O happens in blocks.

questions.text: Which one of the following statements about normal forms is FALSE?

options.t: Lossless, dependency-preserving decomposition into 3NF is always possible
Lossless, dependency-preserving decomposition into BCNF is always possible
Any relation with two attributes is in BCNF

questions.subject: db
questions.solution: A lossless BCNF decomposition always exists but may not preserve dependencies (e.g. R(A,B,C), AB→C, C→B).

questions.text: Let r be a relation instance with scheme R = (A, B, C, D). We define $r_1 = \Pi_{A,B,C}(r)$ and $r_2 = \Pi_{A,D}(r)$. Let $s = r_1 * r_2$ where * denotes natural join. Given that the decomposition for r into $r_1$ and $r_2$ is lossy, which one of the following is True?
questions.subject: db
questions.solution: Joining projections always contains every original tuple; a lossy decomposition adds spurious tuples, so r is a proper subset of s.

questions.subject: pds
questions.solution: Digits are printed after the recursive call returns, so they appear most-significant first: 2,0,4,8; sum is passed by value so main prints 0.

options.t: some compiler-warnings not leading to unintended results
some compiler-warnings due to type-mismatch eventually leading to unintended results

questions.subject: pds
questions.solution: Without the prototype, foo is implicitly declared as returning int at the call; the later definition returning double conflicts with it, giving a 'conflicting types' compile error.

questions.text:
Postorder traversal of a given binary search tree, T produces the following sequence of keys

10, 9, 23, 22, 27, 25, 15, 50, 95, 60, 40, 29

Which one of the following sequences of keys can be the result of an inorder traversal of the tree T?
questions.subject: pds
questions.solution: The inorder traversal of any BST lists its keys in sorted order.

questions.text:
A Priority-Queue is implemented as a Max-Heap. Initially, it has 5 elements. The level-order traversal of the heap is given below:

10, 8, 5, 3, 2

Two new elements '1' and '7' are inserted in the heap in that order. The level-order traversal of the heap after the insertion of the elements is:
questions.subject: pds
questions.solution: Inserting 1 gives 10,8,5,3,2,1; 7 is placed as right child of 5 and swaps with it: 10,8,7,3,2,1,5.

questions.text: How many distinct binary search trees can be created out of 4 distinct keys?
questions.subject: pds
questions.solution: The number of BSTs on n keys is the Catalan number $C_4 = \frac{1}{5}\binom{8}{4} = 14$.

questions.text: In a complete k-ary tree, every internal node has exactly k children. The number of leaves in such a tree with n internal nodes is:
questions.subject: pds
questions.solution: Total nodes $= nk+1$ (every node except the root is a child); leaves $= nk+1-n = n(k-1)+1$.

questions.text:
Suppose $T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n$, $T(0) = T(1) = 1$

Which one of the following is FALSE?
questions.subject: algo
questions.solution: By the master theorem $T(n)=\Theta(n\log n)$, which is $O(n^2)$ but not $\Omega(n^2)$.

questions.text: Let G(V, E) be an undirected graph with positive edge weights. Dijkstra's single source shortest path algorithm can be implemented using the binary heap data structure with time complexity:
questions.subject: algo
questions.solution: With a binary heap, |V| extract-min and up to |E| decrease-key operations each cost $O(\log|V|)$.

questions.text: Suppose there are $\lceil \log n \rceil$ sorted lists of $\lfloor n/\log n \rfloor$ elements each. The time complexity of producing a sorted list of all these elements is: (Hint: Use a heap data structure)
questions.subject: algo
questions.solution: k-way merge with a min-heap of $k=\log n$ list heads costs $O(\log k)=O(\log\log n)$ per element, $O(n\log\log n)$ in total.

questions.text: Let P, Q and R be three atomic propositional assertions. Let X denote $(P \vee Q) \rightarrow R$ and Y denote $(P \rightarrow R) \vee (Q \rightarrow R)$. Which one of the following is a tautology?
questions.subject: dm
questions.solution:
$X \equiv (
eg P\wedge
eg Q)\vee R$ and $Y \equiv 
eg P\vee
eg Q\vee R$; X is stronger than Y, so $Xightarrow Y$ is a tautology.
questions.reviewNote: The reprint prints 'Let K denote (P ∨ Q) → R' — typo for X; transcribed as X.

questions.text:
What is the first order predicate calculus statement equivalent to the following?

Every teacher is liked by some student
questions.subject: dm
questions.solution: For each teacher x there exists a y that is a student and likes x: ∀x [teacher(x) → ∃y (student(y) ∧ likes(y,x))].

questions.text: Let R and S be any two equivalence relations on a non-empty set A. Which one of the following statements is TRUE?

options.t: $R \cup S$, $R \cap S$ are both equivalence relations
Neither $R \cup S$ nor $R \cap S$ is an equivalence relation

questions.subject: dm
questions.solution: Reflexivity, symmetry and transitivity are preserved under intersection; the union may fail transitivity.

questions.text: Let $f: B \rightarrow C$ and $g: A \rightarrow B$ be two functions and let $h = f \circ g$. Given that h is an onto function which one of the following is TRUE?

options.t: f and g should both be onto functions
f should be onto but g need not be onto
g should be onto but f need not be onto
both f and g need not be onto

questions.subject: dm
questions.solution: Every c ∈ C equals f(g(a)) for some a, so f is onto; g need not be (e.g. B may have extra elements).
questions.reviewNote: Reprint prints '&' for g in options (a) and (d); transcribed as g.

questions.text:
What is the minimum number of ordered pairs of non-negative numbers that should be chosen to ensure that there are two pairs (a, b) and (c, d) in the chosen set such that

$a \equiv c \bmod 3$ and $b \equiv d \bmod 5$
questions.subject: dm
questions.solution: There are $3\times5=15$ residue classes for (a mod 3, b mod 5); by pigeonhole 16 pairs guarantee a repeat.

questions.text: Consider three decision problems $P_1$, $P_2$ and $P_3$. It is known that $P_1$ is decidable and $P_2$ is undecidable. Which one of the following is TRUE?

options.t: $P_3$ is decidable if $P_1$ is reducible to $P_3$
$P_3$ is undecidable if $P_3$ is reducible to $P_2$
$P_3$ is undecidable if $P_2$ is reducible to $P_3$
$P_3$ is decidable if $P_3$ is reducible to $P_2$'s complement

questions.subject: toc
questions.solution: If undecidable $P_2$ reduces to $P_3$, a decider for $P_3$ would decide $P_2$; hence $P_3$ is undecidable.

questions.text:
Consider the set H of all 3 × 3 matrices of the type

$$\begin{bmatrix} a & f & e \\ 0 & b & d \\ 0 & 0 & c \end{bmatrix}$$

where a, b, c, d, e and f are real numbers and $abc \ne 0$. Under the matrix multiplication operation, the set H is:

options.t: a monoid but not a group
a semigroup but not a monoid
neither a group nor a semigroup

questions.subject: dm
questions.solution: Invertible upper-triangular matrices are closed under multiplication, contain the identity, and their inverses are upper triangular with nonzero diagonal.

questions.text:
Which one of the following graphs is NOT planar?

G1: ![](fig/cse-2005/cs-47-1.png)

G2: ![](fig/cse-2005/cs-47-2.png)

G3: ![](fig/cse-2005/cs-47-3.png)

G4: ![](fig/cse-2005/cs-47-4.png)

figures.alt: Six vertices on a hexagon (top-left, top-right, right, bottom-right, bottom-left, left) with the six hexagon edges, plus an arc joining left and right vertices, and two crossing chords top-left–bottom-right and top-right–bottom-left; 3-regular graph isomorphic to K3,3.

Six vertices on a hexagon (top, upper-right, lower-right, bottom, lower-left, upper-left) with hexagon edges plus chords: upper-left–upper-right (horizontal), lower-left–lower-right (horizontal), top–bottom (vertical), top–lower-left, upper-right–bottom.

Five vertices as a pentagon (top, upper-right, lower-right, lower-left, upper-left) with pentagon edges, plus chords upper-left–upper-right (horizontal), upper-left–lower-right and upper-right–lower-left (crossing).

Five vertices as a pentagon with all pentagon edges and chords top–lower-left, top–lower-right, upper-left–lower-right, upper-right–lower-left (four of the five pentagram chords; upper-left–upper-right chord absent), i.e. K5 minus one edge.

questions.subject: dm
questions.solution: G1 is 3-regular on 6 vertices and bipartite (hexagon plus the three 'opposite' chords) — it is $K_{3,3}$, hence non-planar; the others can be redrawn without crossings.

questions.text:
Consider the following system of equations in three real variables $x_1$, $x_2$ and $x_3$:

$$2x_1 - x_2 + 3x_3 = 1$$
$$3x_1 + 2x_2 + 5x_3 = 2$$
$$-x_1 + 4x_2 + x_3 = 3$$

This system of equations has

options.t: more than one but a finite number of solutions

questions.subject: la
questions.solution: The coefficient determinant is $2(2-20)+1(3+5)+3(12+2) = 14 \ne 0$, so the solution is unique.
questions.reviewNote: Reprint prints the first equation as '2x1 − x2 = 3x3 = 1' (typo); transcribed as 2x1 − x2 + 3x3 = 1 per the original paper.

questions.text:
What are the eigenvalues of the following 2 × 2 matrix?

$$\begin{bmatrix} 2 & -1 \\ -4 & 5 \end{bmatrix}$$
questions.subject: la
questions.solution: Trace 7, determinant 10-4=6: $\lambda^2-7\lambda+6=0$ gives 1 and 6.

questions.text: Let $G(x) = 1/(1-x)^2 = \sum_{i=0}^{\infty} g(i)x^i$, where $|x| < 1$. What is g(i)?
questions.subject: dm
questions.solution: Differentiating $\frac{1}{1-x}=\sum x^i$ gives $\frac{1}{(1-x)^2}=\sum (i+1)x^i$, so $g(i)=i+1$ (option c in this reprint).
questions.reviewNote: The reprint prints five options (a–e); options a and b are illegible single characters (original paper's options are i, i+1, 2i, 2^i). Answer letter C refers to this reprint's labelling ('i+1'); it is B in the original paper.

questions.text: Box P has 2 red balls and 3 blue balls and box Q has 3 red balls and 1 blue ball. A ball is selected as follows: (i) select a box (ii) choose a ball from the selected box such that each ball in the box is equally likely to be chosen. The probabilities of selecting boxes P and Q are 1/3 and 2/3, respectively. Given that a ball selected in the above process is a red ball, the probability that it came from the box P is:
questions.subject: prob

questions.text: A random bit string of length n is constructed by tossing a fair coin n times and setting a bit to 0 or 1 depending on outcomes head and tail, respectively. The probability that two such randomly generated strings are not identical is:
questions.subject: prob
questions.solution: The second string equals the first with probability $1/2^n$; so they differ with probability $1-1/2^n$.

questions.text:
Consider the machine M:

![](fig/cse-2005/cs-53-1.png)

The language recognized by M is:

options.t: $\{w \in \{a,b\}^* \mid$ every a in w is followed by exactly two b's$\}$
$\{w \in \{a,b\}^* \mid$ every a in w is followed by at least two b's$\}$
$\{w \in \{a,b\}^* \mid$ w does not contain 'aa' as a substring$\}$

figures.alt: DFA with five states: start state q0 (non-final) with self-loop on b; q0 --a--> q1; q1 --b--> q2; q2 --b--> q3 (final, double circle) with self-loop on b; q3 --a--> q1 (curved arc on top); q1 --a--> dead state and q2 --a--> dead state (bottom); dead state has self-loop on a,b. Transition labels are barely legible in this reprint.

questions.subject: toc
questions.solution: From the start state (loop on b), a leads to q1; two b's are needed to reach the final state (loop on b, a returns to q1); an a before two b's goes to the dead state. So every a is followed by at least two b's (strings with at least one a, since the start state is non-final).
questions.reviewNote: Edge labels in the figure are illegible in the reprint; figure structure taken from the original paper (GATE Overflow). Start state is non-final, so strictly the language is option (b) restricted to strings containing at least one a.

questions.text: Let $N_f$ and $N_p$ denote the classes of languages accepted by non-deterministic finite automata and non-deterministic push-down automata, respectively. Let $D_f$ and $D_p$ denote the classes of languages accepted by deterministic finite automata and deterministic push-down automata, respectively. Which one of the following is TRUE?
questions.subject: toc
questions.solution: Subset construction shows DFAs = NFAs in power; DPDAs accept only the deterministic CFLs, a proper subset (e.g. $ww^R$).

questions.text:
Consider the languages

$L_1 = \{a^n b^n c^m \mid n, m > 0\}$ and $L_2 = \{a^n b^m c^m \mid n, m > 0\}$. Which one of the following statements is FALSE?

options.t: $L_1 \cap L_2$ is a context sensitive language

questions.subject: toc
questions.solution: $L_1\cap L_2 = \{a^nb^nc^n\}$, which is context-sensitive but not context-free.

questions.text: Let $L_1$ be a recursive language, and let $L_2$ be a recursively enumerable but not recursive language. Which one of the following is TRUE?

options.t: $\overline{L_1}$ is recursive and $\overline{L_2}$ is recursively enumerable
$\overline{L_1}$ is recursive and $\overline{L_2}$ is not recursively enumerable
$\overline{L_1}$ is recursively enumerable and $\overline{L_2}$ is recursive

questions.subject: toc
questions.solution: Recursive languages are closed under complement; if both $L_2$ and its complement were RE, $L_2$ would be recursive.

questions.text:
Consider the languages:

$L_1 = \{ww^R \mid w \in \{0,1\}^*\}$

$L_2 = \{w\#w^R \mid w \in \{0,1\}^*\}$, where # is a special symbol

$L_3 = \{ww \mid w \in \{0,1\}^*\}$

Which one of the following is TRUE?

options.t: $L_3$ is a CFL, but not a deterministic CFL

questions.subject: toc
questions.solution: The marker # tells a DPDA when to switch from pushing to popping, so $L_2$ is a DCFL; $L_1$ is a non-deterministic CFL and $L_3$ is not context-free.

questions.text:
Consider the following two problems on undirected graphs:

α: Given G(V, E), does G have an independent set of size |V| - 4?

β: Given G(V, E), does G have an independent set of size 5?

Which one of the following is TRUE?

options.t: α is in P and β is NP-complete
α is NP-complete and β is in P
Both α and β are NP-complete
Both α and β are in P

questions.subject: algo
questions.solution: β can be checked over all $\binom{|V|}{5}$ subsets; α is equivalent to a vertex cover of size 4, checkable over $\binom{|V|}{4}$ subsets — both polynomial.

questions.text:
Consider the grammar:

$E \rightarrow E + n \mid E \times n \mid n$

For a sentence $n + n \times n$, the handles in the right-sentential form of the reduction are:

options.t: n, E + n and E + n × n
n, E + n and E + E × n
n, n + n and n + n × n
n, E + n and E × n

questions.subject: cd
questions.solution: Rightmost derivation reversed: n+n×n ⇒ reduce n to E, then E+n to E, then E×n to E; handles n, E+n, E×n.

questions.text:
Consider the grammar:

$S \rightarrow (S) \mid a$

Let the number of states in SLR(1), LR(1) and LALR(1) parsers for the grammar be $n_1$, $n_2$ and $n_3$ respectively. The following relationship holds good:
questions.subject: cd
questions.solution: SLR and LALR both use the LR(0) item sets (6 states); canonical LR(1) splits states inside parentheses by lookahead ')' vs '$' (10 states).
questions.reviewNote: Option (d) is illegible in the reprint (prints 'n1 = n2 = n3', duplicating c); transcribed per the original paper as n1 ≥ n3 ≥ n2.

questions.text:
Consider line number 3 of the following C-program.

```c
int main() {                  /* Line 1 */
  int I, N;                   /* Line 2 */
  fro (I=0, I<N, I++);        /* Line 3 */
}
```

Identify the compiler's response about this line while creating the object-module:
questions.subject: cd
questions.solution: 'fro' is a valid identifier, so no lexical error; per the official key the misspelt for-statement is reported as a syntax error (in C89 it could also parse as a call to an undeclared function, deferring the error to the linker).
questions.reviewNote: Disputed question: in C the line parses as a call to an undeclared function fro(), so strictly no compile error arises; key commonly given as (c).

questions.text:
Consider the following circuit involving a positive edge triggered D FF.

![](fig/cse-2005/cs-62-1.png)

Consider the following timing diagram. Let $A_i$ represent the logic level on the line A in the i-th clock period.

![](fig/cse-2005/cs-62-2.png)

Let $A'$ represent the complement of A. The correct output sequence on Y over the clock periods 1 through 5 is:

figures.alt: Inputs A and X feed a 2-input AND gate; X is also inverted (NOT gate) and ANDed with the flip-flop's Q' output (fed back from the D flip-flop). The two AND outputs go to an OR gate whose output drives D of a positive-edge-triggered D flip-flop clocked by Clk; its Q output is Y.
Clock waveform with six periods numbered 0 to 5 (each starting at a rising edge); X is high during periods 0 and 1, low during period 2, high during periods 3 and 4, and low during period 5.

questions.subject: dl
questions.solution: $D = AX + X'Q'$. Y in period i is D sampled in period i-1: X=1 in periods 0,1,3,4 gives $A_0, A_1, A_3, A_4$; X=0 in period 2 gives $Q' = A_1'$ in period 3.

questions.text:
The following diagram represents a finite state machine which takes as input a binary number from the least significant bit.

![](fig/cse-2005/cs-63-1.png)

Which one of the following is TRUE?

options.t: It computes 1's complement of the input number
It computes 2's complement of the input number

figures.alt: Mealy machine with two states: start state Q0 with self-loop labelled 0/0; transition Q0 to Q1 labelled 1/1; state Q1 with self-loops labelled 0/1 and 1/0.

questions.subject: dl
questions.solution: Bits are copied up to and including the first 1 (Q0: 0/0, 1/1), after which every bit is inverted (Q1: 0/1, 1/0) — the 2's complement rule.

questions.text:
Consider the following circuit:

![](fig/cse-2005/cs-64-1.png)

The flip-flops are positive edge triggered D FFs. Each state is designated as a two bit string $Q_0Q_1$. Let the initial state be 00. The state transition sequence is:

figures.alt: Two positive-edge-triggered D flip-flops sharing clk. The first flip-flop's Q0' output is fed back to its own D0 input. An XOR gate takes Q0 and Q1' (fed back from the second flip-flop) and drives D1 of the second flip-flop, whose outputs are Q1 and Q1'.

questions.subject: dl
questions.reviewNote: Options are drawn as state sequences with a return arrow to 00; transcribed as text.

questions.text:
Consider a three word machine instruction

ADD A[R0], @B

The first operand (destination) "A[R0]" uses indexed addressing mode with R0 as the index register. The second operand (source) "@B" uses indirect addressing mode. A and B are memory addresses residing at the second and the third words, respectively. The first word of the instruction specifies the opcode, the index register designation and the source and destination addressing modes. During execution of ADD instruction, the two operands are added and stored in the destination (first operand).

The number of memory cycles needed during the execution cycle of the instruction is:
questions.subject: coa
questions.solution: Execution needs: read operand at A+[R0], read pointer at B, read the source operand it points to, and write the result — 4 memory cycles.

questions.text:
Match each of the high level language statements given on the left hand side with the most natural addressing mode from those listed on the right hand side.

| Statement | Addressing mode |
|---|---|
| 1. `A[I] = B[J];` | (a) Indirect addressing |
| 2. `while (*A++);` | (b) Indexed addressing |
| 3. `int temp = *x;` | (c) Autoincrement |
questions.subject: coa
questions.solution: Array subscripting uses indexed mode, pointer post-increment uses autoincrement, and dereferencing a pointer uses indirect mode.

questions.text: Consider a direct mapped cache of size 32 KB with block size 32 bytes. The CPU generates 32 bit addresses. The number of bits needed for cache indexing and the number of tag bits are respectively:
questions.subject: coa
questions.solution: 32 KB/32 B = 1024 lines → 10 index bits; offset 5 bits; tag = 32 − 10 − 5 = 17.

questions.text:
A 5 stage pipelined CPU has the following sequence of stages:

IF - Instruction fetch from instruction memory,

RD - Instruction decode and register read,

EX - Execute: ALU operation for data and address computation,

MA - Data memory access — for write access, the register read at RD stage is used,

WB - Register write back.

Consider the following sequence of instructions:

$I_1$: L R0, loc1; R0 <= M[loc1]

$I_2$: A R0, R0; R0 <= R0 + R0

$I_3$: S R2, R0; R2 <= R2 - R0

Let each stage take one clock cycle.

What is the number of clock cycles taken to complete the above sequence of instructions starting from the fetch of $I_1$?
questions.subject: coa
questions.solution: With operand forwarding: I1 IF-RD-EX-MA-WB in cycles 1–5; I2 needs the loaded value, so its EX waits until cycle 5 (one stall) and it completes in cycle 7; I3 gets R0 forwarded from I2's EX and finishes WB in cycle 8.
questions.reviewNote: Answer assumes operand forwarding (not stated in the question); without forwarding the count differs.

questions.text: A device with data transfer rate 10 KB/sec is connected to a CPU. Data is transferred byte-wise. Let the interrupt overhead be 4 μsec. The byte transfer time between the device interface register and CPU or memory is negligible. What is the minimum performance gain of operating the device under interrupt mode over operating it under program controlled mode?
questions.subject: coa
questions.solution: Programmed I/O busy-waits ≈100 μs per byte (1/10 KB/s); interrupt mode costs only the 4 μs overhead per byte: gain ≈ 100/4 = 25.

questions.text:
Consider a disk drive with the following specifications:

16 surfaces, 512 tracks/surface, 512 sectors/track, 1 KB/sector, rotation speed 3000 rpm. The disk is operated in cycle stealing mode whereby whenever one 4 byte word is ready it is sent to memory; similarly, for writing, the disk interface reads a 4 byte word from the memory in each DMA cycle. Memory cycle time is 40 nsec. The maximum percentage of time that the CPU gets blocked during DMA operation is:
questions.subject: coa
questions.solution: One track (512 KB) passes in 20 ms, so a 4-byte word is ready every 20 ms/131072 ≈ 152.6 ns; the CPU is blocked 40/152.6 ≈ 26% ≈ 25%.

questions.text: Suppose n processes, $P_1, \ldots, P_n$ share m identical resource units, which can be reserved and released one at a time. The maximum resource requirement of process $P_i$ is $s_i$, where $s_i > 0$. Which one of the following is a sufficient condition for ensuring that deadlock does not occur?
questions.subject: os
questions.solution: Deadlock requires all m units allocated with every process still waiting, i.e. each holds at most $s_i-1$: $\sum(s_i-1) \ge m$. So $\sum s_i < m+n$ guarantees some process can always finish.
questions.reviewNote: Options (a) and (b) are printed identically ('∀i, s_i < m') in the reprint; the original paper's (b) is ∀i, s_i < n.

questions.subject: os
questions.solution: Child (fork returns 0) prints a+5, parent prints a−5, so x = u + 10; the child's address space is a copy, so &a (a virtual address) is the same: v = y.

questions.text: In a packet switching network, packets are routed from source to destination along a single path having two intermediate nodes. If the message size is 24 bytes and each packet contains a header of 3 bytes, then the optimum packet size is:
questions.subject: cn
questions.solution: With 3 hops and payload p per packet, time ∝ (24/p + 2)(p + 3): packet size 9 (p = 6) gives 6×9 = 54, versus 8×7 = 56 for size 7, 10×6 = 60 for size 6 and 26×4 = 104 for size 4.

questions.text: Suppose the round trip propagation delay for a 10 Mbps Ethernet having 48-bit jamming signal is 46.4 μs. The minimum frame size is:
questions.subject: cn
questions.solution: Bits sent during the round trip: 10 Mbps × 46.4 μs = 464 bits; adding the 48-bit jam signal gives 512 bits.
questions.reviewNote: Reprint prints '46.4 its' (μs). Key is disputed: 464 (ignoring jam) vs 512 (commonly accepted).

questions.text: Let $E_1$ and $E_2$ be two entities in an E/R diagram with simple single-valued attributes. $R_1$ and $R_2$ are two relationships between $E_1$ and $E_2$, where $R_1$ is one-to-many and $R_2$ is many-to-many. $R_1$ and $R_2$ do not have any attributes of their own. What is the minimum number of tables required to represent this situation in the relational model?
questions.subject: db
questions.solution: One table each for $E_1$ and $E_2$ (the one-to-many $R_1$ becomes a foreign key on the many side) plus one table for the many-to-many $R_2$: 3.

questions.text:
The following table has two attributes A and C where A is the primary key and C is the foreign key referencing A with on-delete cascade.

| A | C |
|---|---|
| 2 | 4 |
| 3 | 4 |
| 4 | 3 |
| 5 | 2 |
| 7 | 2 |
| 9 | 5 |
| 6 | 4 |

The set of all tuples that must be additionally deleted to preserve referential integrity when the tuple (2,4) is deleted is:
questions.subject: db
questions.solution: Deleting A=2 cascades to tuples with C=2: (5,2), (7,2); deleting A=5 cascades to (9,5); nothing references 7 or 9.

questions.text:
The relation book(title, price) contains the titles and prices of different books. Assuming that no two books have the same price, what does the following SQL query list?

```sql
select title
from book as B
where (select count(*)
       from book as T
       where T.price > B.price) < 5
```

options.t: Titles of the four most expensive books
Title of the fifth most inexpensive book
Title of the fifth most expensive book
Titles of the five most expensive books

questions.subject: db
questions.solution: A book qualifies if fewer than 5 books cost more, i.e. it is among the 5 most expensive.
questions.reviewNote: Reprint prints the relation name as 'hook'; transcribed as book.

questions.text: Consider a relation scheme R = (A, B, C, D, E, H) on which the following functional dependencies hold: {A→B, BC→D, E→C, D→A}. What are the candidate keys of R?
questions.subject: db
questions.solution: E and H appear on no right-hand side, so every key contains EH; $(EH)^+ = \{E,H,C\}$, and adding A, B or D gives the whole relation: AEH, BEH, DEH.
questions.reviewNote: Reprint prints the FD set as '(A→B, BC→D, E→C C, D→A }' and option (c) as 'AEH, BEE, BCH'; typos normalised.

questions.text:
Consider the following data path of a CPU

![](fig/cse-2005/cs-79-80-1.png)

The ALU, the bus and all the registers in the data path are of identical size. All operations including incrementation of the PC and the GPRs are to be carried out in the ALU. Two clock cycles are needed for memory read operation — the first one for loading address in the MAR and the next one for loading data from the memory bus into the MDR.

The instruction "add R0, R1" has the register transfer interpretation R0 <= R0 + R1. The minimum number of clock cycles needed for execution cycle of this instruction is

figures.alt: Single internal bus connecting MAR, MDR, IR, PC, the GPR file, and two ALU input registers S and T; the ALU takes S and T as inputs and its output is fed back onto the bus.

questions.subject: coa
questions.solution: Single bus: R0→S, R1→T, then ALU output (S+T)→R0 — three bus transfers, 3 cycles.

questions.text:
Consider the following data path of a CPU

![](fig/cse-2005/cs-79-80-1.png)

The ALU, the bus and all the registers in the data path are of identical size. All operations including incrementation of the PC and the GPRs are to be carried out in the ALU. Two clock cycles are needed for memory read operation — the first one for loading address in the MAR and the next one for loading data from the memory bus into the MDR.

The instruction "call Rn, sub" is a two word instruction. Assuming that PC is incremented during the fetch cycle of the first word of the instruction, its register transfer interpretation is

Rn <= PC + 1;

PC <= M[PC];

The minimum number of CPU clock cycles needed during the execution cycle of this instruction is:

figures.alt: Single internal bus connecting MAR, MDR, IR, PC, the GPR file, and two ALU input registers S and T; the ALU takes S and T as inputs and its output is fed back onto the bus.

questions.subject: coa
questions.solution: Cycle 1: PC→MAR and PC→S together (same bus value); cycle 2: memory→MDR while the ALU puts S+1 on the bus into Rn; cycle 3: MDR→PC — 3 cycles.
questions.reviewNote: Answer depends on overlap assumptions (3 with PC→MAR/S in one cycle and the ALU increment overlapped with the memory read; 4 or 5 otherwise); keys differ.

questions.subject: algo
questions.solution: The recursion depth is at most n (foo(n) calls foo(n−1) …), each frame O(1): O(n).

questions.subject: algo
questions.solution: Storing n values plus O(n) recursion depth: O(n) space.

questions.text:
Let s and t be two vertices in an undirected graph G = (V, E) having distinct positive edge weights. Let [X, Y] be a partition of V such that s ∈ X and t ∈ Y. Consider the edge e having the minimum weight amongst all those edges that have one vertex in X and one vertex in Y.

(a) The edge e must definitely belong to:

options.t: the minimum weighted spanning tree of G
the weighted shortest path from s to t
each path from s to t
the weighted longest path from s to t

questions.subject: algo
questions.solution: By the cut property, the unique minimum-weight edge crossing the cut (X, Y) belongs to the (unique) minimum spanning tree.
questions.reviewNote: Reprint prints five options with (a) blank and (b) 'the minimum weighted spanning tree of C' (G); answer letter B refers to this reprint's labelling (it is A in the original paper). Statement typos ('x and r', 'G = (V, S)', '[X, 19') normalised to s, t, G = (V, E), [X, Y].

questions.text:
Let s and t be two vertices in an undirected graph G = (V, E) having distinct positive edge weights. Let [X, Y] be a partition of V such that s ∈ X and t ∈ Y. Consider the edge e having the minimum weight amongst all those edges that have one vertex in X and one vertex in Y.

(b) Let the weight of an edge e denote the congestion on that edge. The congestion on a path is defined to be the maximum of the congestions on the edges of the path. We wish to find the path from s to t having minimum congestion. Which one of the following paths is always such a path of minimum congestion?

options.t: a path from s to t in the minimum weight spanning tree
a weighted shortest path from s to t
an Euler walk from s to t
a Hamiltonian path from s to t

questions.subject: algo
questions.solution: The MST contains a minimum-bottleneck path between every pair of vertices, so its s–t path minimises the maximum edge weight.

questions.text:
Consider the following expression grammar. The semantic rules for expression evaluation are stated next to each grammar production.

| Production | Semantic rule |
|---|---|
| $E \rightarrow$ number | E.val = number.val |
| $\mid E$ '+' $E$ | $E^{(1)}$.val = $E^{(2)}$.val + $E^{(3)}$.val |
| $\mid E$ '×' $E$ | $E^{(1)}$.val = $E^{(2)}$.val × $E^{(3)}$.val |
| ; | |

(a) The above grammar and the semantic rules are fed to a yacc tool (which is an LALR(1) parser generator) for parsing and evaluating arithmetic expressions. Which one of the following is true about the action of yacc for the given grammar?

options.t: It detects recursion and eliminates recursion
It detects reduce-reduce conflict, and resolves
It detects shift-reduce conflict, and resolves the conflict in favor of a shift over a reduce action
It detects shift-reduce conflict, and resolves the conflict in favor of a reduce over a shift action

questions.subject: cd
questions.solution: The ambiguous grammar yields shift-reduce conflicts; by default yacc resolves them in favour of shift.

questions.text:
Consider the following expression grammar. The semantic rules for expression evaluation are stated next to each grammar production.

| Production | Semantic rule |
|---|---|
| $E \rightarrow$ number | E.val = number.val |
| $\mid E$ '+' $E$ | $E^{(1)}$.val = $E^{(2)}$.val + $E^{(3)}$.val |
| $\mid E$ '×' $E$ | $E^{(1)}$.val = $E^{(2)}$.val × $E^{(3)}$.val |
| ; | |

(b) Assume the conflicts in Part (a) of this question are resolved and an LALR(1) parser is generated for parsing arithmetic expressions as per the given grammar. Consider an expression 3 × 2 + 1. What precedence and associativity properties does the generated parser realize?

options.t: Equal precedence and left associativity; expression is evaluated to 7
Equal precedence and right associativity; expression is evaluated to 9
Precedence of '×' is higher than that of '+', and both operators are left associative; expression is evaluated to 7
Precedence of '+' is higher than that of '×', and both operators are left associative; expression is evaluated to 9

questions.subject: cd
questions.solution: Always shifting makes the operators equally precedent and right-associative: 3 × (2 + 1) = 9.
questions.reviewNote: Reprint prints 'does not generated parser realize', '...evaluated to Y' (9) and '...evaluated 107' (to 7); typos normalised.

questions.text:
We are given 9 tasks $T_1, T_2, \ldots, T_9$. The execution of each task requires one unit of time. We can execute one task at a time. Each task $T_i$ has a profit $P_i$ and a deadline $d_i$. Profit $P_i$ is earned if the task is completed before the end of the $d_i^{th}$ unit of time.

| Task | $T_1$ | $T_2$ | $T_3$ | $T_4$ | $T_5$ | $T_6$ | $T_7$ | $T_8$ | $T_9$ |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Profit | 15 | 20 | 30 | 18 | 18 | 10 | 23 | 16 | 25 |
| Deadline | 7 | 2 | 5 | 3 | 4 | 5 | 2 | 7 | 3 |

(a) Are all tasks completed in the schedule that gives maximum profit?
questions.subject: algo
questions.solution: Greedy by profit: T3→slot 5, T9→3, T7→2, T2→1, T4 (deadline 3) no free slot, T5→4, T8→7, T1→6, T6 (deadline 5) no free slot: T4 and T6 are left out.

We are given 9 tasks $T_1, T_2, \ldots, T_9$. The execution of each task requires one unit of time. We can execute one task at a time. Each task $T_i$ has a profit $P_i$ and a deadline $d_i$. Profit $P_i$ is earned if the task is completed before the end of the $d_i^{th}$ unit of time.

| Task | $T_1$ | $T_2$ | $T_3$ | $T_4$ | $T_5$ | $T_6$ | $T_7$ | $T_8$ | $T_9$ |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Profit | 15 | 20 | 30 | 18 | 18 | 10 | 23 | 16 | 25 |
| Deadline | 7 | 2 | 5 | 3 | 4 | 5 | 2 | 7 | 3 |

(b) What is the maximum profit earned?

Consider the following floating point format

![](fig/cse-2005/cs-85-1.png)

Mantissa is a pure fraction in sign-magnitude form.

(a) The decimal number $0.239 \times 2^{13}$ has the following hexadecimal representation (without normalization and rounding off):

figures.alt: 16-bit word: bit 15 sign bit; bits 14 to 8 a 7-bit excess-64 exponent; bits 7 to 0 an 8-bit mantissa.

questions.subject: dl

questions.text:
Consider the following floating point format

![](fig/cse-2005/cs-85-1.png)

Mantissa is a pure fraction in sign-magnitude form.

(b) The normalized representation for the above format is specified as follows. The mantissa has an implicit 1 preceding the binary (radix) point. Assume that only 0's are padded in while shifting a field.

The normalized representation of the above number ($0.239 \times 2^{13}$) is:

figures.alt: 16-bit word: bit 15 sign bit; bits 14 to 8 a 7-bit excess-64 exponent; bits 7 to 0 an 8-bit mantissa.

questions.subject: dl

questions.text: Consider the polynomial $p(x) = a_0 + a_1x + a_2x^2 + a_3x^3$, where $a_i \neq 0,\ \forall i$. The minimum number of multiplications needed to evaluate $p$ on an input $x$ is:
questions.subject: algo
questions.solution: Horner's rule: $a_0 + x(a_1 + x(a_2 + x a_3))$ needs 3 multiplications.

questions.text: Let $X$, $Y$, $Z$ be sets of sizes $x$, $y$ and $z$ respectively. Let $W = X \times Y$ and $E$ be the set of all subsets of $W$. The number of functions from $Z$ to $E$ is:
questions.subject: dm
questions.solution: $|W| = xy$, $|E| = 2^{xy}$; functions $Z \to E$ number $(2^{xy})^z = 2^{xyz}$.
questions.reviewNote: Superscripts in the option exponents are blurred in the scan; options confirmed from the web.

questions.text: The set $\{1, 2, 3, 5, 7, 8, 9\}$ under multiplication modulo 10 is not a group. Given below are four plausible reasons. Which one of them is false?
questions.subject: dm
questions.solution: $2 \times 5 = 10 \equiv 0$ is outside the set (not closed); 2 and 8 have no inverse mod 10 (not coprime to 10), but $3 \times 7 = 21 \equiv 1$, so 3 has an inverse.

questions.text: A relation $R$ is defined on ordered pairs of integers as follows: $(x,y)\,R\,(u,v)$ if $x < u$ and $y > v$. Then $R$ is:

options.t: Neither a Partial Order nor an Equivalence Relation
A Partial Order but not a Total Order

questions.subject: dm
questions.solution: $R$ is irreflexive ($x<x$ is false), so it is not reflexive: neither a partial order nor an equivalence relation.

questions.text: For which one of the following reasons does Internet Protocol (IP) use the time-to-live (TTL) field in the IP datagram header?

options.t: Ensure packets reach destination within that time
Discard packets that reach later than that time
Limit the time for which a packet gets queued in intermediate routers.

questions.subject: cn
questions.solution: TTL is decremented at each hop and the packet is discarded at 0, preventing endless routing loops.

questions.text: Consider three CPU-intensive processes, which require 10, 20 and 30 time units and arrive at times 0, 2 and 6, respectively. How many context switches are needed if the operating system implements a shortest remaining time first scheduling algorithm? Do not count the context switches at time zero and at the end.
questions.subject: os
questions.solution: P1 runs 0-10 without preemption (remaining time always smaller), then P2 (10-30), then P3: 2 context switches.

questions.text:
Consider the following grammar

```
S -> S * E
S -> E
E -> F + E
E -> F
F -> id
```

Consider the following LR(0) items corresponding to the grammar above.

1. $S \rightarrow S * .E$
2. $E \rightarrow F. + E$
3. $E \rightarrow F + .E$

Given the items above, which two of them will appear in the same set in the canonical sets-of-items for the grammar?
questions.subject: cd
questions.solution: Item 1 arises after shifting `*`, item 2 after reducing to F from a state with F, item 3 only after shifting `+`; no two of them ever share a state.

questions.text: You are given a free running clock with a duty cycle of 50% and a digital waveform $f$ which changes only at the negative edge of the clock. Which one of the following circuits (using clocked D flip-flops) will delay the phase of $f$ by $180^\circ$?

figures.alt: f passes through a NOT gate into D of FF1; FF1 clock is clk through an inverter; FF1 output Qbar feeds D of FF2; FF2 clocked directly by clk; output is Q of FF2.
f through a NOT gate into D of FF1; FF1 clocked by clk; Q of FF1 to D of FF2; FF2 clocked by clk through a NOT gate; output Q of FF2.
f directly to D of FF1; FF1 clocked by clk; Q of FF1 to D of FF2; FF2 clocked by clk through a NOT gate; output Q of FF2.
f directly to D of FF1; FF1 clocked by inverted clk; Qbar of FF1 to D of FF2; FF2 clocked directly by clk; output Q of FF2.

questions.subject: dl
questions.solution: Options A and D invert / use the opposite output so f is not preserved, B inverts f; only C reproduces f unchanged, sampling it on the rising edge (half a period after f changes) and then re-clocking on the inverted clock, giving a delay of exactly half a period.
questions.reviewNote: Answer C taken from the accepted answer on gateoverflow (Q8); the option figures are simple but the timing argument is subtle.

questions.text: A CPU has 24-bit instructions. A program starts at address 300 (in decimal). Which one of the following is a legal program counter (all values in decimal)?
questions.subject: coa
questions.solution: Each 24-bit instruction takes 3 bytes, so legal PC values are $300 + 3k$; among the options only 600 is of that form.

questions.text: In a binary max heap containing $n$ numbers, the smallest element can be found in time
questions.subject: pds
questions.solution: The minimum of a max heap is among the $\lceil n/2 \rceil$ leaves and there is no order among them, so $\Theta(n)$ comparisons are needed.

questions.text: Consider a weighted complete graph $G$ on the vertex set $\{v_1, v_2, \ldots, v_n\}$ such that the weight of the edge $(v_i, v_j)$ is $2|i - j|$. The weight of a minimum spanning tree of $G$ is:
questions.subject: algo
questions.solution: The path $v_1 - v_2 - \cdots - v_n$ uses $n-1$ edges of weight 2, total $2(n-1) = 2n-2$, and no cheaper edges exist.

questions.text: To implement Dijkstra's shortest path algorithm on unweighted graphs so that it runs in linear time, the data structure to be used is:
questions.subject: algo
questions.solution: On an unweighted graph Dijkstra degenerates to BFS, which needs only a FIFO queue for $O(V+E)$ time.

questions.text: A scheme for storing binary trees in an array $X$ is as follows. Indexing of $X$ starts at 1 instead of 0. The root is stored at $X[1]$. For a node stored at $X[i]$, the left child, if any, is stored in $X[2i]$ and the right child, if any, in $X[2i+1]$. To be able to store any binary tree on $n$ vertices the minimum size of $X$ should be
questions.subject: pds
questions.solution: A right-skewed tree of $n$ nodes puts its last node at index $2^n - 1$.

questions.text: Which one of the following in place sorting algorithms needs the minimum number of swaps?
questions.subject: algo
questions.solution: Selection sort performs at most $n-1$ swaps, i.e. $O(n)$, fewer than the others.

questions.text:
Consider the following C-program fragment in which $i$, $j$ and $n$ are integer variables.

```c
for (i = n, j = 0; i > 0; i /= 2, j += i);
```

Let $val(j)$ denote the value stored in the variable $j$ after termination of the for loop. Which one of the following is true?
questions.subject: pds
questions.solution: $j = n/2 + n/4 + \cdots \approx n - 1$, hence $\Theta(n)$.

questions.text: Let $S$ be an NP-complete problem and $Q$ and $R$ be two other problems not known to be in NP. $Q$ is polynomial time reducible to $S$ and $S$ is polynomial-time reducible to $R$. Which one of the following statements is true?
questions.subject: algo
questions.solution: Every NP problem reduces to $S$ and $S$ reduces to $R$, so $R$ is NP-hard; membership of $R$ in NP is not known, and $Q \le S$ says nothing about hardness of $Q$.

questions.text: An element in an array $X$ is called a leader if it is greater than all elements to the right of it in $X$. The best algorithm to find all leaders in an array

options.t: Solves it in linear time using a left to right pass of the array
Solves it in linear time using a right to left pass of the array
Solves it using divide and conquer in time $\Theta(n \log n)$

questions.subject: algo
questions.solution: Scan from the right keeping the running maximum; an element is a leader iff it exceeds it. This is $O(n)$.

questions.text: We are given a set $X = \{x_1, \ldots, x_n\}$ where $x_i = 2^i$. A sample $S \subseteq X$ is drawn by selecting each $x_i$ independently with probability $p_i = 1/2$. The expected value of the smallest number in sample $S$ is:
questions.subject: prob
questions.solution: The smallest chosen element is $x_i$ with probability $(1/2)^i$, so $E = \sum_{i=1}^{n} 2^i \cdot 2^{-i} = n$ (ignoring the empty sample).
questions.reviewNote: Answer derived by hand ($E=n$); web summaries disagreed, empty-sample case ignored.

questions.text: Let $L_1 = \{0^{n+m}1^n0^m \mid n, m \ge 0\}$, $L_2 = \{0^{n+m}1^{n+m}0^m \mid n, m \ge 0\}$ and $L_3 = \{0^{n+m}1^{n+m}0^{n+m} \mid n, m \ge 0\}$. Which of these languages are NOT context free?
questions.subject: toc
questions.solution: $L_1 = 0^m(0^n1^n)0^m$ is context free. $L_2$ needs $\#0 = \#1$ and a further comparison of the trailing 0s with a part of the leading 0s, and $L_3 = 0^k1^k0^k$ needs three equal counts; neither is context free.

questions.text:
Consider the following log sequence of two transactions on a bank account, with initial balance 12000, that transfer 2000 to a mortgage payment and then apply a 5% interest.

1. T1 start
2. T1 B old= 1200 new= 10000
3. T1 M old=0 new=2000
4. T1 commit
5. T2 start
6. T2 B old= 10000 new= 10500
7. T2 commit

Suppose the database system crashes just before log record 7 is written. When the system is restarted, which one statement is true of the recovery procedure?

options.t: We must redo log record 6 to set B to 10500
We must undo log record 6 to set B to 10000 and then redo log records 2 and 3
We need not redo log records 2 and 3 because transaction T1 has committed
We can apply redo and undo operations in arbitrary order because they are idempotent.

questions.subject: db
questions.solution: T2 did not commit so it is undone (B back to 10000); T1 committed so its updates (records 2 and 3) are redone.
questions.reviewNote: The printed old value in record 2 reads 1200 (likely a typo for 12000); kept as printed.

questions.text: For each element in a set of size $2n$, an unbiased coin is tossed. The $2n$ coin tosses are independent. An element is chosen if the corresponding coin toss were head. The probability that exactly $n$ elements are chosen is:
questions.subject: prob

questions.text:
Let $E$, $F$ and $G$ be finite sets.

Let $X = (E \cap F) - (F \cap G)$ and $Y = (E - (E \cap G)) - (E - F)$.

Which one of the following is true?
questions.subject: dm
questions.solution: $X = E \cap F \cap \overline{G}$ and $Y = (E \cap \overline{G}) \cap F = E \cap F \cap \overline{G}$, so $X = Y$.

questions.text: $F$ is an $n \times n$ real matrix. $b$ is an $n \times 1$ real vector. Suppose there are two $n \times 1$ vectors, $u$ and $v$ such that $u \neq v$, and $Fu = b$, $Fv = b$. Which one of the following statements is false?

options.t: There are an infinite number of solutions to $Fx = b$

questions.subject: la
questions.solution: $F(u-v) = 0$ with $u - v \ne 0$, so $F$ is singular (a, c true) and $Fx=b$ has infinitely many solutions (b); singular does not force two identical rows.

questions.text: Given a set of elements $N = \{1, 2, \ldots, n\}$ and two arbitrary subsets $A \subseteq N$ and $B \subseteq N$, how many of the $n!$ permutations $\pi$ from $N$ to $N$ satisfy $\min(\pi(A)) = \min(\pi(B))$, where $\min(S)$ is the smallest integer in the set of integers $S$, and $\pi(S)$ is the set of integers obtained by applying permutation $\pi$ to each element of $S$?
questions.subject: dm
questions.solution: The smallest image among $\pi(A\cup B)$ is equally likely to come from any element of $A \cup B$; the two minima agree iff it comes from $A \cap B$, probability $|A\cap B|/|A\cup B|$.

questions.text:
Let $S = \{1, 2, 3, \ldots, m\}$, $m > 3$. Let $X_1, \ldots, X_n$ be subsets of $S$ each of size 3. Define a function $f$ from $S$ to the set of natural numbers as, $f(i)$ is the number of sets $X_j$ that contain the element $i$. That is $f(i) = |\{j \mid i \in X_j\}|$.

Then $\sum_{i=1}^{m} f(i)$ is
questions.subject: dm
questions.solution: Double counting of (element, set) incidences: each of the $n$ sets has 3 elements, so the sum is $3n$.

questions.text:
Which one of the first order predicate calculus statements given below correctly expresses the following English statement?

Tigers and lions attack if they are hungry or threatened.
questions.subject: dm
questions.solution: Any x that is a tiger or a lion and is hungry or threatened attacks: option D. A uses $\wedge$ between tiger and lion (nothing is both), B claims all attack, C reverses the implication.

questions.text:
Consider the following propositional statements:

P1: $((A \wedge B) \rightarrow C) \equiv ((A \rightarrow C) \wedge (B \rightarrow C))$

P2: $((A \vee B) \rightarrow C) \equiv ((A \rightarrow C) \vee (B \rightarrow C))$

Which one of the following is true?

options.t: P1 is a tautology, but not P2
P2 is a tautology, but not P1
P1 and P2 are both tautologies
Both P1 and P2 are not tautologies

questions.subject: dm
questions.solution: P1 fails for $A=T, B=F, C=F$ (LHS true, RHS false); P2 fails for $A=T, B=F, C=F$ as well (LHS $(T)\to F$ = false, RHS $(F)\vee(T)$ = true).

questions.text:
A logical binary relation $\odot$, is defined as follows:

| A | B | A $\odot$ B |
|---|---|---|
| True | True | True |
| True | False | True |
| False | True | False |
| False | False | True |

Let $\sim$ be the unary negation (NOT) operator, with higher precedence than $\odot$. Which one of the following is equivalent to $A \wedge B$?
questions.subject: dm
questions.solution: The table gives $A \odot B = A \vee \sim B$. Then $\sim(\sim A \odot B) = \sim(\sim A \vee \sim B) = A \wedge B$.

questions.text: If $s$ is a string over $(0+1)^*$ then let $n_0(s)$ denote the number of 0-s in $s$ and $n_1(s)$ the number of 1-s in $s$. Which one of the following languages is not regular?

options.t: $L = \{s \in (0+1)^* \mid \text{for every prefix } s' \text{ of } s,\ |n_0(s') - n_1(s')| \le 2\}$

questions.subject: toc
questions.solution: $L \cap 0^*1^* = \{0^a1^b : |a-b| \le 4\}$ is not regular (needs an unbounded counter), so option C is not regular; A is finite, B needs only a bounded counter (5 values) and D is a product of mod counters.

questions.text:
For $s \in (0+1)^*$ let $d(s)$ denote the decimal value of $s$ (e.g. $d(101) = 5$). Let $L = \{s \in (0+1)^* \mid d(s) \bmod 5 = 2 \text{ and } d(s) \bmod 7 = 4\}$.

Which one of the following statements is true?

options.t: $L$ is recursively enumerable, but not recursive

questions.subject: toc
questions.solution: Track $d(s) \bmod 35$ with a DFA (35 states); the condition $d \bmod 5 = 2$ and $d \bmod 7 = 4$ is a set of residues mod 35, so $L$ is regular.

questions.text: Let $SHAM_3$ be the problem of finding a Hamiltonian cycle in a graph $G = (V, E)$ with $|V|$ divisible by 3 and $DHAM_3$ be the problem of determining if a Hamiltonian cycle exists in such graphs. Which one of the following is true?
questions.subject: algo
questions.solution: Padding a general Hamiltonian-cycle instance to make $|V|$ divisible by 3 preserves the answer, so the decision version is NP-complete and the search version is NP-hard.

questions.text:
Consider the following statements about the context-free grammar $G = \{S \rightarrow SS,\ S \rightarrow ab,\ S \rightarrow ba,\ S \rightarrow \epsilon\}$

1. $G$ is ambiguous
2. $G$ produces all strings with equal number of a's and b's
3. $G$ can be accepted by a deterministic PDA.

Which combination below expresses all the true statements about $G$?
questions.subject: toc
questions.solution: $S \Rightarrow SS \Rightarrow SSS$ gives multiple derivations (ambiguous); $aabb$ cannot be generated (so 2 is false); $L(G) = (ab+ba)^*$ is regular, hence accepted by a DPDA.

questions.text: Let $L_1$ be a regular language, $L_2$ be a deterministic context-free language and $L_3$ a recursively enumerable, but not recursive, language. Which one of the following statements is false?
questions.subject: toc
questions.solution: Intersecting an r.e. non-recursive language with a regular language (e.g. $\Sigma^*$) can leave it non-recursive, so B is false; the others follow from closure properties.

questions.text: Consider the regular language $L = (111 + 11111)^*$. The minimum number of states in any DFA accepting this language is
questions.subject: toc
questions.solution: $L$ contains exactly the lengths expressible as $3a+5b$: all except 1, 2, 4, 7. States for lengths 0-7 are pairwise distinguishable and lengths $\ge 8$ collapse into one accepting state: 9 states.

questions.text:
![](fig/cse-2006/cs-35-1.png)

Consider the circuit above. Which one of the following options correctly represents $f(x, y, z)$?

figures.alt: Two 2-to-1 MUXes. MUX1: input 0 = x, input 1 = y-bar, select = z. MUX2: input 0 = output of MUX1, input 1 = x, select = y; output f.

questions.subject: dl
questions.solution: MUX1 = $\overline{z}x + z\overline{y}$; MUX2 with select $y$: $f = \overline{y}(\overline{z}x + z\overline{y}) + xy = x\overline{y}\,\overline{z} + \overline{y}z + xy = x\overline{z} + xy + \overline{y}z$.
questions.reviewNote: Option overlines are hard to read in the scan; expressions taken from the web.

questions.text: Given two three bit numbers $a_2a_1a_0$ and $b_2b_1b_0$ and $c$, the carry in, the function that represents the carry generate function when these two numbers are added is:
questions.subject: dl
questions.solution: Carry out of the 3-bit adder: $c_3 = a_2b_2 + (a_2+b_2)a_1b_1 + (a_2+b_2)(a_1+b_1)a_0b_0$; expanding gives the seven terms of option A.
questions.reviewNote: Option text is a garbled bitmap in the scan; options B-D transcribed from the web and may contain small errors.

questions.text:
Consider the circuit in the diagram. The $\oplus$ operator represents Ex-OR. The D flip-flops are initialized to zeroes (cleared).

![](fig/cse-2006/cs-37-1.png)

The following data: 100110000 is supplied to the "data" terminal in nine clock cycles. After that the values of $q_2q_1q_0$ are:

figures.alt: Three D flip-flops sharing clock. Rightmost FF (q0) has D = data. Middle FF (q1) has D = XOR(q0, q2). Leftmost FF (q2) has D = q1 (Q of middle). The XOR takes q0 from the rightmost FF and q2 fed back from the leftmost FF via a wire along the top.

questions.subject: dl
questions.solution: Next state: $q_0' = data$, $q_1' = q_0 \oplus q_2$, $q_2' = q_1$. Starting from 000 and feeding 1,0,0,1,1,0,0,0,0 the states are 001, 010, 100, 011, 111, 100, 010, 100, 010, so the final $q_2q_1q_0 = 010$.
questions.reviewNote: Wiring read from a low-resolution figure (XOR inputs taken as q0 and q2, output to D of q1); a web summary claimed 101 but hand simulation gives 010.

questions.text: Consider a boolean function $f(w, x, y, z)$. Suppose that exactly one of its inputs is allowed to change at a time. If the function happens to be true for two input vectors $i_1 = \langle w_1, x_1, y_1, z_1 \rangle$ and $i_2 = \langle w_2, x_2, y_2, z_2 \rangle$, we would like the function to remain true as the input changes from $i_1$ to $i_2$ ($i_1$ and $i_2$ differ in exactly one bit position), without becoming false momentarily. Let $f(w, x, y, z) = \Sigma(5, 7, 11, 12, 13, 15)$. Which of the following cube covers of $f$ will ensure that the required property is satisfied?
questions.subject: dl
questions.solution: A hazard-free (static-1) cover must contain a cube covering every pair of adjacent minterms. Cubes $\overline{w}xz$ (5,7), $wx\overline{y}$ (12,13), $x\overline{y}z$ (5,13), $xyz$ (7,15), $wyz$ (11,15) cover all adjacent pairs among the minterms.
questions.reviewNote: Option overlines were partly illegible in the scan; option expressions taken from the web.

questions.text: We consider the addition of two 2's complement numbers $b_{n-1}b_{n-2}\ldots b_0$ and $a_{n-1}a_{n-2}\ldots a_0$. A binary adder for adding unsigned binary numbers is used to add the two numbers. The sum is denoted by $c_{n-1}c_{n-2}\ldots c_0$ and the carry-out by $c_{out}$. Which one of the following options correctly identifies the overflow condition?
questions.subject: dl
questions.solution: Overflow occurs iff both operands have the same sign bit and the sum has the opposite sign: $a_{n-1}b_{n-1}\overline{c_{n-1}} + \overline{a_{n-1}}\,\overline{b_{n-1}}c_{n-1}$.

questions.text: Consider numbers represented in 4-bit gray code. Let $h_3h_2h_1h_0$ be the gray code representation of a number $n$ and let $g_3g_2g_1g_0$ be the gray code of $(n+1)$ (modulo 16) value of the number. Which one of the following functions is correct?
questions.subject: dl
questions.solution: Tabulating gray(n) -> gray(n+1 mod 16): $g_2 = 1$ for $h \in \{2,4,5,6,7,12,13,15\}$. The other listed sets belong to $g_1$, $g_3$ and $g_0$ respectively, so they are attached to wrong function names.

questions.text: A CPU has a cache with block size 64 bytes. The main memory has $k$ banks, each bank being $c$ bytes wide. Consecutive $c$-byte chunks are mapped on consecutive banks with wrap-around. All the $k$ banks can be accessed in parallel, but two accesses to the same bank must be serialized. A cache block access may involve multiple iterations of parallel bank accesses depending on the amount of data obtained by accessing all the $k$ banks in parallel. Each iteration requires decoding the bank numbers to be accessed in parallel and this takes $k/2$ ns. The latency of one bank access is 80 ns. If $c = 2$ and $k = 24$, the latency of retrieving a cache block starting at address zero from main memory is
questions.subject: coa
questions.solution: A 64-byte block is 32 chunks of 2 bytes; 24 banks serve 24 chunks per iteration, so 2 iterations. Each iteration costs $k/2 + 80 = 12 + 80 = 92$ ns, total 184 ns.

questions.text: A CPU has a five stage pipeline and runs at 1 GHz frequency. Instruction fetch happens in the first stage of the pipeline. A conditional branch instruction computes the target address and evaluates the condition in the third stage of the pipeline. The processor stops fetching new instructions following a conditional branch until the branch outcome is known. A program executes $10^9$ instructions out of which 20% are conditional branches. If each instruction takes one cycle to complete on average, the total execution time of the program is
questions.subject: coa
questions.solution: Each branch stalls fetch for 2 extra cycles: cycles $= 10^9 + 0.2 \times 10^9 \times 2 = 1.4 \times 10^9$, i.e. 1.4 s at 1 GHz.

questions.text:
Consider a new instruction named branch-on-bit-set (mnemonic `bbs`). The instruction "`bbs reg, pos, label`" jumps to `label` if bit in position `pos` of register operand `reg` is one. A register is 32 bits wide and the bits are numbered 0 to 31, bit in position 0 being the least significant. Consider the following emulation of this instruction on a processor that does not have `bbs` implemented.

```
temp <- reg & mask
Branch to label if temp is non-zero
```

questions.text: Station A uses 32 byte packets to transmit messages to Station B using a sliding window protocol. The round trip delay between A and B is 80 milliseconds and the bottleneck bandwidth on the path between A and B is 128 kbps. What is the optimal window size that A should use?
questions.subject: cn
questions.solution: Bandwidth-delay product $= 128\,000 \times 0.08 = 10\,240$ bits $= 1280$ bytes $= 40$ packets of 32 bytes (transmission time 2 ms, RTT 80 ms): window of 40.

questions.text: Let $T$ be a depth first search tree in an undirected graph $G$. Vertices $u$ and $v$ are leaves of this tree $T$. The degrees of both $u$ and $v$ in $G$ are at least 2. Which one of the following statements is true?

options.t: There must exist a vertex $w$ adjacent to both $u$ and $v$ in $G$
There must exist a vertex $w$ whose removal disconnects $u$ and $v$ in $G$
There must exist a cycle in $G$ containing $u$ and $v$
There must exist a cycle in $G$ containing $u$ and all its neighbours in $G$

questions.subject: algo
questions.solution: In an undirected DFS all non-tree edges join a vertex to an ancestor.
```
      subroutine swap(ix, iy)
         it = ix
L1:      ix = iy
L2:      iy = it
      end
      ia = 3
      ib = 8

      end
```

Exactly the following set of statement(s) is correct:

questions.subject: cd

questions.text: A computer system supports 32-bit virtual addresses as well as 32-bit physical addresses. Since the virtual address space is of the same size as the physical address space, the operating system designers decide to get rid of the virtual memory entirely. The processor cache organization can be made more efficient now
Hardware support for memory management is no longer needed

questions.text: Consider three processes (process id 0, 1, 2 respectively) with compute time bursts 2, 4, and 8 time units. All processes arrive at time zero. Consider the longest remaining time first (LRTF) scheduling algorithm. In LRTF ties are broken by giving priority to the process with the lowest process id. The average turn around time is
questions.subject: os
questions.solution: Simulating unit by unit, the processes with bursts 2, 4, 8 finish at times 12, 13 and 14; average turnaround $= (12+13+14)/3 = 13$.

questions.text: Consider three processes, all arriving at time zero, with total execution time of 10, 20, and 30 units, respectively. Each process spends the first 20% of execution time doing I/O, the next 70% of time doing computation, and the last 10% of time doing I/O again. The operating system uses a shortest remaining compute time first scheduling algorithm and schedules a new process either when the running process gets blocked on I/O or when the running process finishes its compute burst. Assume that all I/O operations can be overlapped as much as possible. For what percentage of time does the CPU remain idle?
questions.subject: os
questions.solution: P1: I/O 0-2, compute 2-9; P2 compute 9-23 (its I/O ended at 4); P3 compute 23-44; P3's final I/O ends at 47. CPU idle 0-2 and 44-47 = 5 of 47 units $\approx 10.6\%$.

questions.text: Consider the following snapshot of a system running $n$ processes. Process $i$ is holding $x_i$ instances of a resource $R$, for $1 \le i \le n$. Currently, all instances of $R$ are occupied. Further, for all $i$, process $i$ has placed a request for an additional $y_i$ instances while holding the $x_i$ instances it already has. There are exactly two processes $p$ and $q$ such that $y_p = y_q = 0$. Which one of the following can serve as a necessary condition to guarantee that the system is not approaching a deadlock?
questions.subject: os
questions.solution: $p$ and $q$ can finish and release $x_p + x_q$ instances; for some other process to be able to proceed, this must be at least what that process requests, so a condition of the form $x_p + x_q \ge y_k$ is what is needed (option B is the only one of this form).
