questions.text:
Consider the relation account (customer, balance) where customer is a primary key and there are no null values. We would like to rank customers according to decreasing balance. The customer with the largest balance gets rank 1. Ties are not broken but ranks are skipped: if exactly two customers have the largest balance they each get rank 1 and rank 2 is not assigned.

Query1:

```sql
select A.customer, count(B.customer)
from account A, account B
where A.balance <= B.balance
group by A.customer
```

Query2:

```sql
select A.customer, 1+count(B.customer)
from account A, account B
where A.balance < B.balance
group by A.customer
```

Consider these statements about Query1 and Query2.

1. Query1 will produce the same row set as Query2 for some but not all databases
2. Both Query1 and Query2 are correct implementations of the specification
3. Query1 is a correct implementation of the specification but Query2 is not
4. Neither Query1 nor Query2 is a correct implementation of the specification
5. Assigning rank with a pure relational query takes less time than scanning in decreasing balance order and assigning ranks using ODBC

Which two of the above statements are correct?
questions.subject: db
questions.solution: Query1 counts customers with balance >= own (includes itself and ties), giving wrong ranks with ties; Query2 drops the top-balance customers (no strictly greater balance, so no join rows) so it is incomplete. Neither is correct (4), and they coincide only on trivial databases such as the empty one (1). Statement 5 is false (a cursor scan is cheaper).

questions.text:
Consider the relation enrolled (student, course) in which (student, course) is the primary key, and the relation paid (student, amount) where student is the primary key. Assume no null values and no foreign keys or integrity constraints. Given the following four queries:

Query1: `select student from enrolled where student in (select student from paid)`

Query2: `select student from paid where student in (select student from enrolled)`

Query3: `select E.student from enrolled E, paid P where E.student = P.student`

Query4: `select student from paid where exists (select * from enrolled where enrolled.student = paid.student)`

Which one of the following statements is correct?

options.t: All queries return identical row sets for any database
Query2 and Query4 return identical row sets for all databases but there exist databases for which Query1 and Query2 return different row sets
There exist databases for which Query3 returns strictly fewer rows than Query2
There exist databases for which Query4 will encounter an integrity violation at runtime

questions.subject: db
questions.solution: Queries 2 and 4 return each paid student that is enrolled once. Queries 1 and 3 return a student once per enrolled course, so they can have duplicates and differ from Query2; Query3 never returns fewer rows than Query2.

questions.text:
Consider the relation enrolled (student, course) in which (student, course) is the primary key, and the relation paid (student, amount) where student is the primary key. Assume no null values and no foreign keys or integrity constraints. Assume that amounts 6000, 7000, 8000, 9000 and 10000 were each paid by 20% of the students. Consider these query plans (Plan 1 on left, Plan 2 on right) to "list all courses taken by students who have paid more than $x$".

![](fig/cse-2006/cs-69-1.png)

A disk seek takes 4 ms, disk data transfer bandwidth is 300 MB/s and checking a tuple to see if amount is greater than $x$ takes 10 $\mu$s.

Which of the following statements is correct?

options.t: Plan 1 and Plan 2 will not output identical row sets for all databases
A course may be listed more than once in the output of Plan 1 for some databases
For $x = 5000$, Plan 1 executes faster than Plan 2 for all databases
For $x = 9000$, Plan 1 executes slower than Plan 2 for all databases

figures.alt: Plan 1 (left): enrolled -> probe index on student; paid -> sequential scan with select amount > x; both feed an indexed nested loop join, then project on course. Plan 2 (right): enrolled -> probe index on student; paid -> sequential scan; indexed nested loop join; then select on amount > x; then project on course.

questions.subject: db
questions.solution: Both plans compute the same join and selection, so the row sets are identical (A false). No duplicate elimination is done, so a course taken by several qualifying students appears several times (B true). The speed claims in C and D do not hold for all databases.

Consider two cache organizations: The first one is 32 KB 2-way set associative with 32-byte block size. The second one is of the same size but direct mapped. The size of an address is 32 bits in both cases. A 2-to-1 multiplexer has a latency of 0.6 ns while a $k$-bit comparator has a latency of $k/10$ ns. The hit latency of the set associative organization is $h_1$ while that of the direct mapped one is $h_2$.

The value of $h_1$ is
questions.subject: coa

questions.text:
Consider two cache organizations: The first one is 32 KB 2-way set associative with 32-byte block size. The second one is of the same size but direct mapped. The size of an address is 32 bits in both cases. A 2-to-1 multiplexer has a latency of 0.6 ns while a $k$-bit comparator has a latency of $k/10$ ns. questions.text:

A 3-ary heap can be represented by an array as follows: The root is stored in the first location, $a[0]$, nodes in the next level, from left to right, is stored from $a[1]$ to $a[3]$. questions.text:
Consider the diagram shown below where a number of LANs are connected by (transparent) bridges. In order to avoid packets looping through circuits in the graph, the bridges organize themselves in a spanning tree. First, the root bridge is identified as the bridge with the least serial number. Next, the root sends out (one or more) data units to enable the setting up of the spanning tree of shortest paths from the root bridge to each bridge.

Each bridge identifies a port (the root port) through which it will forward frames to the root bridge. Port conflicts are always resolved in favour of the port with the lower index value. When there is a possibility of multiple bridges forwarding to the same LAN (but not through the root port), ties are broken as follows: bridges closest to the root get preference and between such bridges, the one with the lowest serial number is preferred.

![](fig/cse-2006/cs-82-1.png)

For the given connection of LANs by bridges, which one of the following choices represents the depth first traversal of the spanning tree of bridges?

figures.alt: Bridge B1 (ports 1,2) connects to two top LANs: LAN-L (hosts H1,H2) via port 1 and LAN-R (hosts H3,H4) via port 2. B5 connects port 2 to LAN-L and port 3 (crossing) to LAN-R; B3 connects port 3 to LAN-R and port 4 (crossing) to LAN-L. B5 ports 1 and 4 and B3 port 1 connect to the middle-left LAN (hosts H5,H6); B3 port 2 connects to the middle-right LAN (hosts H7,H8). B4: port 1 to the middle-left LAN, port 2 to the middle-right LAN, port 3 to a LAN with H9,H10. B2: port 1 to the middle-right LAN, port 2 to the middle-left LAN, port 3 to a LAN with H11,H12.

questions.subject: cn
questions.solution: B1 is root. B5 and B3 are both one hop away (root ports 2 and 3). On the middle LANs B3 (lower serial than B5) is the designated bridge, so B4 and B2 hang below B3 (root ports 1). DFS from B1 visits B5, then B3, then B4, B2.

Consider the diagram shown below where a number of LANs are connected by (transparent) bridges. In order to avoid packets looping through circuits in the graph, the bridges organize themselves in a spanning tree. First, the root bridge is identified as the bridge with the least serial number. Next, the root sends out (one or more) data units to enable the setting up of the spanning tree of shortest paths from the root bridge to each bridge.

Each bridge identifies a port (the root port) through which it will forward frames to the root bridge. Port conflicts are always resolved in favour of the port with the lower index value. When there is a possibility of multiple bridges forwarding to the same LAN (but not through the root port), ties are broken as follows: bridges closest to the root get preference and between such bridges, the one with the lowest serial number is preferred.

![](fig/cse-2006/cs-82-1.png)

Consider the correct spanning tree for the previous question. Let host H1 send out a broadcast ping packet. Which of the following options represents the correct forwarding table on B3?

figures.alt: Bridge B1 (ports 1,2) connects to two top LANs: LAN-L (hosts H1,H2) via port 1 and LAN-R (hosts H3,H4) via port 2. B5 connects port 2 to LAN-L and port 3 (crossing) to LAN-R; B3 connects port 3 to LAN-R and port 4 (crossing) to LAN-L. questions.subject: cn
questions.solution: In the spanning tree B3's root port is 3 (towards B1); port 4 is blocked. H1-H4 are reached via port 3, H5, H6, H9, H10 via port 1 (middle-left LAN and B4), H7, H8, H11, H12 via port 2 (middle-right LAN and B2).

questions.text: Which one of the following grammars generates the language $L = \{a^ib^j \mid i \neq j\}$?

options.t:
```
S -> AC | CB
C -> aCb | a | b
A -> aA | epsilon
B -> Bb | epsilon
```

```
S -> AC | CB
C -> aCb | epsilon
A -> aA | epsilon
B -> Bb | epsilon
```

```
S -> AC | CB
C -> aCb | epsilon
A -> aA | a
B -> bB | b
```

questions.subject: toc
questions.solution: $C$ generates $a^kb^k$; $A \to aA \mid a$ adds at least one extra $a$ and $B \to bB \mid b$ at least one extra $b$, so $S \to AC \mid CB$ generates exactly $a^ib^j$ with $i \ne j$. Options A and C also generate strings with $i = j$.

questions.text: In the correct grammar above, what is the length of the derivation (number of steps starting from $S$) to generate the string $a^lb^m$ with $l \neq m$?
questions.subject: toc
questions.solution: For $l > m$: $S \to AC$ (1), $C \to aCb$ ($m$ steps), $C \to \epsilon$ (1), and $A$ produces $a^{l-m}$ in $l-m$ steps: total $l + 2$. Symmetrically $m + 2$ for $m > l$, i.e. $\max(l,m) + 2$.
questions.reviewNote: Option D is printed as 'max(l, m) + 2' in the scan (duplicate of A); the web version reads 'max(l, m) + 3'. Option A is the answer either way.

questions.text:
Consider the following two statements about the function $f(x)=|x|$:

P. $f(x)$ is continuous for all real values of $x$

Q. $f(x)$ is differentiable for all real values of $x$

Which of the following is **TRUE**?

options.t: P is true and Q is false.
P is false and Q is true.
Both P and Q are true.
Both P and Q are false.

questions.subject: calc
questions.solution: $|x|$ is continuous everywhere but not differentiable at $x=0$ (left and right derivatives are -1 and +1).

questions.text: Let S be a set of $n$ elements. The number of ordered pairs in the largest and the smallest equivalence relations on S are
questions.subject: dm
questions.solution: Largest is the universal relation $S\times S$ ($n^2$ pairs); smallest is the identity relation ($n$ pairs, needed for reflexivity).

questions.text: What is the maximum number of different Boolean functions involving $n$ Boolean variables?
questions.subject: dl
questions.solution: There are $2^n$ input combinations and each can map to 0 or 1, giving $2^{2^n}$ functions.

questions.text: Let G be the non-planar graph with the minimum possible number of edges. Then G has
questions.subject: dm
questions.solution: By Kuratowski, minimal non-planar graphs are $K_5$ (10 edges) and $K_{3,3}$ (9 edges, 6 vertices); the minimum edge count is 9.

questions.text:
Consider the DAG with $V=\{1,2,3,4,5,6\}$, shown below.

![DAG](fig/cse-2007/cs-5-1.png)

Which of the following is **NOT** a topological ordering?

figures.alt: Directed acyclic graph on vertices 1-6 with edges 1->2, 1->3, 2->5, 2->4, 3->4, 3->6, 4->5, 4->6.

questions.subject: algo

questions.text: Which of the following problems is undecidable?
questions.subject: toc
questions.solution: Membership (CYK), finiteness and equivalence of FSAs are decidable; ambiguity of a CFG is undecidable.

questions.text: Which of the following is **TRUE**?

options.t: Every subset of a regular set is regular.
Every finite subset of a non-regular set is regular.
The union of two non-regular sets is not regular.
Infinite union of finite sets is regular.

questions.subject: toc
questions.solution: Every finite set is regular. Subsets of regular sets need not be regular, union of non-regular sets can be regular (L and complement), and an infinite union of finite sets can be non-regular (e.g. $\{a^nb^n\}$).

questions.text: How many 3-to-8 line decoders with an enable input are needed to construct a 6-to-64 line decoder without using any other logic gates?
questions.subject: dl
questions.solution: One decoder decodes 3 MSBs and drives the enables of 8 decoders for the 3 LSBs: 1 + 8 = 9.

questions.text:
Consider the following Boolean function of four variables:

$f(w,x,y,z)=\sum(1,3,4,6,9,11,12,14)$

The function is
questions.subject: dl
questions.solution: $f = x'z + xz' = x\oplus z$, so $f$ is independent of $w$ and $y$.

questions.text: Consider a 4-way set associative cache consisting of 128 lines with a line size of 64 words. The CPU generates a 20-bit address of a word in main memory. The number of bits in the TAG, LINE and WORD fields are respectively:
questions.subject: coa
questions.solution: Word offset = $\log_2 64 = 6$; sets = 128/4 = 32, so 5 bits; tag = 20 - 6 - 5 = 9.

questions.text: Consider a disk pack with 16 surfaces, 128 tracks per surface and 256 sectors per track. 512 bytes of data are stored in a bit serial manner in a sector. The capacity of the disk pack and the number of bits required to specify a particular sector in the disk are respectively:
questions.subject: coa
questions.solution: Capacity = $16\cdot128\cdot256\cdot512 = 2^{28}$ B = 256 MB; sectors = $2^{4+7+8}$, so 19 bits.

questions.text: The height of a binary tree is the maximum number of edges in any root to leaf path. The maximum number of nodes in a binary tree of height $h$ is:
questions.subject: pds
questions.solution: Levels 0..h hold $1+2+\dots+2^h = 2^{h+1}-1$ nodes.

questions.text: The maximum number of binary trees that can be formed with three unlabeled nodes is:
questions.subject: pds
questions.solution: Catalan number $C_3 = \frac{1}{4}\binom{6}{3} = 5$.

questions.text: Which of the following sorting algorithms has the lowest worst-case complexity?
questions.subject: algo
questions.solution: Merge sort is $O(n\log n)$ in the worst case; the others are $O(n^2)$.

questions.subject: algo
questions.solution: $j$ takes values $1,2,4,\dots$; the body executes $\lfloor\log_2 n\rfloor+1$ times (counting the true tests), which matches option D as the intended key.
questions.reviewNote: Strictly the loop condition is evaluated $\lfloor\log_2 n\rfloor+2$ times (including the final false test), which matches no option; D is the intended/official answer as far as known but this is unconfirmed.

questions.text:
Group 1 contains some CPU scheduling algorithms and Group 2 contains some applications. Match entries in Group 1 to entries in Group 2.

| Group 1 | Group 2 |
|---|---|
| P. Gang Scheduling | 1. Guaranteed Scheduling |
| Q. Rate Monotonic Scheduling | 2. Real-time Scheduling |
| R. Fair Share Scheduling | 3. Thread Scheduling |
questions.subject: os
questions.solution: Gang scheduling schedules related threads together; rate monotonic is real-time; fair share gives guaranteed share per user.

questions.text: Consider the following statements about user level threads and kernel level threads. Which one of the following statements is **FALSE**?

options.t: Context switch time is longer for kernel level threads than for user level threads.
User level threads do not need any hardware support.
Related kernel level threads can be scheduled on different processors in a multi-processor system.
Blocking one kernel level thread blocks all related threads.

questions.subject: os
questions.solution: Blocking one kernel-level thread does not block its siblings; it is user-level threads that all block when one makes a blocking system call.

questions.text: Which one of the following is a top-down parser?
questions.subject: cd
questions.solution: Recursive descent is top-down; operator precedence, LR and LALR are bottom-up.

questions.text: In Ethernet when Manchester encoding is used, the bit rate is:
questions.subject: cn
questions.solution: Manchester uses two signal elements per bit, so baud rate = 2 x bit rate, i.e. bit rate is half the baud rate.

questions.text: Which one of the following uses UDP as the transport protocol?
questions.subject: cn
questions.solution: DNS queries normally use UDP; HTTP, Telnet and SMTP use TCP.

questions.text: How many different non-isomorphic Abelian groups of order 4 are there?
questions.subject: dm
questions.solution: $\mathbb{Z}_4$ and $\mathbb{Z}_2\times\mathbb{Z}_2$.

questions.text: Let $Graph(x)$ be a predicate which denotes that $x$ is a graph. Let $Connected(x)$ be a predicate which denotes that $x$ is connected. Which of the following first order logic sentences **DOES NOT** represent the statement: "Not every graph is connected"?
questions.subject: dm
questions.solution: A, B and C are all equivalent to 'some graph is not connected'; D says every graph is disconnected.

questions.text: Which of the following graphs has an Eulerian circuit?

options.t: Any $k$-regular graph where $k$ is an even number.
The complement of a cycle on 25 vertices.

questions.subject: dm
questions.solution: Complement of $C_{25}$ is connected with every vertex of degree $24-2=22$ (even), so it has an Eulerian circuit. $K_{90}$ has odd degree 89; a $k$-regular graph may be disconnected.

questions.text: Suppose we uniformly and randomly select a permutation from the $20!$ permutations of $1,2,3,\dots,20$. What is the probability that 2 appears at an earlier position than any other even number in the selected permutation?
questions.subject: prob
questions.solution: Each of the 10 even numbers is equally likely to appear first among the evens, so probability is 1/10.

questions.text: Let $A$ be a $4\times4$ matrix with eigenvalues $-5,-2,1,4$. Which of the following is an eigenvalue of $\begin{bmatrix}A&I\\I&A\end{bmatrix}$, where $I$ is the $4\times4$ identity matrix?
questions.subject: la
questions.solution: Eigenvalues of the block matrix are $\lambda\pm1$: $-6,-4,-3,-1,0,2,3,5$; only 2 is listed.

questions.text: Consider the set $S=\{a,b,c,d\}$. Consider the following 4 partitions $\pi_1,\pi_2,\pi_3,\pi_4$ on $S$: $\pi_1=\{\overline{abcd}\}$, $\pi_2=\{\overline{ab},\overline{cd}\}$, $\pi_3=\{\overline{abc},\overline{d}\}$, $\pi_4=\{\overline{a},\overline{b},\overline{c},\overline{d}\}$. Let $\prec$ be the partial order on the set of partitions $S'=\{\pi_1,\pi_2,\pi_3,\pi_4\}$ defined as follows: $\pi_i\prec\pi_j$ if and only if $\pi_i$ refines $\pi_j$. The poset diagram for $(S',\prec)$ is

figures.alt: Poset diagram (chain): pi1 at top, then pi2, pi3, pi4 at bottom in a single vertical line.
Poset diagram: pi1 at top connected to pi4 and to pi2; pi2 connected to pi3 (pi3 lowest left); pi3 connected to pi4.
Diamond poset: pi1 at top, pi2 and pi3 in the middle, pi4 at the bottom.
Poset diagram: pi1, pi2, pi3 at the top level, all connected to pi4 at the bottom.

questions.subject: dm
questions.solution: $\pi_4$ refines everything, $\pi_2$ and $\pi_3$ both refine $\pi_1$ and are incomparable: a diamond with $\pi_1$ top, $\pi_4$ bottom.

questions.text: Consider the set of (column) vectors defined by $X=\{x\in R^3\mid x_1+x_2+x_3=0,\text{ where }x^T=[x_1,x_2,x_3]^T\}$. Which of the following is **TRUE**?

options.t: $\{[1,-1,0]^T,[1,0,-1]^T\}$ is a basis for the subspace X.
$\{[1,-1,0]^T,[1,0,-1]^T\}$ is a linearly independent set, but it does not span X and therefore is not a basis of X.
X is not a subspace of $R^3$.

questions.subject: la
questions.solution: X is a plane through the origin (dimension 2); the two given vectors lie in X and are independent, hence a basis.

questions.text: Consider the series $x_{n+1}=\frac{x_n}{2}+\frac{9}{8x_n}$, $x_0=0.5$ obtained from the Newton-Raphson method. The series converges to
questions.subject: legacy
questions.solution: At the limit $x=x/2+9/(8x)$, so $x^2=9/4$ and $x=1.5$ (positive start).

questions.text: A minimum state deterministic finite automaton accepting the language $L=\{w\mid w\in\{0,1\}^*,\text{ number of 0s and 1s in }w\text{ are divisible by 3 and 5, respectively}\}$ has
questions.subject: toc
questions.solution: Product of a mod-3 counter and a mod-5 counter gives 15 pairwise distinguishable states.

questions.text: The language $L=\{0^i21^i\mid i\ge0\}$ over the alphabet $\{0,1,2\}$ is

options.t: is recursive and is a deterministic CFL.
is not a deterministic CFL but a CFL.

questions.subject: toc
questions.solution: The marker 2 lets a DPDA push 0s and pop for 1s: it is a DCFL, hence recursive, and not regular.

questions.text: Which of the following languages is regular?
questions.subject: toc
questions.solution: $ww^Rx$: any string starting with 00 or 11 of length at least 3 works (take $|w|=1$), so it is regular; the others are not.

questions.text:
Let $f(w,x,y,z)=\sum(0,4,5,7,8,9,13,15)$. Which of the following expressions are **NOT** equivalent to $f$?

(P) $x'y'z'+w'xy'+wy'z+xz$

(Q) $w'y'z'+wx'y'+xz$

(R) $w'y'z'+wx'y'+xyz+xy'z$

(S) $x'y'z'+wx'y'+w'y$
questions.subject: dl
questions.solution: P, Q and R each expand to exactly minterms 0,4,5,7,8,9,13,15. S contains $w'y$ = minterms 2,3,6,7, so it differs from $f$.

questions.text:
Define the connective $*$ for the Boolean variables $X$ and $Y$ as: $X*Y=XY+X'Y'$. Let $Z=X*Y$. Consider the following expressions $P$, $Q$ and $R$.

$P: X=Y*Z$  $Q: Y=X*Z$  $R: X*Y*Z=1$

Which of the following is **TRUE**?
questions.subject: dl
questions.solution: $*$ is XNOR (associative, commutative, $A*A=1$). $Y*(X*Y)=X$, $X*(X*Y)=Y$, and $(X*Y)*Z=Z*Z=1$.

questions.text: Suppose only one multiplexer and one inverter are allowed to be used to implement any Boolean function of $n$ variables. What is the minimum size of the multiplexer needed?
questions.subject: dl
questions.solution: Use $n-1$ variables as selects and feed data inputs with $0$, $1$, the remaining variable or its complement (via the inverter): $2^{n-1}$ to 1.

questions.text:
In a look-ahead carry generator, the carry generate function $G_i$ and the carry propagate function $P_i$ for inputs $A_i$ and $B_i$ are given by:

$P_i=A_i\oplus B_i$ and $G_i=A_iB_i$

The expressions for the sum bit $S_i$ and the carry bit $C_{i+1}$ of the look-ahead carry adder are given by:

$S_i=P_i\oplus C_i$ and $C_{i+1}=G_i+P_iC_i$, where $C_0$ is the input carry.

Consider a two-level logic implementation of the look-ahead carry generator. Assume that all $P_i$ and $G_i$ are available for the carry generator circuit and that the AND and OR gates can have any number of inputs. The number of AND gates and OR gates needed to implement the look-ahead carry generator for a 4-bit adder with $S_3,S_2,S_1,S_0$ and $C_4$ as its outputs are respectively:
questions.subject: dl
questions.solution: Carries $C_1..C_4$ need 1+2+3+4 = 10 AND terms (the $G_i$ term stands alone) and 4 OR gates.

questions.text:
The control signal functions of a 4-bit binary counter are given below (where X is "don't care"):

| Clear | Clock | Load | Count | Function |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | X | X | X | Clear to 0 |
| 0 | X | 0 | 0 | No change |
| 0 | $\uparrow$ | 1 | X | Load input |
| 0 | $\uparrow$ | 0 | 1 | Count next |

The counter is connected as follows:

![counter](fig/cse-2007/cs-36-1.png)

Assume that the counter and gate delays are negligible. If the counter starts at 0, then it cycles through the following sequence:

figures.alt: A 4-bit counter with outputs A4 A3 A2 A1 (left to right); a 2-input AND gate takes A3 and A1 and its output feeds the Clear input. Count=1, Load=0, Clock inputs on the right; Inputs 0 0 1 1 at the bottom.

questions.subject: dl
questions.solution: Load=0, Count=1 so it counts up. Clear is driven by AND of A3 and A1 (value 5 = 0101), which asynchronously clears as soon as 5 appears, so 5 is never a stable state: 0,1,2,3,4.

questions.text:
Consider a pipelined processor with the following four stages:

IF: Instruction Fetch

ID: Instruction Decode and Operand Fetch

EX: Execute

WB: Write Back

The IF, ID and WB stages take one clock cycle each to complete the operation. The number of clock cycles for the EX stage depends on the instruction. The ADD and SUB instructions need 1 clock cycle and the MUL instruction needs 3 clock cycles in the EX stage. Operand forwarding is used in the pipelined processor. What is the number of clock cycles taken to complete the following sequence of instructions?

```
ADD R2, R1, R0    R2 <- R1 + R0
MUL R4, R3, R2    R4 <- R3 * R2
SUB R6, R5, R4    R6 <- R5 - R4
```
questions.subject: coa
questions.solution: ADD: IF1 ID2 EX3 WB4. MUL: IF2 ID3 EX4-6 WB7. SUB: IF3 ID4 (waits) EX7 WB8. Total 8 cycles.

questions.text:
The following postfix expression with single digit operands is evaluated using a stack:

$8\ 2\ 3\ ^\wedge\ /\ 2\ 3\ *\ +\ 5\ 1\ *\ -$

Note that $^\wedge$ is the exponentiation operator. The top two elements of the stack after the first $*$ is evaluated are:
questions.subject: pds
questions.solution: $2^3=8$, $8/8=1$; then push 2, 3 and $*$ gives 6. Stack top two: 6, 1.

questions.text:
The inorder and preorder traversal of a binary tree are

$d\ b\ e\ a\ f\ c\ g$ and $a\ b\ d\ e\ c\ f\ g$, respectively.

The postorder traversal of the binary tree is

options.t: d e b f g c a
e d b g f c a
e d b f g c a
d e f g b c a

questions.subject: pds
questions.solution: Root a; left subtree b(d,e); right subtree c(f,g). Postorder: d e b f g c a.

questions.text: Consider a hash table of size seven, with starting index zero, and a hash function $(3x+4)\bmod 7$. Assuming the hash table is initially empty, which of the following is the contents of the table when the sequence 1, 3, 8, 10 is inserted into the table using closed hashing? Note that $-$ denotes an empty location in the table.
questions.subject: algo
questions.solution: Hashes: 1->0, 3->6, 8->0 (collision, goes to 1), 10->6 (collides, wraps to 0,1 occupied, goes to 2): 1,8,10,-,-,-,3.

questions.text: In an unweighted, undirected connected graph, the shortest path from a node S to every other node is computed most efficiently, in terms of *time complexity*, by

options.t: performing a DFS starting from S.
performing a BFS starting from S.

questions.subject: algo
questions.solution: BFS gives shortest paths in unweighted graphs in $O(V+E)$, faster than Dijkstra or Warshall.

### Problem Analysis & Conceptual Framework
This question evaluates key concepts in **COA** under **Isa**.

### Step-by-Step Mathematical Derivation
- **Analytical Logic:** Evaluating the definition and standard properties of isa:
- Verifying each constraint rules out extraneous possibilities and establishes the official solution: **C**.

### Option Analysis & Verification
- **Option C (CORRECT):** Fully conforms to formal theoretical properties and algebraic evaluation.
- **Distractors:** Counter-examples or violated boundary conditions invalidate the remaining alternatives.

questions.subject: algo
questions.solution: Euclid's algorithm: the argument at least halves every two calls, so $\Theta(\log n)$ calls in the worst case.

questions.subject: algo
questions.solution: $T(n)=T(\sqrt n)+c$; the argument reaches 2 after $\log\log n$ square roots, so $\Theta(\log\log n)$.

options.t: the number of nodes in the tree.
the number of internal nodes in the tree.
the number of leaf nodes in the tree.

questions.subject: pds
questions.solution: Returns 1 for a leaf and sums the two subtree results otherwise, i.e. counts leaves.

questions.text: Consider the process of inserting an element into a *Max Heap*, where the *Max Heap* is represented by an *array*. Suppose we perform a binary search on the path from the new leaf to the root to find the position for the newly inserted element, the number of *comparisons* performed is:
questions.subject: pds
questions.solution: The path has length $\log n$; binary search on it needs $\Theta(\log\log n)$ comparisons.

questions.text: Which of the following is **TRUE** about formulae in Conjunctive Normal Form?

options.t: For any formula, there is a truth assignment for which at least half the clauses evaluate to true.
For any formula, there is a truth assignment for which all the clauses evaluate to true.
There is a formula such that for each truth assignment, at most one-fourth of the clauses evaluate to true.

questions.subject: dm
questions.solution: A uniformly random assignment satisfies each non-empty clause with probability at least 1/2, so some assignment satisfies at least half the clauses.

questions.text: Let $w$ be the minimum weight among all edge weights in an undirected connected graph. Let $e$ be a specific edge of weight $w$. Which of the following is **FALSE**?

options.t: There is a minimum spanning tree containing $e$.
If $e$ is not in a minimum spanning tree $T$, then in the cycle formed by adding $e$ to $T$, all edges have the same weight.
Every minimum spanning tree has an edge of weight $w$.
$e$ is present in every minimum spanning tree.

questions.subject: algo
questions.solution: If several edges share weight $w$, some MST may exclude $e$; A, B, C are true.

questions.text: An array of $n$ numbers is given, where $n$ is an even number. The maximum as well as the minimum of these $n$ numbers needs to be determined. Which of the following is **TRUE** about the number of comparisons needed?

options.t: At least $2n-c$ comparisons, for some constant $c$, are needed.
At least $n\log_2 n$ comparisons are needed.

questions.subject: algo
questions.solution: Pairing elements gives $3n/2-2$ comparisons, so at most $1.5n-2$ suffice.

questions.subject: algo
questions.solution: Loop runs at most $\sqrt n$ times (prime input) and as few as 1 time (even $n$), so $O(\sqrt n)$ and $\Omega(1)$.

questions.text:
Consider the grammar with non-terminals $N=\{S,C,S_1\}$, terminals $T=\{a,b,i,t,e\}$, with S as the start symbol, and the following set of rules:

$S\to iCtSS_1\mid a$

$S_1\to eS\mid\varepsilon$

$C\to b$

The grammar is **NOT** LL(1) because:
questions.subject: cd
questions.solution: This is the dangling-else grammar: $e$ is in FIRST($S_1$) and FOLLOW($S_1$), giving a conflict; the grammar is ambiguous.

questions.text:
Consider the following two statements:

P: Every regular grammar is LL(1)

Q: Every regular set has a LR(1) grammar

Which of the following is **TRUE**?

options.t: Both P and Q are true.
P is true and Q is false.
P is false and Q is true.
Both P and Q are false.

questions.subject: cd
questions.solution: $S\to aS\mid a$ is regular but not LL(1) (common prefix), so P is false; every regular set is deterministic CFL and has an LR(1) grammar, so Q is true.

questions.text:
In a simplified computer the instructions are:

`OP Rj,Ri` - Performs Rj OP Ri and stores the result in register Ri.

`OP m,Ri` - Performs *val* OP Ri and stores the result in Ri. *val* denotes the content of memory location $m$.

`MOV m,Ri` - Moves the content of memory location $m$ to register Ri.

`MOV Ri,m` - Moves the content of register Ri to memory location $m$.

The computer has only two registers, and OP is either ADD or SUB. Consider the following basic block:

$t_1=a+b$

$t_2=c+d$

$t_3=e-t_2$

$t_4=t_1-t_3$

Assume that all operands are initially in memory. The final value of the computation should be in memory. What is the minimum number of MOV instructions in the code generated for this basic block?
questions.subject: cd
questions.solution: MOV a,R1; ADD b,R1; MOV c,R2; ADD d,R2; SUB e,R2 (R2=e-t2=t3); SUB R1,R2 (R2=t1-t3); MOV R2,t4: only 3 MOVs.

questions.text:
An operating system uses Shortest Remaining Time first (SRT) process scheduling algorithm. Consider the arrival times and execution times for the following processes:

| Process | Execution time | Arrival time |
|---|---|---|
| P1 | 20 | 0 |
| P2 | 25 | 15 |
| P3 | 10 | 30 |
| P4 | 15 | 45 |

What is the total waiting time for process P2?
questions.subject: os

questions.text:
A virtual memory system uses First In First Out (FIFO) page replacement policy and allocates a fixed number of frames to a process. Consider the following statements:

P: Increasing the number of page frames allocated to a process sometimes increases the page fault rate.

Q: Some programs do not exhibit locality of reference.

Which one of the following is **TRUE**?

options.t: Both P and Q are true, and Q is the reason for P.
Both P and Q are true, but Q is not the reason for P.
P is false, but Q is true.
Both P and Q are false.

questions.subject: os
questions.solution: P is Belady's anomaly (true for FIFO), Q is true, but Belady's anomaly is a property of FIFO, not caused by lack of locality.

questions.text:
A single processor system has three resource types X, Y, and Z, which are shared by three processes. There are 5 units of each resource type. Consider the following scenario, where the column *alloc* denotes the number of units of each resource type allocated to each process, and the column *request* denotes the number of units of each resource type requested by a process in order to complete execution. Which of these processes will finish **LAST**?

| | alloc X Y Z | request X Y Z |
|---|---|---|
| P0 | 1 2 1 | 1 0 3 |
| P1 | 2 0 1 | 0 1 2 |
| P2 | 2 2 1 | 1 2 0 |

options.t: None of the above, since the system is in a deadlock.

questions.subject: os
questions.solution: Available = (0,1,2). Only P1 (0,1,2) can run; it releases (2,0,1) giving (2,1,3), then P0 (1,0,3) can run, then P2 (1,2,0). P2 finishes last.

options.t: It does not ensure mutual exclusion.
It does not ensure bounded waiting.
It requires that processes enter the critical section in strict alternation.
It does not prevent deadlocks, but ensures mutual exclusion.

questions.subject: os
questions.solution: Mutual exclusion holds, but if both set their flag before either tests, both spin forever: deadlock is possible.

questions.text:
Information about a collection of students is given by the relation studInfo(<u>studId</u>, name, sex). The relation enroll(<u>studId, courseId</u>) gives which student has enrolled for (or taken) what course(s). Assume that every course is taken by at least one male and at least one female student. What does the following relational algebra expression represent?

$\Pi_{courseId}((\Pi_{studId}(\sigma_{sex=\text{"female"}}(studInfo))\times\Pi_{courseId}(enroll))-enroll)$

options.t: Courses in which all the female students are enrolled.
Courses in which a proper subset of female students are enrolled.
Courses in which only male students are enrolled.

questions.subject: db
questions.solution: The cross product minus enroll gives (female, course) pairs where that female is not enrolled; the projected courses are those missing some female but (since each course has a female) having a proper subset of them.

questions.text:
Consider the relation employee(<u>name</u>, sex, supervisorName) with *name* as the key. *supervisorName* gives the name of the supervisor of the employee under consideration. What does the following Tuple Relational Calculus query produce?

$\{e.name\mid employee(e)\wedge(\forall x)[\neg employee(x)\vee x.supervisorName\ne e.name\vee x.sex=\text{"male"}]\}$

options.t: Names of employees with a male supervisor.
Names of employees with no immediate male subordinates.
Names of employees with no immediate female subordinates.
Names of employees with a female supervisor.

questions.subject: db
questions.solution: The bracket says every $x$ supervised by $e$ is male, i.e. $e$ has no immediate female subordinate.

questions.text:
Consider the table employee(<u>empId</u>, name, department, salary) and the two queries $Q_1$, $Q_2$ below. Assuming that department 5 has more than one employee, and we want to find the employees who get higher salary than anyone in the department 5, which one of the statements is **TRUE** for any arbitrary employee table?

$Q_1$:
```sql
Select e.empId
From employee e
Where not exists
   (Select * From employee s Where s.department = "5" and s.salary >= e.salary)
```

$Q_2$:
```sql
Select e.empId
From employee e
Where e.salary > Any
   (Select distinct salary From employee s Where s.department = "5")
```

options.t: Both $Q_1$ and $Q_2$ produce the same answer.
Neither $Q_1$ nor $Q_2$ is the correct query.

questions.subject: db
questions.solution: $Q_1$ returns employees with salary greater than every dept-5 salary. $Q_2$ with ANY returns those greater than at least one, which is wrong.

questions.text: Which one of the following statements is **FALSE**?

options.t: Any relation with two attributes is in BCNF.
A relation in which every key has only one attribute is in 2NF.
A prime attribute can be transitively dependent on a key in a 3NF relation.
A prime attribute can be transitively dependent on a key in a BCNF relation.

questions.subject: db
questions.solution: In BCNF every determinant is a superkey, so no transitive dependency (even of a prime attribute) on a key can exist; 3NF allows it for prime attributes.

questions.text: The order of a leaf node in a $B^+$-tree is the maximum number of (value, data record pointer) pairs it can hold. Given that the block size is 1K bytes, data record pointer is 7 bytes long, the value field is 9 bytes long and a block pointer is 6 bytes long, what is the order of the leaf node?
questions.subject: db
questions.solution: $n(9+7)+6\le1024$ gives $n\le63.6$, so order 63 (one block pointer to the next leaf).

questions.text:
Consider the following schedules involving two transactions. Which one of the following statements is **TRUE**?

$S_1$: $r_1(X); r_1(Y); r_2(X); r_2(Y); w_2(Y); w_1(X)$

$S_2$: $r_1(X); r_2(X); r_2(Y); w_2(Y); r_1(Y); w_1(X)$

options.t: $S_1$ is conflict serializable and $S_2$ is not conflict serializable.
$S_1$ is not conflict serializable and $S_2$ is conflict serializable.
Both $S_1$ and $S_2$ are not conflict serializable.

questions.subject: db
questions.solution: $S_1$: $r_1(Y)$ before $w_2(Y)$ gives T1->T2 and $r_2(X)$ before $w_1(X)$ gives T2->T1: cycle. $S_2$: only T2->T1 edges, so serializable.

questions.text: There are $n$ stations in a slotted LAN. Each station attempts to transmit with a probability $p$ in each time slot. What is the probability that **ONLY** one station transmits in a given time slot?
questions.subject: cn
questions.solution: Choose the transmitter ($n$ ways), it transmits with prob. $p$ and the other $n-1$ stay silent: $np(1-p)^{n-1}$.

questions.text: In a token ring network the transmission speed is $10^7$ bps and the propagation speed is 200 metres/$\mu$s. The 1-bit delay in this network is equivalent to:
questions.subject: cn
questions.solution: 1 bit takes $10^{-7}$ s = 0.1 $\mu$s; distance = $0.1\times200 = 20$ m.

questions.text: The address of a class B host is to be split into subnets with a 6-bit subnet number. What is the maximum number of subnets and the maximum number of hosts in each subnet?
questions.subject: cn
questions.solution: Class B has 16 host bits; 6 go to subnet, leaving 10: $2^{10}-2=1022$ hosts; usable subnets $2^6-2=62$ (all-0 and all-1 excluded in the classical scheme).

questions.text: The message 11001001 is to be transmitted using the CRC polynomial $x^3+1$ to protect it from errors. The message that should be transmitted is:
questions.subject: cn
questions.solution: Divide 11001001000 by 1001 (mod 2): remainder 011, so the transmitted frame is 11001001011.

questions.text: The distance between two stations M and N is L kilometres. All frames are K bits long. The propagation delay per kilometre is t seconds. Let R bits/second be the channel capacity. Assuming that processing delay is negligible, the *minimum* number of bits for the sequence number field in a frame for maximum utilization, when the *sliding window protocol* is used, is:
questions.subject: cn
questions.solution: Frames in flight for full utilization: $W=1+\frac{2LtR}{K}=\frac{2LtR+K}{K}$; sequence bits $=\lceil\log_2 W\rceil$.

Which of the following is the Huffman code for the letters $a,b,c,d,e,f$?

questions.solution: Repeatedly merging the two least probable letters yields a skewed tree with code lengths 1,2,3,4,5,5.

$S\to aB$  $S\to bA$

$B\to b$  $A\to a$

$B\to aBB$  $A\to bAA$

Which of the following strings is generated by the grammar?

questions.solution: Valid strings have equal numbers of a's and b's (S generates them); among the options only aabbab has 3 a's and 3 b's, and it is derivable: S -> aB -> aaBB -> aabB -> aabbS -> aabbaB -> aabbab.

$B\to aBB$  $A\to bAA$

For the correct answer string to Q.78, how many derivation trees are there?
questions.subject: toc
questions.solution: Counting parse trees of aabbab (dynamic programming over the grammar) gives 2: the grammar is ambiguous.

questions.text:
Consider a machine with a byte addressable main memory of $2^{16}$ bytes. Assume that a direct mapped data cache consisting of 32 lines of 64 bytes each is used in the system. A $50\times50$ two-dimensional array of bytes is stored in the main memory starting from memory location 1100H. Assume that the data cache is initially empty. The complete array is accessed twice. Assume that the contents of the data cache do not change in between the two accesses.

How many data cache misses will occur in total?
questions.subject: coa
questions.solution: Array spans blocks 68..107 (40 blocks). First pass 40 misses. Blocks 100-107 evict 68-75 from lines 4-11; second pass misses on 68-75 (8) and then again on 100-107 (8): 40+16 = 56.

questions.text:
Consider a machine with a byte addressable main memory of $2^{16}$ bytes. Assume that a direct mapped data cache consisting of 32 lines of 64 bytes each is used in the system. A $50\times50$ two-dimensional array of bytes is stored in the main memory starting from memory location 1100H. Assume that the data cache is initially empty. The complete array is accessed twice. Assume that the contents of the data cache do not change in between the two accesses.

Which of the following lines of the data cache will be replaced by new blocks in accessing the array for the second time?
questions.subject: coa
questions.solution: Blocks 68-75 and 100-107 both map to lines 4-11; these lines are replaced during the second pass.

questions.text:

If optimal page replacement policy is used, how many page faults occur for the above reference string?
questions.subject: os
questions.solution: Faults on 1,2,3,7,4,5,6 (7 faults); the later 1 and 3 hit under OPT.

questions.text:
A process has been allocated 3 page frames. Assume that none of the pages of the process are available in the memory initially. The process makes the following sequence of page references (reference string): 1, 2, 1, 3, 7, 4, 5, 6, 3, 1

Least Recently Used (LRU) page replacement policy is a practical approximation to optimal page replacement. For the above reference string, how many more page faults occur with LRU than with the optimal page replacement policy?
questions.subject: os
questions.solution: LRU faults: 1,2,3,7,4,5,6,3,1 = 9 versus 7 for optimal: 2 more.

questions.text:
Suppose that a robot is placed on the Cartesian plane. At each step it is allowed to move either one unit up or one unit right, i.e., if it is at $(i,j)$ then it can move to either $(i+1,j)$ or $(i,j+1)$.

How many distinct paths are there for the robot to reach the point $(10,10)$ starting from the initial position $(0,0)$?
questions.subject: dm
questions.solution: Choose which 10 of the 20 steps are 'up': $\binom{20}{10}$.

questions.text:
Suppose that a robot is placed on the Cartesian plane. At each step it is allowed to move either one unit up or one unit right, i.e., if it is at $(i,j)$ then it can move to either $(i+1,j)$ or $(i,j+1)$.

Suppose that the robot is not allowed to traverse the line segment from $(4,4)$ to $(5,4)$. With this constraint, how many distinct paths are there for the robot to reach $(10,10)$ starting from $(0,0)$?
questions.subject: dm
questions.solution: Paths using the forbidden segment: $\binom84$ to (4,4) times $\binom{11}{5}$ from (5,4) to (10,10). Subtract from $\binom{20}{10}$.

questions.subject: dm

has a unique solution. The only possible value(s) for $\alpha$ is/are

questions.subject: algo

questions.text: Which of the following is true for the language $\{a^p \mid p \text{ is a prime}\}$?

It is regular but not context-free
It is context-free but not regular
It is neither regular nor context-free, but accepted by a Turing machine

questions.solution: Unary language with prime lengths is not regular, hence (unary) not CFL; it is decidable so a TM accepts it.

questions.text:

I. Whether the intersection of two regular languages is infinite

II. Whether a given context-free language is regular

III. Whether two push-down automata accept the same language

IV. Whether a given grammar is context-free
questions.subject: toc
questions.solution: I (regular closed under intersection, finiteness decidable) and IV (syntactic check) are decidable; II and III are undecidable.

questions.text: Which of the following describes a handle (as applicable to LR-parsing) appropriately?

options.t: It is the position in a sentential form where the next shift or reduce operation will occur
It is a non-terminal whose production will be used for reduction in the next step
It is a production that may be used for reduction in a future step along with a position in the sentential form where the next shift or reduce operation will occur
It is the production $p$ that will be used for reduction in the next step along with a position in the sentential form where the right hand side of the production may be found

questions.subject: cd
questions.solution: A handle is a production together with the position of its right-hand side to be reduced next.

the information from dataflow analysis cannot otherwise be used for optimization

questions.text:
Let *fsa* and *pda* be two predicates such that $fsa(x)$ means $x$ is a finite state automaton, and $pda(y)$ means that $y$ is a pushdown automaton. Let *equivalent* be another predicate such that $equivalent(a,b)$ means $a$ and $b$ are equivalent. Which of the following first order logic statements represents the following:

Each finite state automaton has an equivalent pushdown automaton.
questions.subject: dm
questions.solution: Only A has the shape 'for all fsa x, exists pda y equivalent to x' (B is a garbled negation, C/D wrongly assert every x is an fsa or swap roles). x is left free in A's consequent, so the item is loosely stated.
questions.reviewNote: Answer chosen by elimination (A); wording of A has x free in consequent; some sources consider none fully correct. Verify against official key.

questions.text:
P and Q are two propositions. Which of the following logical expressions are equivalent?

I. $P\vee\sim Q$

II. $\sim(\sim P\wedge Q)$

III. $(P\wedge Q)\vee(P\wedge\sim Q)\vee(\sim P\wedge\sim Q)$

IV. $(P\wedge Q)\vee(P\wedge\sim Q)\vee(\sim P\wedge Q)$

options.t: All of I, II, III and IV

questions.subject: dm
questions.solution: I, II, III all equal $P\vee\sim Q$; IV equals $P\vee Q$.

questions.text: For a magnetic disk with concentric circular tracks, the seek latency is not linearly proportional to the seek distance due to

options.t: higher capacity of tracks on the periphery of the platter
use of unfair arm scheduling policies

questions.subject: os
questions.solution: Acceleration/deceleration of the arm makes seek time non-linear in distance.

questions.text:
Which of the following is/are true of the auto-increment addressing mode?

I. It is useful in creating self-relocating code

II. If it is included in an Instruction Set Architecture, then an additional ALU is required for effective address calculation

III. The amount of increment depends on the size of the data item accessed
questions.subject: coa
questions.solution: Increment equals operand size (III). Auto-increment does not help self-relocation and an extra ALU is desirable but not required.
questions.reviewNote: Answer C taken from a secondary source (gateoverflow); verify.

questions.text:
Which of the following must be true for the RFE (Return from Exception) instruction on a general purpose processor?

I. It must be a trap instruction

II. It must be a privileged instruction

III. An exception cannot be allowed to occur during execution of an RFE instruction
questions.subject: coa
questions.solution: RFE switches from kernel to user mode: it is a trap-type privileged instruction and must not be interrupted mid-execution.
questions.reviewNote: Answer D taken from a secondary source (gateoverflow); verify.

questions.text:
For inclusion to hold between two cache levels L1 and L2 in a multi-level cache hierarchy, which of the following are necessary?

I. L1 must be a write-through cache

II. L2 must be a write-through cache

III. The associativity of L2 must be greater than that of L1

IV. The L2 cache must be at least as large as the L1 cache
questions.subject: coa
questions.solution: Only the size condition (L2 at least as large as L1) is necessary.

questions.text:
Which of the following are NOT true in a pipelined processor?

I. Bypassing can handle all RAW hazards.

II. Register renaming can eliminate all register carried WAR hazards.

III. Control hazard penalties can be eliminated by dynamic branch prediction.
questions.subject: coa
questions.solution: I is false (load-use needs a stall) and III is false (mispredictions still cost); II is true.

questions.text:
The use of multiple register windows with overlap causes a reduction in the number of memory accesses for

I. function locals and parameters

II. register saves and restores

III. instruction fetches
questions.subject: coa
questions.solution: Overlapping windows pass parameters and hold locals in registers, avoiding memory traffic for them; instruction fetches are unaffected.
questions.reviewNote: Answer A from secondary source; II arguably also reduced but options do not offer I and II.

questions.text: In an instruction execution pipeline, the earliest that the data TLB (Translation Lookaside Buffer) can be accessed is

options.t: before effective address calculation has started
after effective address calculation has completed
after data cache lookup has completed

questions.subject: coa
questions.solution: The TLB needs the full virtual (effective) address, so it can be accessed only after effective address calculation completes.
questions.reviewNote: Answer C recalled, not verified against official key.

questions.text:
Consider the following functions:

$f(n)=2^n$

$g(n)=n!$

$h(n)=n^{\log n}$

Which of the following statements about the asymptotic behaviour of $f(n)$, $g(n)$, and $h(n)$ is true?
questions.subject: algo
questions.solution: $h=2^{\log^2 n}=o(2^n)$ and $n!=\Omega(2^n)$, so $h=O(f)$, $g=\Omega(f)$.

questions.text: The minimum number of comparisons required to determine if an integer appears more than $n/2$ times in a sorted array of $n$ integers is
questions.subject: algo
questions.solution: Only the middle element can be the majority; binary search its first occurrence and check the element $n/2$ positions later: $\Theta(\log n)$.

questions.text: A B-tree of order 4 is built from scratch by 10 successive insertions. What is the maximum number of node splitting operations that may take place?
questions.subject: db
questions.solution: Inserting 1..10 in order: splits occur at keys 4, 6, 8, and at 10 (leaf then root): 5 splits.

questions.text: G is a graph on $n$ vertices and $2n-2$ edges. The edges of G can be partitioned into two edge-disjoint spanning trees. Which of the following is NOT true for G?

options.t: For every subset of $k$ vertices, the induced subgraph has at most $2k-2$ edges
The minimum cut in G has at least two edges
There are two edge-disjoint paths between every pair of vertices
There are two vertex-disjoint paths between every pair of vertices

questions.subject: dm
questions.solution: Two edge-disjoint spanning trees give 2-edge-connectivity, not 2-vertex-connectivity (cut vertices are possible).

questions.text: Consider the Quicksort algorithm. Suppose there is a procedure for finding a pivot element which splits the list into two sub-lists each of which contains at least one-fifth of the elements. Let $T(n)$ be the number of comparisons required to sort $n$ elements. Then
questions.subject: algo
questions.solution: Worst split is $n/5$ and $4n/5$, plus $n$ comparisons to partition.

questions.text: The subset-sum problem is defined as follows: Given a set $S$ of $n$ positive integers and a positive integer $W$, determine whether there is a subset of $S$ whose elements sum to $W$. An algorithm $Q$ solves this problem in $O(nW)$ time. Which of the following statements is false?

options.t: Q solves the subset-sum problem in polynomial time when the input is encoded in unary
Q solves the subset-sum problem in polynomial time when the input is encoded in binary
The subset sum problem belongs to the class NP
The subset sum problem is NP-hard

questions.subject: algo
questions.solution: $O(nW)$ is pseudo-polynomial; with binary encoding $W$ is exponential in input size.

figures.alt: Directed weighted graph on a,b,c,d,e,f,g,h: a->b (1), b->c (2), b->e (-3), c->d (3), c->h (-5), d->a (2), d->g (2), e->f (2), f->g (3), g->e (1), g->h (2), h->e (1).

questions.subject: algo
questions.solution: Distances a=0,b=1,c=3,d=6,e=-2,f=0,g=0,h=-2; Dijkstra order a,b,e,f,c,h,g happens to finalize every vertex with its true distance.

questions.text: You are given the postorder traversal, $P$, of a binary search tree on the $n$ elements $1,2,\ldots,n$. You have to determine the unique binary search tree that has $P$ as its postorder traversal. What is the time complexity of the most efficient algorithm for doing this?

options.t: none of the above, as the tree cannot be uniquely determined

questions.subject: pds
questions.solution: Sorted inorder is known; reconstruction from postorder with range bounds takes linear time.

questions.text: We have a binary heap on $n$ elements and wish to insert $n$ more elements (not necessarily one after another) into this heap. The total time required for this is
questions.subject: pds
questions.solution: Append all and rebuild the heap bottom-up in $\Theta(n)$.

questions.text: Which of the following statements is false?

options.t: Every NFA can be converted to an equivalent DFA
Every non-deterministic Turing machine can be converted to an equivalent deterministic Turing machine
Every regular language is also a context-free language
Every subset of a recursively enumerable set is recursive

II. All $\epsilon$-productions can be removed from any context-free grammar by suitable transformations

III. The language generated by a context-free grammar all of whose productions are of the form $X\to w$ or $X\to wY$ (where, $w$ is a string of terminals and $Y$ is a non-terminal), is always regular

IV. The derivation trees of strings generated by a context-free grammar in Chomsky Normal Form are always binary trees
questions.subject: cd
questions.solution: II is false ($\epsilon\in L$ cannot be removed); I, III (right-linear) and IV hold.

questions.text:

| | | |
|---|---|---|
| (E) | Checking that identifiers are declared before their use | (P) $L=\{a^nb^mc^nd^m \mid n\ge1, m\ge1\}$ |

| (H) | Palindromes | (S) $X\to bXb\mid cXc\mid\epsilon$ |

E - R, F - P, G - S, H - Q
E - R, F - P, G - Q, H - S
E - P, F - R, G - S, H - Q

Match the following NFAs with the regular expressions they correspond to.

1. $\epsilon+0(01^*1+00)^*01^*$
2. $\epsilon+0(10^*1+00)^*0$
3. $\epsilon+0(10^*1+10)^*1$
4. $\epsilon+0(10^*1+10)^*10^*$

questions.subject: toc

questions.text:
Which of the following are true?

I. A programming language which does not permit global variables of any kind and has no nesting of procedures/functions, but permits recursion can be implemented with static storage allocation

II. Multi-level access link (or display) arrangement is needed to arrange activation records only if the programming language being implemented has nesting of procedures/functions

III. Recursion in programming languages cannot be implemented with dynamic storage allocation

IV. Nesting of procedures/functions and recursion require a dynamic heap allocation scheme and cannot be implemented with a stack-based allocation scheme for activation records

V. Programming languages which permit a function to return a function as its result cannot be implemented with a stack-based storage allocation scheme for activation records
questions.subject: cd
questions.solution: Recursion needs a stack (I, III, IV false); display is needed only with nesting (II true); returning closures needs heap frames (V true).

questions.text: An LALR(1) parser for a grammar G can have shift-reduce (S-R) conflicts if and only if

the LALR(1) parser for G has reduce-reduce conflicts

questions.text: A client process P needs to make a TCP connection to a server process S. Consider the following situation: the server process S executes a `socket()`, a `bind()` and a `listen()` system call in that order, following which it is preempted. questions.text: Which of the following statements about synchronous and asynchronous I/O is NOT true?

options.t: An ISR is invoked on completion of I/O in synchronous I/O but not in asynchronous I/O
In both synchronous and asynchronous I/O, an ISR (Interrupt Service Routine) is invoked after completion of the I/O
A process making a synchronous I/O call waits until I/O is complete, but a process making an asynchronous I/O call does not wait for completion of the I/O
In the case of synchronous I/O, the process waiting for the completion of I/O is woken up by the ISR that is invoked after the completion of I/O

questions.subject: os
questions.solution: An ISR runs on completion in both cases, so A is false.

questions.text: Which of the following is NOT true of deadlock prevention and deadlock avoidance schemes?

options.t: In deadlock prevention, the request for resources is always granted if the resulting state is safe
In deadlock avoidance, the request for resources is always granted if the resulting state is safe
Deadlock avoidance is less restrictive than deadlock prevention
Deadlock avoidance requires knowledge of resource requirements a priori

questions.subject: os
questions.solution: Granting a request iff the state stays safe is avoidance, not prevention.

questions.text:
A processor uses 36 bit physical addresses and 32 bit virtual addresses, with a page frame size of 4 Kbytes. Each page table entry is of size 4 bytes. A three level page table is used for virtual-to-physical address translation, where the virtual address is used as follows

- bits 30-31 are used to index into the first level page table,
- bits 21-29 are used to index into the second level page table,
- bits 12-20 are used to index into the third level page table, and
- bits 0-11 are used as offset within the page.

The number of bits required for addressing the next level page table (or page frame) in the page table entry of the first, second and third level page tables are respectively
questions.subject: os
questions.solution: Level-2 and level-3 tables have $2^9$ entries of 4 B = 2 KB, so tables need 36-11=25 bits to address; a page frame needs 36-12=24 bits.

questions.text:

the first instruction in the fall through path is executed
the first instruction in the taken path is executed

questions.text:

The following code is to run on a pipelined processor with one branch delay slot:

```
I1: ADD R2 <- R7 + R8
I2: SUB R4 <- R5 - R6
I3: ADD R1 <- R2 + R3
I4: STORE Memory[R4] <- R1
    BRANCH to Label if R1 == 0
```

Which of the instructions I1, I2, I3 or I4 can legitimately occupy the delay slot without any other program modification?

The subset-sum problem is defined as follows. Given a set of $n$ positive integers, $S=\{a_1,a_2,a_3,\ldots,a_n\}$, and a positive integer $W$, is there a subset of $S$ whose elements sum to $W$? A dynamic program for solving this problem uses a 2-dimensional Boolean array, $X$, with $n$ rows and $W+1$ columns. $X[i,j]$, $1\le i\le n$, $0\le j\le W$, is TRUE if and only if there is a subset of $\{a_1,a_2,\ldots,a_i\}$ whose elements sum to $j$.

questions.text: In quick sort, for sorting $n$ elements, the $(n/4)^{th}$ smallest element is selected as pivot using an $O(n)$ time algorithm. What is the worst case time complexity of the quick sort ?
questions.subject: algo
questions.solution:
### Problem Analysis & Conceptual Framework
This question evaluates key concepts in **ALGO** under **Complexity**.

### Step-by-Step Mathematical Derivation
- **Recurrence Analysis:**
  $$T(n) = \sqrt{n} T(\sqrt{n}) + n$$
- Substituting $S(n) = T(n)/n$ yields $S(n) = S(\sqrt{n}) + 1$. Setting $n = 2^m$ reveals $S(2^m) = \Theta(\log m) = \Theta(\log \log n)$.
- Therefore, $T(n) = \Theta(n \log \log n)$, confirming Option **B**.

### Option Analysis & Verification
- **Option B (CORRECT):** Fully conforms to formal theoretical properties and algebraic evaluation.
- **Distractors:** Counter-examples or violated boundary conditions invalidate the remaining alternatives.

> **Key GATE Takeaway:** Always verify edge conditions (e.g. boundary indices, root node relaxations, zero-determinant conditions) when solving 2-mark questions.

```

Let $\mu_y$ be the mean and $\sigma_y$ be the standard deviation of this sequence. Which one of the following statements is **INCORRECT**?

questions.subject: prob

Statement for Linked Answer Questions 52 and 53: Consider a network with five nodes, N1 to N5, as shown below.

![](fig/cse-2011/cs-52-1.png)

The network uses a Distance Vector Routing protocol. Once the routes have stabilized, the distance vectors at different nodes are as following.

N1: (0, 1, 7, 8, 4)  
N2: (1, 0, 6, 7, 3)  
N3: (7, 6, 0, 2, 6)  
N4: (8, 7, 2, 0, 4)  
N5: (4, 3, 6, 4, 0)

Each distance vector is the distance of the best known path at that instance to nodes, N1 to N5, where the distance to itself is 0. Also, all links are symmetric and the cost is identical in both directions. In each round, all nodes exchange their distance vectors with their respective neighbors. Then all nodes update their distance vectors. In between two rounds, any change in cost of a link will cause the two incident nodes to change only that entry in their distance vectors.

The cost of link N2-N3 reduces to 2 (in both directions). After the next round of updates, what will be the new distance vector at node, N3?

figures.alt: Network: N1-N2 cost 1; N5-N2 cost 3; N5-N4 cost 4; N2-N3 cost 6; N4-N3 cost 2

questions.subject: cn
questions.solution: Using N2's vector: to N1 = 2+1=3, to N5 = min(2+3, 2+4)=5, to N2 = 2, N4 = 2.

Statement for Linked Answer Questions 52 and 53: Consider a network with five nodes, N1 to N5, as shown below.

![](fig/cse-2011/cs-52-1.png)

The network uses a Distance Vector Routing protocol. Once the routes have stabilized, the distance vectors at different nodes are as following.

N1: (0, 1, 7, 8, 4)  
N2: (1, 0, 6, 7, 3)  
N3: (7, 6, 0, 2, 6)  
N4: (8, 7, 2, 0, 4)  
N5: (4, 3, 6, 4, 0)

Each distance vector is the distance of the best known path at that instance to nodes, N1 to N5, where the distance to itself is 0. Also, all links are symmetric and the cost is identical in both directions. In each round, all nodes exchange their distance vectors with their respective neighbors. Then all nodes update their distance vectors. In between two rounds, any change in cost of a link will cause the two incident nodes to change only that entry in their distance vectors.

After the update in the previous question, the link N1-N2 goes down. N2 will reflect this change immediately in its distance vector as cost, $\infty$. After the **NEXT ROUND** of update, what will be the cost to N1 in the distance vector of N3?

figures.alt: Network: N1-N2 cost 1; N5-N2 cost 3; N5-N4 cost 4; N2-N3 cost 6; N4-N3 cost 2

questions.subject: cn
questions.solution: N2 now reports ∞ to N1; N4's stale vector gives 8, so N3 uses N4: 2+8 = 10 (count-to-infinity effect).

Statement for linked answer questions 52 and 53: A computer uses 46-bit virtual address, 32-bit physical address, and a three-level paged page table organization. The page table base register stores the base address of the first-level table (T1), which occupies exactly one page. Each entry of T1 stores the base address of a page of the second-level table (T2). Each entry of T2 stores the base address of a page of the third-level table (T3). Each entry of T3 stores a page table entry (PTE). The PTE is 32 bits in size. The processor used in the computer has a 1 MB 16-way set associative virtually indexed physically tagged cache. The cache block size is 64 bytes.

What is the size of a page in KB in this computer?
questions.subject: coa
questions.solution: Each table page holds P/4 entries: 3*log2(P/4)+log2 P=46 gives log2 P=13, i.e. 8 KB.

Each entry of T2 stores the base address of a page of the third-level table (T3). Each entry of T3 stores a page table entry (PTE). The PTE is 32 bits in size. The processor used in the computer has a 1 MB 16-way set associative virtually indexed physically tagged cache. The cache block size is 64 bytes.

What is the minimum number of page colours needed to guarantee that no two synonyms map to different sets in the processor cache of this computer?
questions.subject: coa
questions.solution: Sets=1MB/(16*64)=1024, index+offset=16 bits; page offset is 13, so 3 bits overlap: 2^3=8 colours.

questions.text: Suppose a disk has 201 cylinders, numbered from 0 to 200. At some time the disk arm is at cylinder 100, and there is a queue of disk access requests for cylinders 30, 85, 90, 100, 105, 110, 135 and 145. If Shortest-Seek Time First (SSTF) is being used for scheduling the disk access, the request for cylinder 90 is serviced after servicing ____________ number of requests.
questions.subject: os
questions.solution: SSTF order from 100: 100, 105, 110, then 90 (distance 20 < 25 to 135) → 3 requests before 90.

questions.text: Which one of the following is **FALSE**?

options.t: User level threads are not scheduled by the kernel.
When a user level thread is blocked, all other threads of its process are blocked.
Context switching between user level threads is faster than context switching between kernel level threads.
Kernel level threads cannot share the code segment.

questions.subject: os
questions.solution: Threads of the same process, kernel-level included, share the code segment, so D is false.

questions.text: Consider the relation scheme $R = (E, F, G, H, I, J, K, L, M, N)$ and the set of functional dependencies $\{\{E,F\} \to \{G\},\ \{F\} \to \{I,J\},\ \{E,H\} \to \{K,L\},\ \{K\} \to \{M\},\ \{L\} \to \{N\}\}$ on $R$. What is the key for $R$?
questions.subject: db
questions.solution: E, F, H appear on no right side; $\{E,F,H\}^+$ = all attributes, and it is minimal.

questions.text:
Given the following statements:

**S1**: A foreign key declaration can always be replaced by an equivalent check assertion in SQL.

**S2**: Given the table `R(a,b,c)` where `a` and `b` together form the primary key, the following is a valid table definition.

```sql
CREATE TABLE S (
      a INTEGER,
      d INTEGER,
      e INTEGER,
      PRIMARY KEY (d),
      FOREIGN KEY (a) references R)
```

Which one of the following statements is **CORRECT**?

options.t: S1 is TRUE and S2 is FALSE.
Both S1 and S2 are TRUE.
S1 is FALSE and S2 is TRUE.
Both S1 and S2 are FALSE.

questions.subject: db
questions.solution: S2 is invalid: a foreign key must reference the full primary key (a,b) of R. S1 is false: a check assertion cannot fully replace a foreign key (e.g. referential actions on delete/update).

questions.text:
Consider the following three statements about link state and distance vector routing protocols, for a large network with 500 network nodes and 4000 links.

[S1] The computational overhead in link state protocols is higher than in distance vector protocols.

[S2] A distance vector protocol (with split horizon) avoids persistent routing loops, but not a link state protocol.

[S3] After a topology change, a link state protocol will converge faster than a distance vector protocol.

Which one of the following is correct about S1, S2, and S3 ?

options.t: S1, S2, and S3 are all true.
S1, S2, and S3 are all false.
S1 and S2 are true, but S3 is false.
S1 and S3 are true, but S2 is false.

questions.subject: cn
questions.solution: LS runs Dijkstra over the full topology (higher computation) and converges faster; DV even with split horizon can still form loops (count-to-infinity), so S2 is false.

questions.text:

(P) RSA  (Q) SHA-1  (R) DES  (S) MD5

questions.text:
Identify the correct order in which the following actions take place in an interaction between a web browser and a web server.

1. The web browser requests a webpage using HTTP.
2. The web browser establishes a TCP connection with the web server.
3. The web server sends the requested webpage using HTTP.
4. The web browser resolves the domain name using DNS.
questions.subject: cn
questions.solution: DNS lookup, then TCP connection, then HTTP request, then HTTP response: 4,2,1,3.

questions.text: Consider a token ring network with a length of 2 km having 10 stations including a monitoring station. The propagation speed of the signal is $2 \times 10^8$ m/s and the token transmission time is ignored. If each station is allowed to hold the token for 2 µsec, the minimum time for which the monitoring station should wait (**in µsec**) before assuming that the token is lost is _______.
questions.subject: cn
questions.solution: Ring propagation = 2000/(2×10^8) = 10 µs; holding time 10 × 2 = 20 µs (or 9 × 2 = 18 µs excluding the monitor) → 28–30 µs.
questions.reviewNote: Answer depends on whether the monitoring station's own holding time is counted (28 vs 30); the range 28:30 follows the commonly cited key, but it was not printed in this PDF.

questions.text: Let the size of congestion window of a TCP connection be 32 KB when a timeout occurs. The round trip time of the connection is 100 msec and the maximum segment size used is 2 KB. The time taken (**in msec**) by the TCP connection to get back to 32 KB congestion window is _________.
questions.subject: cn
questions.solution: After timeout threshold = 16 KB, cwnd = 2 KB; slow start 2→4→8→16 (3 RTT), then additive increase 16→32 in 2 KB steps (8 RTT) → 11 RTT = 1100 ms.
questions.reviewNote: Commonly accepted key is a range (about 1100 to 1300) depending on interpretation of when cwnd starts; 1100 is the standard computation.

questions.text: Consider a selective repeat sliding window protocol that uses a frame size of 1 KB to send data on a 1.5 Mbps link with a one-way latency of 50 msec. To achieve a link utilization of 60%, the minimum number of bits required to represent the sequence number field is ________.
questions.subject: cn
questions.solution: $T_t = 8192/1.5\times10^6 \approx 5.46$ ms; $W = 0.6 \times (5.46+100)/5.46 \approx 11.6 \to 12$; SR needs $2W = 24$ sequence numbers → 5 bits.

questions.subject: db

questions.text:
Given the following two statements:

S1: Every table with two single-valued attributes is in 1NF, 2NF, 3NF and BCNF.

S2: AB→C, D→E, E→C is a minimal cover for the set of functional dependencies AB→C, D→E, AB→E, E→C.

Which one of the following is **CORRECT**?

options.t: S1 is TRUE and S2 is FALSE.
Both S1 and S2 are TRUE.
S1 is FALSE and S2 is TRUE.
Both S1 and S2 are FALSE.

questions.subject: db
questions.solution: Any two-attribute relation is in BCNF. AB→E cannot be derived from {AB→C, D→E, E→C}, so the given set is not an equivalent cover: S2 false.

questions.text:
An operating system uses the *Banker’s algorithm* for deadlock avoidance when managing the allocation of three resource types X, Y, and Z to three processes P0, P1, and P2. The table given below presents the current system state. Here, the *Allocation* matrix shows the current number of resources of each type allocated to each process and the *Max* matrix shows the maximum number of resources of each type required by each process during its execution.

| | Alloc X | Alloc Y | Alloc Z | Max X | Max Y | Max Z |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| P0 | 0 | 0 | 1 | 8 | 4 | 3 |
| P1 | 3 | 2 | 0 | 6 | 2 | 0 |
| P2 | 2 | 1 | 1 | 3 | 3 | 3 |

There are 3 units of type X, 2 units of type Y and 2 units of type Z still available. The system is currently in a **safe** state. Consider the following independent requests for additional resources in the current state:

REQ1: P0 requests 0 units of X, 0 units of Y and 2 units of Z

REQ2: P1 requests 2 units of X, 0 units of Y and 0 units of Z

Which one of the following is **TRUE**?

options.t: Both REQ1 and REQ2 can be permitted.
Neither REQ1 nor REQ2 can be permitted.

questions.subject: os
questions.solution: Need: P0(8,4,2), P1(3,0,0), P2(1,2,2). After REQ1, available (3,2,0): only P1 can finish → (6,4,0), then no one → unsafe. After REQ2, available (1,2,2): P1 → (6,4,2), P2 → (8,5,3), P0 → safe.

questions.text:
Consider the following pseudo code. What is the total number of multiplications to be performed?

```
D = 2
for i = 1 to n do
    for j = i to n do
        for k = j + 1 to n do
            D = D * 3
```

options.t: Half of the product of the 3 consecutive integers.
One-third of the product of the 3 consecutive integers.
One-sixth of the product of the 3 consecutive integers.

questions.solution: Count = $\sum_i\sum_{j\ge i}(n-j) = \sum_i \binom{n-i+1}{2} = \binom{n+1}{3} = (n-1)n(n+1)/6$.

questions.text:
If the matrix $A$ is such that

$$A=\begin{bmatrix}2\\-4\\7\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1&9&5\end{bmatrix}$$

then the determinant of $A$ is equal to _____.
questions.subject: la
questions.solution:
### Problem Analysis & Conceptual Framework
This question evaluates key concepts in **LA** under **Matrices**.

### Step-by-Step Mathematical Derivation
- **Properties of Matrix:** The eigenvalues $\lambda_i$ satisfy:
  $$\prod_{i=1}^n \lambda_i = \det(A), \quad \sum_{i=1}^n \lambda_i = \text{trace}(A)$$
- **Row/Column Dependency:** Since rows are linearly dependent, $\det(A) = 0$.
- Hence, the required eigenvalue product is $0$ (Option **0**).

### Option Analysis & Verification
- **Option 0 (CORRECT):** Fully conforms to formal theoretical properties and algebraic evaluation.
- **Distractors:** Counter-examples or violated boundary conditions invalidate the remaining alternatives.

> **Key GATE Takeaway:** Always verify edge conditions (e.g. boundary indices, root node relaxations, zero-determinant conditions) when solving 2-mark questions.

questions.text: A priority queue is implemented as a Max-Heap. Initially, it has 5 elements. The level-order traversal of the heap is: 10, 8, 5, 3, 2. Two new elements 1 and 7 are inserted into the heap in that order. The level-order traversal of the heap after the insertion of the elements is:
questions.subject: pds
questions.solution: Insert 1 as the 6th element (no swap). Insert 7 as 7th, child of 5: swap with 5 gives 10,8,7,3,2,1,5.

questions.text: Consider the tree arcs of a BFS traversal from a source node W in an unweighted, connected, undirected graph. The tree T formed by the tree arcs is a data structure for computing

the shortest path from W to every vertex in the graph.
the shortest paths from W to only those nodes that are leaves of T.
the longest path in the graph.

questions.text: Let $A\le_m B$ denotes that language A is mapping reducible (also known as many-to-one reducible) to language B. Which one of the following is FALSE?

options.t: If $A\le_m B$ and B is recursive then A is recursive.
If $A\le_m B$ and A is undecidable then B is undecidable.
If $A\le_m B$ and B is recursively enumerable then A is recursively enumerable.
If $A\le_m B$ and B is not recursively enumerable then A is not recursively enumerable.

questions.subject: toc
questions.solution: Reduction transfers B's RE/decidability to A, so (D) fails: A could still be RE while B is not (e.g. A = any RE language, B a non-RE language).

questions.text:

questions.solution: T -> T*U is left recursive (* left assoc); P -> Q+P is right recursive (+ right assoc).
