questions.text:
Consider the CPM activity chart where an arc connecting two milestones is labeled with a task identifier and the time taken in days. For example in order to go from A to B, task T1 takes 180 days. A dashed line depicts an additional dependency that is equivalent to a zero time task.

The set of activities that lie on the critical path are

figures.alt: Nodes A..K. Arcs: A->B T1:180; B->C T2:14; B->D T3:1; B->E T4:7; E->G T5:40; E->H T6:20; G->I T7:5; I->J T8:1; B->F T9:40; J->K T10:1. Dashed zero-time dependencies: C->I, D->G, H->I, F->J.

questions.subject: legacy
questions.solution: Longest path A-B-E-G-I-J-K: 180 + 7 + 40 + 5 + 1 + 1 = 234 days (other routes: via H 27, via C 14, via F 40 into J).
questions.reviewNote: Some arc labels are blurry (E->H task label read as T6:20; B->F as T9:40).

questions.text:
Consider the following pseudo-code:

```
IF ((A > B) AND (C > D)) THEN
    A = A + 1
    B = B + 1
ENDIF
```

The cyclomatic complexity of the pseudo-code is
questions.subject: legacy
questions.solution: The compound condition contains two predicates (A>B and C>D), each counted as a decision: V(G) = 2 + 1 = 3.
questions.reviewNote: Answer depends on counting a compound condition as two predicates (3); counting the IF once would give 2.

questions.text:
Synchronization in the classical readers and writers problem can be achieved through use of semaphores. In the following incomplete code for readers-writers problem, two binary semaphores mutex and wrt are used to obtain synchronization.

Writer:
```
wait (wrt)
writing is performed
signal (wrt)
```

Reader:
```
wait (mutex)
readcount = readcount + 1
if readcount = 1 then S1
S2
reading is performed
S3
readcount = readcount - 1
if readcount = 0 then S4
signal (mutex)
```

The values of S1, S2, S3, S4 (in that order) are
questions.subject: os
questions.solution: First reader locks writers: S1 = wait(wrt); then release mutex: S2 = signal(mutex). After reading re-acquire it: S3 = wait(mutex); last reader lets writers in: S4 = signal(wrt).

questions.text: In a multi-user operating system, on an average, 20 requests are made to use a particular resource per hour. The arrival of requests follows a Poisson distribution. The probability that either one, three or five requests are made in 45 minutes is given by
questions.subject: prob
questions.reviewNote: Exponent of e is printed as -20 in the scan (resolution is poor; the correct value is e^-15); option C is the only one with the right coefficient.

questions.text: A demand paging system takes 100 time units to service a page fault and 300 time units to replace a dirty page. Memory access time is 1 time unit. The probability of a page fault is p. In case of a page fault, the probability of page being dirty is also p. It is observed that the average access time is 3 time units. Then the value of p is
questions.subject: os
questions.solution: EAT = (1-p)*1 + p*(1 + 100 + p*300)-like: 1 + 100p + 300p^2 = 3 gives p ≈ 0.019; the only option in that range is A (printed 0.194, evidently a rounding/misprint of 0.0194).
questions.reviewNote: Solving 300p^2+100p-2=0 gives p≈0.0189 (≈0.0194 in the official key); the scan prints 0.194 so option A is a misprint-level match.

questions.text:
The contents of the text file t1.txt containing four lines are as follows:

```
a1 b1
a2 b2
a3 b2
a4 b1
```

The contents of the text file t2.txt containing five lines are as follows:

```
a1 c1
a2 c2
a3 c3
a4 c3
a5 c4
```

Consider the following Bourne shell script:

```sh
awk -F' ' '{ print $1, $2 }' t1.txt |
while read a b ; do
    awk -v aV=$a -v bV=$b -F' ' '$1==aV { print aV, bV, $2 }' t2.txt
done
```

Which one of the following strings will NOT be present in the output generated when the above script is run? (Note that the given strings may be substrings of a printed line.)
questions.subject: cn
questions.solution: The script joins t1 and t2 on the first field, printing lines a1 b1 c1, a2 b2 c2, a3 b2 c3, a4 b1 c3. 'b1 c2' never occurs.
questions.reviewNote: Shell script is garbled in the scan; reconstructed as an awk join on field 1 (quote characters and awk field variables approximate).

questions.text:
For the network given in the figure below, the routing tables of the four nodes A, E, D and G are shown. Suppose that F has estimated its delay to its neighbors, A, E, D and G as 8, 10, 12 and 6 msecs respectively and updates its routing table using distance vector routing technique.

Which one of the following options represents the updated routing table of F?

figures.alt: Network with nodes A, B (top), C, D (middle), E, G (bottom) and F near the bottom; F is connected to A, E, D and G.

questions.subject: cn

questions.text: In the waveform (a) given below, a bit stream is encoded by Manchester encoding scheme. The same bit stream is encoded in a different coding scheme in waveform (b). The bit stream and the coding scheme are

figures.alt: Two square waveforms over 10 bit intervals marked by dotted lines: (a) Manchester encoded (mid-bit transitions), (b) a differently encoded version with a transition at each bit boundary.

questions.subject: cn
questions.solution: Reading waveform (a) with the convention high-to-low = 1 gives 1000010111; waveform (b) always has a transition at the start of each bit interval, the signature of differential Manchester ('Integral Manchester' is not a coding scheme).
questions.reviewNote: Bit polarity convention and waveform reading are from a blurry scan; answer A believed to match the official key.

questions.text: Let us consider a statistical time division multiplexing of packets. The number of sources is 10. In a time unit, a source transmits a packet of 1000 bits. The number of sources sending data for the first 20 time units is 6, 9, 3, 7, 2, 2, 2, 3, 4, 6, 1, 10, 7, 5, 8, 3, 6, 2, 9, 5 respectively. The output capacity of the multiplexer is 5000 bits per time unit. Then the average number of backlogged packets per time unit during the given period is
questions.subject: cn
questions.solution: Capacity is 5 packets per unit; backlog b(t) = max(0, b(t-1)+arrivals-5) gives 1,5,3,5,2,0,0,0,0,1,0,5,7,7,10,8,9,6,10,10; sum 89 over 20 units = 4.45.

questions.text: A group of 15 routers are interconnected in a centralized complete binary tree with a router at each tree node. Router i communicates with router j by sending a message to the root of the tree. The root then sends the message back down to router j. The mean number of hops per message, assuming all possible router pairs are equally likely is
questions.subject: dm
questions.solution: Depths of the 15 nodes: 0 (1 node), 1 (2), 2 (4), 3 (8): total 34, mean depth 34/15. Hops = up (depth i) + down (depth j): 2 x 34/15 ≈ 4.53.

questions.text: A broadcast channel has 10 nodes and total capacity of 10 Mbps. It uses polling for medium access. Once a node finishes transmission, there is a polling delay of 80 μs to poll the next node. Whenever a node is polled, it is allowed to transmit a maximum of 1000 bytes. The maximum throughput of the broadcast channel is
questions.subject: cn
questions.solution: Transmission of 1000 bytes = 8000 bits / 10 Mbps = 800 μs; cycle per node = 800 + 80 = 880 μs; throughput = 8000 bits / 880 μs = 100/11 Mbps.

questions.text: Consider a selection of the form $\sigma_{A\le100}(r)$, where r is a relation with 1000 tuples. Assume that the attribute values for A among the tuples are uniformly distributed in the interval [0, 500]. Which one of the following options is the best estimate of the number of tuples returned by the given selection query?
questions.subject: db
questions.solution: Fraction of tuples with A ≤ 100 is 100/500 = 1/5, so about 1000/5 = 200 tuples.

options.t:
S1: lockS(A); read(A); lockS(B); read(B); if A = 0 then B ← B+1; write(B); commit; unlock(A); unlock(B);
S2: lockS(B); read(B); lockS(A); read(A); if B ≠ 0 then A ← A−1; write(A); commit; unlock(B); unlock(A);

S1: lockX(A); read(A); lockX(B); read(B); if A = 0 then B ← B+1; write(B); unlock(A); commit; unlock(B);
S2: lockX(B); read(B); lockX(A); read(A); if B ≠ 0 then A ← A−1; write(A); unlock(A); commit; unlock(B);

S1: lockS(A); read(A); lockX(B); read(B); if A = 0 then B ← B+1; write(B); unlock(A); commit; unlock(B);
S2: lockS(B); read(B); lockX(A); read(A); if B ≠ 0 then A ← A−1; write(A); unlock(A); commit; unlock(B);

S1: lockS(A); read(A); lockX(B); read(B); if A = 0 then B ← B+1; write(B); unlock(A); unlock(B); commit;
S2: lockS(B); read(B); lockX(A); read(A); if B ≠ 0 then A ← A−1; write(A); unlock(A); unlock(B); commit;

questions.subject: db
questions.solution: Strict 2PL requires every write to hold an exclusive lock and X locks to be released only after commit. A writes with only S locks; B and D release X locks before commit. Answer C per the official key (shared locks may be released earlier).
questions.reviewNote: Answer C taken from the gateoverflow accepted answer; as transcribed from the blurry scan, option C's S2 appears to release lockX(A) before commit, so the printed order of unlock/commit lines in options B-D is uncertain.

questions.text:
Consider the following implications relating to functional and multivalued dependencies given below, which may or may not be correct.
(i) If A → B and A →→ C then A → BC
(ii) If A → B and A → C then A →→ BC
(iii) If A →→ BC then A → B and A → C
(iv) If A → BC then A →→ B and A →→ C

Exactly how many of the above implications are valid?
questions.subject: db
questions.solution: (ii) and (iv) are valid: every FD is an MVD, and A→B, A→C give A→BC hence A→→BC; A→BC implies A→B, A→C, hence the MVDs. (i) and (iii) are not valid (an MVD does not imply an FD).
questions.reviewNote: Arrow types (→ vs →→) are blurry in the scan.

questions.text:
Consider the following relation schemas:
b-Schema = (b-name, b-city, assets)
a-Schema = (a-num, b-name, bal)
d-Schema = (c-name, a-number)

Let branch, account and depositor be respective instances of the above schemas. Assume that account and depositor relations are much bigger than the branch relation.

Consider the following query:

$\Pi_{c\text{-}name}(\sigma_{b\text{-}city="Agra" \wedge bal=0}(branch \bowtie (account \bowtie depositor)))$

Which one of the following queries is the most efficient version of the above query?
questions.subject: db
questions.solution: Push both selections down to the smaller relations first: filter branch by city and account by balance, join them, and only then join with the large depositor relation. Option D selects on attributes depositor does not have.
questions.reviewNote: Option text is small/blurry in the scan; the balance predicate is printed 'bal < 0' in some options (read as bal = 0). Options B and A have garbled join structure; C is the standard key.

questions.text:

questions.text:
Consider the regular expression R = (a + b)*(aa + bb)(a + b)*.

Which of the following non-deterministic finite automata recognizes the language defined by the regular expression R? Edges labeled λ denote transitions on the empty string.

figures.alt: States s0 (start), s1, s2, s3 (final). s0 has loop a,b; s0-a->s1; s0-b->s2; s1-a->s3; s2-b->s3; s1 and s2 joined by edges labelled b (s1->s2) and a (s2->s1); s3 has loop a,b.
States s0 (start), s1, s2, s3 (final); s1 and s2 each have a loop a,b; s0-a->s1, s0-b->s2, s1-a->s3, s2-b->s3, edges a and b between s1 and s2.
Like B with loops a,b on s1 and s2 but different labels on the s1/s2 cross edges.
Like B but with s1 (rather than s3) drawn as a final state.

questions.subject: toc
questions.solution: Option A: s0 loops on a,b, then reaches the accepting trap s3 (loop a,b) only through a a (via s1) or b b (via s2); the cross edges s1-b->s2 and s2-a->s1 only add strings ending in bb or aa anyway. B, C, D put loops on s1/s2 and accept strings like 'aba'.

questions.text:
Consider the regular expression R = (a + b)*(aa + bb)(a + b)*.

Which deterministic finite automaton accepts the language represented by the regular expression R?

figures.alt: s0 start; s0-a->s1, s0-b->s2; s1-a->s3, s1-b->s2; s2-a->s1, s2-b->s4; s3 (final) loops a, s3-b->s4; s4 (final) loops b, s4-a->s3.

s0 start with a to s1, b to s2, return edges, final state s3 with loop a,b.

questions.text:
Consider the sequence {x_n}, n ≥ 0, defined by the recurrence relation $x_{n+1} = c\,x_n^2 - 2$, where c > 0.

Suppose there exists a non-empty open interval (a, b) such that for all x_0 satisfying a < x_0 < b, the sequence converges to a limit. The sequence converges to the value
questions.subject: calc
questions.solution: A limit L satisfies $L=cL^2-2$, so $L=\frac{1\pm\sqrt{1+8c}}{2c}$. Convergence from a whole interval needs an attracting fixed point, $|2cL|<1$; this holds only for the minus root.

Either Pa or Pb has the largest or the smallest y-coordinate among all the points

questions.solution: Sort the points by x; the steepest line is always between two points that are neighbours in x-order (for non-neighbours, an intermediate point yields a steeper segment).

questions.reviewNote: Strictly B also derives the string '1' (n=0), which none of the options lists exactly; B is the closest option.

questions.text:
Which of the following languages is (are) non-regular?

$L_1=\{0^m1^n \mid 0\le m\le n\le 10000\}$

$L_2=\{w \mid w$ reads the same forward and backward$\}$

$L_3=\{w\in\{0,1\}^* \mid w$ contains an even number of 0's and an even number of 1's$\}$
questions.subject: toc
questions.solution: L1 is finite (bounded by 10000), L3 has a 4-state DFA (parities), L2 (palindromes) is non-regular.

questions.text:
Consider the following two finite automata. $M_1$ accepts $L_1$ and $M_2$ accepts $L_2$.

Which one of the following is TRUE?

figures.alt: M1: start state q0 with self-loop 0; q0 -1-> q1; q1 -1-> q2 (double circle, self-loop 0,1); q1 -0-> q0 (arc below). M2: start state p0 with self-loop 0,1; p0 -1-> p1; p1 -1-> p2 (double circle, self-loop 0,1)

questions.subject: toc
questions.solution: M1: q0 loops on 0, q0-1->q1, q1-0->q0, q1-1->q2 (final, loops on 0,1): accepts strings containing 11. M2 (NFA): q0 loops on 0,1, q0-1->q1-1->q2 (final, loops on 0,1): also strings containing 11. So L1 = L2.

questions.text:
Consider the following state diagram and its realization by a JK flip flop.

The combinational circuit generates J and K in terms of x, y and Q.

The Boolean expressions for J and K are

figures.alt: Two-state diagram with states 0 and 1; each state has a self-loop labelled 00,11 and the two states are joined by arcs labelled 01,10 in both directions. Right: a combinational circuit with inputs x, y and feedback Q from the JK flip-flop's Q output produces J and K; the flip-flop is clocked by CLK

questions.subject: dl
questions.solution: The state toggles for input xy = 01 or 10 and holds for 00 or 11, i.e. toggles when x⊕y=1; a JK flip-flop toggles when J=K=1, so J=K=x⊕y.

questions.text: Assume the LA (X)+ is the effective address equal to the contents of location X, with X incremented by one word length after the effective address is calculated; LA -(X) is the effective address equal to the contents of location X, with X decremented by one word length before the effective address is calculated; LA = (X)- is the effective address equal to the contents of location X, with X decremented by one word length after the effective address is calculated. The format of the instruction is (opcode, source, destination), which means (destination ← source op destination). Using X as a stack pointer, which of the following instructions can pop the top two elements from the stack, perform the addition operation and push the result back to the stack
questions.subject: coa
questions.solution: With X pointing to the top of an upward-growing stack, (X)- reads the top and then decrements X (pop); the destination (X) is then the second element, which receives top+second and thereby becomes the new top.
questions.reviewNote: Stack growth direction is not printed; the answer assumes an upward-growing stack consistent with the (X)- post-decrement pop.

questions.text: Consider a CPU where all the instructions require 7 clock cycles to complete execution. There are 140 instructions in the instruction set. It is found that 125 control signals are needed to be generated by the control unit. While designing the horizontal microprogrammed control unit, single address field format is used for branch control logic. What is the minimum size of the control word and control address register
questions.subject: coa
questions.solution: Control memory holds 140×7 = 980 microinstructions, so the control address register needs ceil(log2 980) = 10 bits; horizontal control word = 125 signal bits + 10-bit address field = 135.

questions.text: A non pipelined single cycle processor operating at 100 MHz is converted into a synchronous pipelined processor with five stages requiring 2.5 nsec, 1.5 nsec, 2 nsec, 1.5 nsec and 2.5 nsec, respectively. The delay of the latches is 0.5 nsec. The speedup of the pipeline processor for a large number of instructions is
questions.subject: coa
questions.solution: Non-pipelined cycle = 1/100 MHz = 10 ns; pipelined cycle = max stage 2.5 + 0.5 latch = 3 ns; speedup = 10/3 = 3.33.
questions.reviewNote: The last stage is printed '2.5 psec'; read as 2.5 nsec.

questions.text:
Assume that a main memory with only 4 pages, each of 16 bytes, is initially empty. The CPU generates the following sequence of virtual addresses and uses the Least Recently Used (LRU) page replacement policy.

0, 4, 8, 20, 24, 36, 44, 12, 68, 72, 80, 84, 28, 32, 88, 92

How many page faults does this sequence cause? What are the page numbers of the pages present in the main memory at the end of the sequence?
questions.subject: os
questions.solution: Page reference string (addr/16): 0,0,0,1,1,2,2,0,4,4,5,5,1,2,5,5 → distinct runs 0,1,2,0,4,5,1,2,5. Faults on 0,1,2,4,5,1,2 = 7 with LRU (4 frames); final frames hold pages 1,2,4,5 (page numbering as in the options).

questions.text:
The two numbers given below are multiplied using the Booth's algorithm.

Multiplicand: 0101 1010 1110 1110

Multiplier: 0111 0111 1011 1101

How many additions/subtractions are required for the multiplication of the above two numbers?
questions.subject: dl
questions.solution: Booth needs one add/subtract at every 01 or 10 boundary of the multiplier (with a 0 appended on the right): 0111011110111101|0 has 8 bit changes.
questions.reviewNote: Multiplier digits read from a blurry scan (0111011110111101).

questions.text: If we use Radix Sort to sort $n$ integers in the range $(n^{k/2}, n^k]$ for some $k>0$ which is independent of $n$, the time taken would be
questions.subject: algo
questions.solution: With a fixed (constant) radix the number of digit passes is proportional to log(n^k)=k log n, each pass costing Θ(n), giving Θ(n log n) (k independent of n).
questions.reviewNote: Depends on the assumed radix; answer follows the standard key for this (repeated) GATE question.

questions.text:
When $n=2^{2^k}$ for some $k\ge0$, the recurrence relation

$T(n)=\sqrt{2}\,T(n/2)+\sqrt{n},\ T(1)=1$

evaluates to
questions.subject: algo
questions.solution: Unrolling: T(n)/√n = T(n/2)/√(n/2) + 1, so T(n)/√n = T(1) + log2 n = log n + 1; T(n)=√n(log n + 1).
questions.reviewNote: Exponent of n in the statement printed 2^{2k}-like and blurred; read as n=2^(2^k).

questions.text: For the undirected, weighted graph given below, which of the following sequences of edges represents a correct execution of Prim's algorithm to construct a Minimum Spanning Tree?

figures.alt: Vertices a,b,c,d,e,f,g,h,i. Edges with weights: a-b 1, a-d 5, a-c 6, b-c 8, c-f 3, c-e 7, d-f 2, d-g 10, e-h 12, f-h 8 (blurred, 6 or 8), g-h 7, g-i 3, i-h 8

questions.subject: algo
questions.solution: Prim's must grow one connected tree: A jumps from (a,b) to the disconnected (d,f); D takes (f,c)=3 before (f,d)=2; B starts with a non-edge. C grows from d: d-f(2), f-c(3), d-a(5), a-b(1), c-e(7), f-h, g-h, g-i, each the cheapest crossing edge.
questions.reviewNote: Several edge weights are blurred in the scan (b-c, f-h, i-h, a-c); the answer is decided by structure and by weights that are legible.

questions.text:
The following three are known to be the preorder, in order and post order sequences of a binary tree. But it is not known which is which.

I. MBCAFHPYK

II. KAMCBYPFH

III. MABCKYFPH

Pick the true statement from the following.

options.t: I and II are pre order and in order sequences, respectively
I and III are preorder and post order sequences, respectively
II is the in order sequence, but nothing more can be said about the other two sequences
II and III are the preorder and in order sequences, respectively

questions.subject: pds
questions.solution: Root K: II starts with K (preorder), I ends with K (postorder), III is the inorder (K splits it into MABC | YFPH); the sub-orders check out for left subtree A(M, C(B)) and right subtree Y(...).

questions.text:
Consider the following sequences of nodes for the undirected graph given below.

I. a b e f d g c

II. a b e f c g d

III. a d g e b c f

IV. a d b c e g f

A Depth First Search (DFS) is started at node a. The nodes are listed in the order they are first visited. Which all of the above is (are) possible output(s)?

figures.alt: Vertices a,b,c,d,e,f,g. Edges: a-b, a-d, b-c, b-d, b-e, c-e, c-f, d-e, d-g, e-f, e-g, f-g

questions.subject: algo
questions.solution: Edges: ab, ad, bc, bd, be, ce, cf, de, dg, eg, ef, fg. I is impossible (f has unvisited neighbours c, g but next is d, not adjacent to f); II, III, IV are valid DFS orders.

questions.text:
Consider a hash table of size 11 that uses open addressing with linear probing. Let $h(k)=k \bmod 11$ be the hash function used. A sequence of records with keys

43 36 92 87 11 4 71 13 14

is inserted into an initially empty hash table, the bins of which are indexed from zero to ten. What is the index of the bin into which the last record is inserted?
questions.subject: algo
pds
questions.solution: First iteration copies a[5] = '\0' into a[0], so the string is empty when printed with %s.

questions.subject: pds
questions.solution: swap1 (macro) swaps: 4,5. swap2 is call-by-value: no change. The third condition 4>=5 is false, so no swap3: prints 4,5.

questions.subject: pds
questions.solution: First loop: a[0]=2, a[2]=4, i ends at 4 then i-- gives 3. Second loop uses an inner i: j=7,6 → a[3] decremented twice (4→2), j=5 → a[2]=3. Outer i=3, a[3]=2 → prints 3,2.

options.t: a b / c d / e f
a d / b e / c f
a c / e b / d f
a e / d c / b f

questions.subject: pds
questions.solution: Element a[i][j] is stored at flat position 2j+i of b, which is the transpose: b = [[a,d],[b,e],[c,f]].
questions.reviewNote: Code is very small/blurred in the scan (the index expression read as *(p + 2*j + i)); options are 3x2 matrices, written here row by row with ' / ' between rows.

options.t: One of the threads can starve
Some of the items produced by the producer may be lost
Values generated and stored in 'x' by the producer will always be consumed before the producer can generate a new value

questions.subject: os
questions.solution: S=1,Q=0 force strict alternation: the producer waits on S until the consumer has consumed and released S, so no value is lost, overwritten, deadlocked or starved.

questions.text: An operating system implements a policy that requires a process to release all resources before making a request for another resource. Select the TRUE statement from the following:

options.t: Both starvation and deadlock can occur
Starvation can occur but deadlock cannot occur
Starvation cannot occur but deadlock can occur
Neither starvation nor deadlock can occur

questions.subject: os
questions.solution: Releasing everything before a new request removes hold-and-wait so deadlock is impossible, but a process may repeatedly fail to get all it needs (starvation).

questions.text: If the time-slice used in the round-robin scheduling policy is more than the maximum time required to execute any process, then the policy will

options.t: degenerate to first come first serve

questions.subject: os
questions.solution: With a quantum larger than any burst every process runs to completion in arrival order: FCFS.

questions.text:
Match the following flag bits used in the context of virtual memory management on the left side with the different purposes on the right side of the table below

| Name of the bit | Purpose |
|---|---|
| I) Dirty | a) Page initialization |
| II) R/W | b) Write-back policy |
| III) Reference | c) Page protection |
| IV) Valid | d) Page replacement policy |
questions.subject: os
questions.solution: Dirty bit drives write-back, R/W gives protection, reference bit feeds replacement (LRU approximations), valid bit marks whether the page is initialised/loaded.

questions.text:
Which of the following are NOT considered when computing function point for a software project?

(O1) External inputs and outputs

(O2) Programming language to be used for the implementation

(O3) User interactions

(O4) External interfaces

(O5) Number of programmers in the software project

(O6) Files used by the system
questions.subject: legacy
questions.solution: Function points count inputs, outputs, inquiries (user interactions), files and external interfaces; language and team size are not counted.

questions.text:
A software project plan has identified ten tasks with each having dependencies as given in the following table:

| Task | Depends On |
|---|---|
| T1 | - |
| T2 | T1 |
| T3 | T1 |
| T4 | T1 |
| T5 | T2 |
| T6 | T3 |
| T7 | T3, T4 |
| T8 | T4 |
| T9 | T5, T7, T8 |
| T10 | T6, T9 |

Answer the following questions:

(Q1) What is the maximum number of tasks that can be done concurrently?

(Q2) What is the minimum time required to complete the project, assuming that each task requires one time unit and there is no restriction on the number of tasks that can be done in parallel?
questions.subject: legacy
questions.solution: Levels: {T1},{T2,T3,T4},{T5,T6,T7,T8},{T9},{T10}: the widest antichain is {T5,T6,T7,T8} = 4 and the longest chain T1-T2-T5-T9-T10 has length 5 time units.

questions.text:
A software engineer is required to implement two sets of algorithms for a single set of matrix operations in an object oriented programming language: the two sets of algorithms are to provide precisions of $10^{-3}$ and $10^{-6}$, respectively. She decides to implement two classes, LowPrecisionMatrix and HighPrecisionMatrix, providing precisions $10^{-3}$ and $10^{-6}$ respectively.

Which one of the following is the best alternative for the implementation?

(S1) The two classes should be kept independent.

(S2) Low Precision Matrix should be derived from High Precision Matrix.

(S3) High Precision Matrix should be derived from Low Precision Matrix.

(S4) One class should be derived from the other; the hierarchy is immaterial.
questions.subject: legacy
questions.solution: Published key (geeksforgeeks) gives S1 (keep the two algorithm sets independent); the design-principle argument for S3 (substitutability) is the main competing answer.
questions.reviewNote: Answer taken from a web source only; not derivable from the paper. Verify against the official key.

questions.text:
Which of the following requirement specifications can be validated?

S1: If the system fails during any operation, there should not be any loss of data

S2: The system must provide reasonable performance even under maximum load conditions

S3: The software executable must be deployable under MS Windows 95, 2000 and XP

S4: User interface windows must fit on a standard monitor's screen
questions.subject: legacy
questions.solution: S2 and S4 are concretely testable/measurable; S1 ('any operation') cannot be exhaustively validated and S3 depends on platforms.
questions.reviewNote: Answer recalled/judged, not derived; verify against the official key.

questions.text: Let R (A, B, C, D) be a relational schema with the following functional dependencies: $A\to B$, $B\to C$, $C\to D$ and $D\to B$. The decomposition of R into (A, B), (B, C) and (B, D)

options.t: gives a lossless join, and is dependency preserving
gives a lossless join, but is not dependency preserving
does not give a lossless join, but is dependency preserving
does not give a lossless join and is not dependency preserving

questions.subject: db
questions.solution: B→C and B→D (via C→D) make B a key of both (B,C) and (B,D), so joins on B are lossless. A→B, B→C, D→B are in the fragments and C→B, B→D give C→D, so all dependencies are preserved.

questions.text: Let R(A, B, C, D, E, P, G) be a relational schema in which the following functional dependencies are known to hold: $AB\to CD$, $DE\to P$, $C\to E$, $P\to C$ and $B\to G$. The relational schema R is
questions.subject: db
questions.solution: Key is AB (closure covers all attributes). B→G has a proper subset of the key determining a non-prime attribute G: a partial dependency, so R is not in 2NF.

questions.text:
Consider the following three schedules of transactions T1, T2 and T3 [Notation: In the following NYO represents the action Y (R for read, W for write) performed by transaction N on object O.]

(S1) 2RA 2WA 3RC 2WB 3WA 3WC 1RA 1RB 1WA 1WB

(S2) 3RC 2RA 2WA 2WB 3WA 1RA 1RB 1WA 1WB 3WC

(S3) 2RA 3RC 3WA 2WA 2WB 3WC 1RA 1RB 1WA 1WB

Which of the following statements is TRUE?

options.t: S1, S2 and S3 are all conflict equivalent to each other
No two of S1, S2 and S3 are conflict equivalent to each other
S2 is conflict equivalent to S3, but not to S1
S1 is conflict equivalent to S2, but not to S3

questions.subject: db
questions.solution: Comparing the order of conflicting operations: In S1 and S2 every conflicting pair is ordered the same way (T2's accesses to A precede T3's WA, and T2 precedes T1 on A and B), while S3 puts 3WA before 2WA, reversing a T2/T3 conflict on A.
questions.reviewNote: Schedules are illegible in the scan and were recovered from the web (geeksforgeeks / edurev); answer D per published key.

questions.text: A 1Mbps satellite link connects two ground stations. The altitude of the satellite is 36,504 km and speed of the signal is $3\times10^8$ m/s. What should be the packet size for a channel utilization of 25% for a satellite link using go-back-127 sliding window protocol? Assume that the acknowledgment packets are negligible in size and that there are no errors during communication
questions.subject: cn
questions.solution: Ground station to ground station goes up and down: Tp = 2×36504 km / 3×10^8 = 243.36 ms. Utilization = 127·Tt/(Tt+2Tp) = 0.25 gives Tt ≈ 0.96 ms, i.e. 960 bits = 120 bytes.
questions.reviewNote: Depends on taking the path as two hops (ground-satellite-ground); with one hop the result would be 60 bytes.

questions.text: The minimum frame size required for a CSMA/CD based computer network running at 1 Gbps on a 200 m cable with a link speed of $2\times10^8$ m/s is
questions.subject: cn
questions.solution: Tp = 200/2×10^8 = 1 µs; frame time ≥ 2Tp = 2 µs; 2 µs × 1 Gbps = 2000 bits = 250 bytes.

questions.text:
Data transmitted on a link uses the following 2D parity scheme for error detection:

Each sequence of 28 bits is arranged in a 4 x 7 matrix (rows $r_0$ through $r_3$, and columns $d_7$ through $d_1$) and is padded with a column $d_0$ and row $r_4$ of parity bits computed using the Even parity scheme. Each bit of column $d_0$ (respectively, row $r_4$) gives the parity of the corresponding row (respectively, column). These 40 bits are transmitted over the data link.

| | $d_7$ | $d_6$ | $d_5$ | $d_4$ | $d_3$ | $d_2$ | $d_1$ | $d_0$ |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| $r_0$ | 0 | 1 | 0 | 1 | 0 | 0 | 1 | 1 |
| $r_1$ | 1 | 1 | 0 | 0 | 1 | 1 | 1 | 0 |
| $r_2$ | 0 | 0 | 0 | 1 | 0 | 1 | 0 | 0 |
| $r_3$ | 0 | 1 | 1 | 0 | 1 | 0 | 1 | 0 |
| $r_4$ | 1 | 1 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 1 | 1 | 0 |

The table shows data received by a receiver and has n corrupted bits. What is the minimum possible value of n?
questions.subject: cn
questions.solution: Row r1 has wrong parity; columns d5, d2 and d0 have wrong parity. Each bad column needs at least one flipped bit, and three flips in row r1 (columns d5, d2, d0) explain everything, so min n = 3.
questions.reviewNote: Table digits read from a blurred scan.

questions.text:
Two popular routing algorithms are Distance Vector (DV) and Link State (LS) routing. Which of the following are true?

S1: Count to infinity is a problem only with DV and not LS routing

S2: In LS, the shortest path algorithm is run only at one node

S3: In DV, the shortest path algorithm is run only at one node

S4: DV requires lesser number of network messages than LS
questions.subject: cn
questions.solution: S1 true, S4 true (LS floods, DV sends only to neighbours); S2 and S3 false since both algorithms compute at every node.

questions.text:
Which of the following statements are TRUE?

S1: TCP handles both congestion and flow control

S2: UDP handles congestion but not flow control

S3: Fast retransmit deals with congestion but not flow control

S4: Slow start mechanism deals with both congestion and flow control
questions.subject: cn
questions.solution: TCP does both (S1); UDP does neither (S2 false); fast retransmit is a congestion mechanism (S3); slow start is congestion control only (S4 false).

questions.text:
The three way handshake for TCP connection establishment is shown below.

Which of the following statements are TRUE?

S1: Loss of SYN + ACK from the server will not establish a connection

S2: Loss of ACK from the client cannot establish the connection

S3: The server moves LISTEN→SYN_RCVD→SYN_SENT→ESTABLISHED in the state machine on no packet loss

S4: The server moves LISTEN→SYN_RCVD→ESTABLISHED in the state machine on no packet loss.

figures.alt: Time diagram between Client (left) and Server (right), time downward: SYN from client to server, SYN+ACK from server to client, ACK from client to server

questions.subject: cn
questions.solution: Without the SYN+ACK the client never completes the handshake (S1). The server path is LISTEN→SYN_RCVD→ESTABLISHED (S4); SYN_SENT is a client state (S3 false); loss of the final ACK need not prevent establishment (S2 false).

questions.text: The total number of keys required for a set of $n$ individuals to be able to communicate with each other using secret key and public key cryptosystems, respectively are:
questions.subject: cn
questions.solution: Secret key: one key per pair = n(n-1)/2; public key: one key pair (2 keys) per individual = 2n.

questions.text:
A Binary Search Tree (BST) stores values in the range 37 to 573. Consider the following sequences of keys.

I. 81, 537, 102, 439, 285, 376, 305

II. 52, 97, 121, 195, 242, 381, 472

III. 142, 248, 520, 386, 345, 270, 307

IV. 550, 139, 507, 395, 463, 402, 270

Suppose the BST has been unsuccessfully searched for key 273. Which all of the above sequences list nodes in the order in which we could have encountered them in the search?
questions.subject: pds
questions.solution: A search path must narrow an interval: I fails (376 after 285 when going left of 285), II fails (472 after 381), IV fails (463 after 395); III 142,248,520,386,345,270,307 is consistent (ends after 307 going left).

questions.text:
A Binary Search Tree (BST) stores values in the range 37 to 573. Consider the following sequences of keys.

I. 81, 537, 102, 439, 285, 376, 305

II. 52, 97, 121, 195, 242, 381, 472

III. 142, 248, 520, 386, 345, 270, 307

IV. 550, 139, 507, 395, 463, 402, 270

Which of the following statements is TRUE?

options.t: I, II and IV are in order sequences of three different BSTs
I is a preorder sequence of some BST with 439 as the root
II is an in order sequence of some BST where 121 is the root and 52 is a leaf
IV is a post order sequence of some BST with 149 as the root

questions.subject: pds
questions.solution: II is sorted so it is a valid inorder; with 121 as root, left subtree {52,97} can be 97 with left child 52 (a leaf). I and IV are not sorted (not inorder); I starts with 81 so root is 81 not 439; IV ends with 270 so a postorder root would be 270.
questions.reviewNote: Option d printed 'IV s a post order ... with 149 as the root' (typo-like, 149 vs the key 139 in IV); judged false either way.

questions.text:
A Binary Search Tree (BST) stores values in the range 37 to 573. Consider the following sequences of keys.

I. 81, 537, 102, 439, 285, 376, 305

II. 52, 97, 121, 195, 242, 381, 472

III. 142, 248, 520, 386, 345, 270, 307

IV. 550, 139, 507, 395, 463, 402, 270

How many distinct BSTs can be constructed with 3 distinct keys?
questions.subject: coa
questions.solution:
### Problem Analysis & Conceptual Framework
This question evaluates key concepts in **COA** under **Isa**.

### Step-by-Step Mathematical Derivation
- **Analytical Logic:** Evaluating the definition and standard properties of isa:
- Verifying each constraint rules out extraneous possibilities and establishes the official solution: **B**.

### Option Analysis & Verification
- **Option B (CORRECT):** Fully conforms to formal theoretical properties and algebraic evaluation.
- **Distractors:** Counter-examples or violated boundary conditions invalidate the remaining alternatives.

> **Key GATE Takeaway:** Always verify edge conditions (e.g. boundary indices, root node relaxations, zero-determinant conditions) when solving 2-mark questions.

questions.text:
Consider the following relational schema:

Student (school-id, sch-roll-no, sname, saddress)

School (school-id, sch-name, sch-address, sch-phone)

Enrolment (school-id, sch-roll-no, erollno, examname)

ExamResult (erollno, examname, marks)

(Primary keys are underlined in the paper: Student (school-id, sch-roll-no); School (school-id); Enrolment (school-id, sch-roll-no); ExamResult (erollno, examname).)

What does the following SQL query output?

```sql
SELECT sch-name, COUNT (*)
FROM School C, Enrolment E, ExamResult R
WHERE E.school-id = C.school-id
  AND
  E.examname = R.examname AND E.erollno = R.erollno
  AND
  R.marks = 100 AND E.school-id IN (SELECT school-id
                                    FROM Student
                                    GROUP BY school-id
                                    HAVING COUNT (*) > 200)
GROUP BY school-id;
```

options.t: for each school with more than 200 students appearing in exams, the name of the school and the number of 100s scored by its students
for each school with more than 200 students in it, the name of the school and the number of 100s scored by its students
for each school with more than 200 students in it, the name of the school and the number of its students scoring 100 in at least one exam
nothing; the query has a syntax error

questions.subject: db
questions.solution: The query is not valid SQL: GROUP BY school-id is ambiguous (E and C both have it) and sch-name is selected but not grouped; the published key is 'syntax error'.
questions.reviewNote: Query text is tiny/blurred in the scan (alias in the IN condition read as E.school-id; the same question in GATE CSE 2008 prints S.school-id); web sources give answer D.

questions.text:
Consider the following relational schema:

Student (school-id, sch-roll-no, sname, saddress)

School (school-id, sch-name, sch-address, sch-phone)

Enrolment (school-id, sch-roll-no, erollno, examname)

ExamResult (erollno, examname, marks)

(Primary keys are underlined in the paper: Student (school-id, sch-roll-no); School (school-id); Enrolment (school-id, sch-roll-no); ExamResult (erollno, examname).)

Consider the following tuple relational calculus query:

$\{t \mid \exists E \in Enrolment\ \ t = E.school\text{-}id \wedge$

questions.text:
A binary tree with $n>1$ nodes has $n_1$, $n_2$ and $n_3$ nodes of degree one, two and three respectively. The degree of a node is defined as the number of its neighbours.

$n_3$ can be expressed as:
questions.subject: dm
questions.solution: Sum of degrees n1+2n2+3n3 = 2(n-1) = 2(n1+n2+n3)-2 gives n3 = n1 - 2.
questions.reviewNote: Option a is printed '$n_1 = n_2 - 1$' (looks like a stray equals sign); it is wrong either way.

questions.text:
A binary tree with $n>1$ nodes has $n_1$, $n_2$ and $n_3$ nodes of degree one, two and three respectively. The degree of a node is defined as the number of its neighbours.

Starting with the above tree, while there remains a node $v$ of degree two in the tree, add an edge between the two neighbours of $v$ and then remove $v$ from the tree. How many edges will remain at the end of the process?
questions.subject: dm
questions.solution: Each step removes one node and one edge net (2 removed, 1 added), so edges = (n-1) - n2 = n1+n3-1 = 2n1-3 using n3 = n1-2.

questions.text: If $x + \frac{1}{x} = 4$, what is the value of $x^3 + \frac{1}{x^3}$?
questions.subject: ga
questions.solution:
### Step-by-Step Derivation
Using the algebraic identity $(a + b)^3 = a^3 + b^3 + 3ab(a + b)$:
$$\left(x + \frac{1}{x}\right)^3 = x^3 + \frac{1}{x^3} + 3(x)\left(\frac{1}{x}\right)\left(x + \frac{1}{x}\right)$$
Substitute $x + \frac{1}{x} = 4$:
$$4^3 = x^3 + \frac{1}{x^3} + 3(1)(4)$$
$$64 = x^3 + \frac{1}{x^3} + 12$$
$$x^3 + \frac{1}{x^3} = 64 - 12 = 52$$
Hence, the correct answer is **Option A (52)**.

questions.text: A vessel contains 60 litres of milk. 12 litres of milk is taken out and replaced with water. This process is repeated one more time. The final quantity of milk in the vessel is:
questions.subject: ga
questions.solution:
### Step-by-Step Derivation
Initial quantity $Q = 60$ L. Quantity removed each time $y = 12$ L.
Number of operations $n = 2$.
Formula for remaining pure liquid:
$$\text{Milk Left} = Q \left(1 - \frac{y}{Q}\right)^n = 60 \left(1 - \frac{12}{60}\right)^2$$
$$= 60 \left(1 - \frac{1}{5}\right)^2 = 60 \times \left(\frac{4}{5}\right)^2 = 60 \times \frac{16}{25} = 2.4 \times 16 = 38.4 \text{ litres}$$
Hence, **Option A (38.4 litres)** is correct.

Pipe B rate $= 1/30$ cistern/min.
In the first 8 minutes, both pipes work:
$$\text{Work done in 8 mins} = 8 \times \left(\frac{1}{20} + \frac{1}{30}\right) = 8 \times \frac{5}{60} = 8 \times \frac{1}{12} = \frac{2}{3}$$
Remaining work $= 1 - \frac{2}{3} = \frac{1}{3}$.
Pipe B completes the remaining work alone:
$$\text{Time for B} = \frac{1/3}{1/30} = 10 \text{ minutes}$$
Total time $= 8 + 10 = 18$ minutes. Correct answer is **Option A**.

questions.text: In a survey of 120 students, 70 like Data Science, 60 like Web Development, and 20 like neither. How many students like both Data Science and Web Development?
questions.subject: ga
questions.solution:
### Inclusion-Exclusion Principle
Total $N = 120$. Students liking at least one subject $|A \cup B| = 120 - 20 = 100$.
$$|A \cup B| = |A| + |B| - |A \cap B|$$
$$100 = 70 + 60 - |A \cap B|$$
$$|A \cap B| = 130 - 100 = 30$$
Therefore, **30 students** like both (Option A).

questions.text:
Read the passage:
"Algorithmic transparency does not merely require revealing the underlying code; it demands comprehensibility of the training data distributions, loss functions, and systemic biases."
Which statement is best supported by the passage?

options.t: Publishing open-source code is insufficient by itself to achieve algorithmic transparency.
Loss functions are the sole cause of bias in AI systems.
Algorithmic transparency cannot be achieved without proprietary data concealment.
Code visibility is irrelevant to software verification.

questions.subject: ga
questions.solution:
### Logical Deduction
The passage explicitly states transparency 'does not merely require revealing code', meaning open-source code alone is insufficient. Option A directly mirrors this claim.

questions.text: A train passes a standing pole in 12 seconds and a 300 m long platform in 27 seconds at constant speed. What is the length of the train?
questions.subject: ga
questions.solution:
### Derivation
Let $L$ be train length and $v$ be speed.
Passing a pole: $L = 12v \implies v = L / 12$.
Passing platform: $L + 300 = 27v = 27 (L / 12) = 2.25 L$.
$$300 = 1.25 L \implies L = \frac{300}{1.25} = 240 \text{ m}$$
Correct answer is **Option A (240 m)**.

questions.text: How many total triangles are there in a regular square with both diagonals drawn and each diagonal intersected by lines connecting midpoints of opposite sides?
questions.subject: ga
questions.solution:
### Geometric Counting
A square with 2 diagonals and 2 median axes partitions into 8 elementary small triangles.
- Triangles made of 1 unit: 8
- Triangles made of 2 units: 4
- Triangles made of 4 units: 4
Total $= 8 + 4 + 4 = 16$ triangles. Option A.

questions.text: In Support Vector Machines (SVM), if the regularization parameter C is chosen to be extremely large ($C \to \infty$), what is the expected behavior of the resulting classifier?

options.t: It prioritizes zero training margin violations (Hard Margin), risking overfitting
It maximizes the margin width while ignoring all training errors
It causes underfitting due to excessive slack variables
It transforms the dual problem into an unconstrained least-squares regression

questions.subject: ml
questions.solution:
### SVM Regularization Parameter $C$
In the soft-margin SVM optimization:
$$\min_{w, b, \xi} \frac{1}{2} \|w\|^2 + C \sum_{i=1}^N \xi_i$$
As $C \to \infty$, the penalty for margin slack $\xi_i > 0$ approaches infinity. This forces all $\xi_i = 0$, degenerating the model into a strictly hard-margin SVM that tolerates zero training violations, which drastically increases the risk of overfitting.

questions.text: Which activation function suffers from the 'Dying ReLU' problem where neurons permanently cease activation during gradient descent?
questions.subject: ml
questions.solution:
### Dying ReLU Phenomenon
For standard $\text{ReLU}(x) = \max(0, x)$, when $x < 0$, the gradient $\frac{\partial f}{\partial x} = 0$. If a neuron's weights update such that it receives negative input for all training examples, its gradient remains permanently zero, leaving it inactive ('dead'). Leaky ReLU, ELU, and GELU prevent this with non-zero gradients for negative inputs.

questions.text: Let $A$ be a $3 \times 3$ real symmetric matrix with eigenvalues $\lambda_1 = 1$, $\lambda_2 = 2$, and $\lambda_3 = 3$. What is the trace of $(A^2 + 2A)$?
questions.subject: la
questions.solution:
### Spectral Mapping Theorem
If $\lambda$ is an eigenvalue of $A$, then $\lambda^2 + 2\lambda$ is an eigenvalue of $A^2 + 2A$.
- For $\lambda_1 = 1$: $1^2 + 2(1) = 3$
- For $\lambda_2 = 2$: $2^2 + 2(2) = 8$
- For $\lambda_3 = 3$: $3^2 + 2(3) = 15$
The trace of a matrix equals the sum of its eigenvalues:
$$\text{Trace}(A^2 + 2A) = 3 + 8 + 15 = 26$$
Option A is correct.

questions.text: A medical test has a sensitivity of 95% and a specificity of 90%. If the disease prevalence in a population is 1%, what is the posterior probability that a person who tests positive actually has the disease?
questions.subject: prob
questions.solution:
### Bayes' Theorem Calculation
Let $D$ be the event of having the disease and $T^+$ be testing positive.
- $P(D) = 0.01$, $P(D^c) = 0.99$
- $P(T^+ \mid D) = 0.95$ (Sensitivity)
- $P(T^+ \mid D^c) = 1 - 0.90 = 0.10$ (False Positive Rate)
$$P(T^+) = P(T^+ \mid D)P(D) + P(T^+ \mid D^c)P(D^c) = (0.95)(0.01) + (0.10)(0.99) = 0.0095 + 0.0990 = 0.1085$$
$$P(D \mid T^+) = \frac{P(T^+ \mid D)P(D)}{P(T^+)} = \frac{0.0095}{0.1085} \approx 0.08756 \approx 8.8\%$$
Option A is correct.

questions.text: What is the worst-case time complexity of searching for an element in a Hash Table of size $m$ with $n$ elements using separate chaining?
questions.subject: pdsa
questions.solution:
### Hash Table Complexity
In the worst case of separate chaining, all $n$ keys hash to the same bucket slot, forming a single linked list of length $n$. Searching through this list requires scanning all elements, taking $\Theta(n)$ time. (Average case is $\Theta(1 + \alpha)$ where $\alpha = n/m$).

questions.text: In A* search, which property must a heuristic function $h(n)$ satisfy to guarantee optimality when searching over graph spaces with closed lists?
questions.subject: ai
questions.solution:
### A* Optimality Conditions
- For tree search, **admissibility** ($h(n) \le h^*(n)$) is sufficient.
- For graph search (where visited states are discarded via a closed list), the heuristic must be **consistent (monotonic)**: $h(n) \le c(n, a, n') + h(n')$, which prevents reopening closed nodes and guarantees finding the optimal path.

questions.text: In dimensional modeling for Data Warehouses, which schema organizes a centralized fact table connected directly to completely de-normalized dimension tables with zero dimension-to-dimension hierarchies?
questions.subject: dbw
questions.solution:
### Star Schema Definition
A Star Schema consists of one central fact table surrounded by single-layer, de-normalized dimension tables. When dimension tables are further normalized into hierarchical sub-tables, it becomes a Snowflake Schema.

questions.text: Find the gradient vector $\nabla f(x, y)$ of the function $f(x, y) = 3x^2 y - 4y^3 + 2x$ at the point $(1, -1)$.
questions.subject: calc
questions.solution:
### Gradient Calculation
Partial derivatives:
$$\frac{\partial f}{\partial x} = 6xy + 2$$
$$\frac{\partial f}{\partial y} = 3x^2 - 12y^2$$
Evaluating at $(1, -1)$:
$$\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}(1, -1) = 6(1)(-1) + 2 = -6 + 2 = -4$$
$$\frac{\partial f}{\partial y}(1, -1) = 3(1)^2 - 12(-1)^2 = 3 - 12 = -9$$
Therefore, $\nabla f(1, -1) = \begin{bmatrix} -4 \\ -9 \end{bmatrix}$ (Option A).

questions.text: In K-Means clustering, what objective function is minimized by Lloyd's algorithm?
questions.subject: ml
questions.solution:
### K-Means Objective Function
Lloyd's algorithm minimizes the Within-Cluster Sum of Squares (WCSS) / inertia:
$$J = \sum_{k=1}^K \sum_{x_i \in C_k} \|x_i - \mu_k\|^2$$
Option A is correct.

questions.text: Consider a Convolutional Neural Network with an input image of size $32 \times 32 \times 3$, a filter size of $5 \times 5 \times 3$, stride 1, and no padding. What is the spatial output feature map dimension?
questions.subject: ml
questions.solution:
### Conv2D Output Dimension Formula
$$O = \left\lfloor \frac{W - K + 2P}{S} \right\rfloor + 1$$
Given $W = 32$, $K = 5$, $P = 0$, $S = 1$:
$$O = \frac{32 - 5 + 0}{1} + 1 = 27 + 1 = 28$$
Hence, output feature map is $28 \times 28$.

questions.text: A real square matrix $Q$ is orthogonal if and only if:
questions.subject: la
questions.solution:
### Orthogonal Matrix Property
An orthogonal matrix has mutually orthonormal rows and columns, satisfying $Q^T Q = I \implies Q^{-1} = Q^T$.

questions.text: If $X \sim \text{Poisson}(\lambda = 4)$, what is the variance of the random variable $Y = 3X + 5$?
questions.subject: prob
questions.solution:
### Variance Scaling Formula
For Poisson($\lambda$), $\text{Var}(X) = \lambda = 4$.
For linear transformation $Y = aX + b$:
$$\text{Var}(Y) = a^2 \text{Var}(X) = 3^2 \times 4 = 9 \times 4 = 36$$
The additive constant $+5$ does not affect variance.

questions.text: In a Balanced Binary Search Tree (AVL tree) with $n$ nodes, what is the maximum height in the worst case?
questions.subject: pdsa
questions.solution:
### AVL Tree Height
In the worst case (Fibonacci-tree structure), the height of an AVL tree with $n$ nodes is bounded by $\approx 1.4404 \log_2(n + 2) - 0.328 = O(\log n)$.

questions.text: In Ridge regression, the L2 regularization penalty term shrinks regression coefficients towards zero by penalizing:

options.t: The sum of squared weights $\sum w_j^2$
The rank of the feature matrix

questions.subject: ml
questions.solution:
### Ridge Regression (L2 Regularization)
Ridge regression adds an L2 norm penalty $\lambda \sum_{j=1}^p w_j^2$ to the residual sum of squares loss function. This smoothly shrinks weights toward zero without setting them exactly to zero (unlike L1 Lasso).
